# 3. `run-report-guide.html` — "The run report: one run, one record, written by the run"

Subtitle: *"What happened, recorded by the thing it happened to"* / "One run, one record, written by the run." Header metadata: **Written by** — "Hooks and runtimes record; the orchestrator assembles; checks and the reviewer judge"; **Read by** — "The human at the final gate; the run log's diagnosis; the next run's orchestrator".

### Purpose
The run report is "the system-generated account of an orchestrated run in Claude Code… Assembled from recorded events, not narrated from memory" — the answer to "what happened in there?" for a run the human did not watch. It supplies the factual body from which the human decides acceptance and from which the run log's diagnosis is written.

### Foundations (verbatim)
- **Provenance is the central premise:** "The single most important property of a run report is provenance. A line that says 'all agents completed successfully' means one thing if a hook counted the stop events and another if the orchestrator recalled it. The report should make that difference visible on every line, so the human can weigh a fact by its source."
- **Three-document distinction (the load-bearing paragraph):** "The **evidence display** is the live view the human reads during and at the end of the run. The **run report** is that view frozen at completion, made complete, and persisted with the code. The **run log** entry is the short human diagnosis written afterwards from the report: which axis failed and what changed in the setup. The report is the factual body; the log entry is the judgement. The report can exist without the log; the log is worthless without the report."
- **Evidence over assertion:** "Official guidance asks the agent to show evidence rather than assert success: the test output, the command it ran and what it returned. The run report is that principle applied to the whole run rather than a single check."
- **Orchestrator does not author:** "Nobody writes it, in the sense of composing it." · "The orchestrator's role is assembly, not authorship." · "A report in which most lines are stated is a report whose harness needs more hooks." · "The test of a good harness is the ratio of recorded to stated lines in the report. Each run, pick the stated line that mattered most and ask which hook or structured return would have recorded it instead."
- **The human's role — the decision is not in the report:** "The report carries every fact needed for the acceptance decision and does not make it. The moment a report says 'this run is ready to merge' in its own voice, it has become narrative, and the reader has to re-verify everything to know whether to believe it." Judgement table's last row: "The run should be accepted — Judged by: **The human**, reading the ledger and the open findings — Source in the report: **Not in the report; in the run log entry**."
- **Critic independence:** "A reviewer prompted to find gaps will report some even when the work is sound. The report records findings as returned, with their severity, and leaves it to the human to decide which matter. Filtering them before they reach the report is the orchestrator grading the critic."
- **Three inherited rules:** *From tracing* — "One run, one trace… every step is a span, and if the report cannot say which step spent the money or the time, it is not a report." *From CI* — "Counts first, detail on demand… every check is listed with its result and its raw output, and skipped checks are as visible as failed ones." *From incident timelines* — "Chronology, not story… events in order, each with where it was observed, and interpretation kept separate from record."
- **What is preserved / versioned:** the report is "a markdown file committed with the run", "one file per run, committed alongside the code at the run's final commit"; header carries "spec path @ commit · kickoff name @ version".
- **Iteration across runs:** "Read it, then write the log entry… The next run's kickoff points the orchestrator at the previous reports for the same spec."
- **Failure axes:** referenced obliquely — the Failures and interventions section "is where the run log's diagnosis usually starts"; the log entry is "which axis failed and what changed in the setup". Axes themselves are not defined here.

### Prescriptions

**Four provenance sources (marks on every line):**
- **Recorded** — "Hooks and runtimes. Deterministic. Subagent start and stop events, task creation and completion, tool failures, permission denials, stop-hook blocks, worktree lifecycle, session boundaries, token usage from the CLI's JSON output, stage results from a workflow runtime. Written by scripts the model does not control."
- **Checked** — "Verification commands. Deterministic. The exit code and output of every check the spec names, the diff boundary result, the list of test files that changed. Produced by running commands, captured verbatim."
- **Reviewed** — "The reviewer subagent. Model judgement in a fresh context. Findings against the spec, each with a severity and a resolution state. Not deterministic, but independent of the implementer and bounded by a mandate."
- **Stated** — "The orchestrator. Model narrative from the run's own context. Confined to one labelled section… The only part of the report that can be wrong in the way a person's recollection is wrong."
- Only the orchestrator can produce "the reconciliation of plan against outcome: which planned units landed, which did not, and what landed that was never planned. Even there, each verdict points at a checked or reviewed source, so the orchestrator is joining records rather than judging its own work."

**Eight sections, in order, with provenance and fields:**
1. **Header** *[recorded]* — "run id · spec path @ commit · kickoff name @ version · started / ended · outcome (accepted | accepted-with-reservations | abandoned at \&lt;gate\&gt;) · total tokens or cost · agents spawned · phases completed / planned".
2. **Ledger** *[checked · reviewed · stated]* — four lists, always: "Planned and landed" (units whose mapped checks pass); "Planned and not landed" (checks fail/skipped/never attempted, "each with the reason as recorded (gate block, stall, abandoned phase)"); "Unplanned and landed" ("surfaced by the diff boundary check and by reviewer findings of behaviour the spec did not ask for"); "Attempted and discarded" ("from worktree removal or discarded branches"). Row shape: "unit · plan ref · spec refs (B/E numbers) · verdict · deciding source (check name / finding id / diff path) · agent(s)". "This is the section the human reads to decide whether to accept the run."
3. **Verification** *[checked]* — "passed / failed / skipped · per check: name · command · exit · output excerpt · covers · ran at commit; unverified behaviours · test-file changes · diff boundary: files outside allowed paths". Plus "the three things agents will not volunteer: spec behaviours with no mapped check, checks skipped or pending, and any test file that changed during the run with the diff."
4. **Review** *[reviewed]* — "The reviewer's findings as returned, unedited by the orchestrator"; "finding id · severity · spec ref · description · state (resolved @ commit | open | disputed)"; "Findings the implementer disputed are marked as disputed, not deleted."
5. **Phases** *[recorded · stated]* — "phase · started / ended · gate · gate result · agents · tokens · ended by (gate pass | stop-hook block ×n | stall | human | error)".
6. **Agents** *[recorded · stated]* — "agent id · type / role · model · phase · task (stated) · outcome (returned | failed | blocked | stalled) · duration · tokens · artefacts · transcript path". "'What it produced' is the artefacts it wrote or the structured result it returned, as paths or schema-validated payloads, not a summary of its summary."
7. **Failures and interventions** *[recorded]* — "time · phase · agent · event · detail (verbatim from hook input)"; covers "tool failures, permission denials, stop-hook blocks and their count, subagent failures, context compactions, retries, worktree conflicts."
8. **Orchestrator notes** *[stated]* — "The only narrative section, kept short and clearly marked… It may refer to records above; it may not restate them as if they were its own observations."

**Claims/judgement table (claim → judged by → source):** planned unit landed → mapped checks pass at final commit; did not land → mapped check fails/skipped/none ran; something unplanned landed → diff boundary path with no owning unit, or review finding; feature works end to end → "the spec's acceptance script exits 0"; scope respected → diff boundary passes + reviewer reports no out-of-scope change; tests not weakened → "Test-file change list is empty, or each change is accounted for"; agent completed → "Its stop event fired with a returned result that validated against the expected schema"; phase abandoned for a reason → the recorded event that ended it; run should be accepted → the human, not in the report.

**Build sequence (6 steps in Claude Code):** record events to a per-run JSONL file (hooks on `SubagentStart`, `SubagentStop`, `TaskCreated`, `TaskCompleted`, `PostToolUseFailure`, `PermissionDenied`, `Stop`, `PreCompact`, `WorktreeCreate`, `WorktreeRemove`) → capture every check's output verbatim through a wrapper → return structured results from workers ("a result in a fixed shape (unit, spec refs, artefacts written, status), validated by a schema check at the handoff") → capture cost (`--output-format json`, per-stage tally) → assemble at the end ("A final orchestrator step, or a `SessionEnd` hook that invokes a skill… Every line marked with its source") → read it, then write the log entry.

**Annotated template:** full markdown skeleton headed `# Run report · export-html · run 3` with sections `## Ledger`, `## Verification`, `## Review`, `## Phases`, `## Agents`, `## Failures and interventions`, `## Orchestrator notes`, provenance marks in brackets.

**Anti-patterns (8):** narrated, not recorded; no provenance; summaries of summaries; the missing "not landed"; filtered findings; no cost column; the verdict in the report's own voice; the wall of transcript.

### Vocabulary defined
- **Recorded / Checked / Reviewed / Stated** — the four provenance marks (definitions quoted above).
- **Evidence display / run report / run log entry** — the three-document distinction quoted above.
- **Ledger** — "The plan reconciled against the result. Four lists, each entry pointing at the check or review finding that decides it."
- **Outcome values** — "accepted | accepted-with-reservations | abandoned at \&lt;gate\&gt;".
- **Agent outcome values** — "returned | failed | blocked | stalled".
- **Phase "ended by" values** — "gate pass | stop-hook block ×n | stall | human | error".
- **Finding state values** — "resolved @ commit | open | disputed".

### Cross-references
- "The **run log** entry is the short human diagnosis written afterwards from the report… The report is the factual body; the log entry is the judgement. The report can exist without the log; the log is worthless without the report."
- "This section is where the run log's diagnosis usually starts." (Failures and interventions)
- "**Read by**: The human at the final gate; the run log's diagnosis; the next run's orchestrator."
- Footer: "Related: the field review · verification · the run log."
- Sources: *Best practices for Claude Code* (evidence over assertion, Stop-hook gate and eight-block cap, JSON output, adversarial review caveat); *Intercept and control agent behavior with hooks* (Agent SDK); *Orchestrate subagents at scale with dynamic workflows*; hook lifecycle practitioner guides; OpenTelemetry AI agent observability.

### Where artefacts live
- `runs/&lt;id&gt;/events.jsonl` — hook-appended event stream, timestamped.
- `runs/&lt;id&gt;/checks/` — "command, exit code and output" of each verification command, written by a wrapper.
- The report itself: "a markdown file committed with the run, and the same content as the HTML evidence page"; "Markdown, one file per run, committed alongside the code at the run's final commit."
- Referenced: `docs/specs/export-html.md @ a1b2c3d`, `kickoffs/feature-parallel.md v7`; per-agent `transcript path` recorded in the Agents table (transcripts linked, never pasted).

# Closing: what the three pages together say the foundations are

1. **A run is an experiment, and it is disposable.** "A run is over the moment you stop trusting it." Endings are chosen at defined moments (gate, evidence, fired trigger) — never by momentum. Cheap endings are *engineered* in advance: small vertical units, one branch and one worktree each, triggers written when calm.

2. **The product of a failed run is the diagnosis, not the code.** "The product is the diagnosis. The code was only ever the packaging." Abandonment only pays if something remembers why — hence the run log.

3. **Setup survives; output does not.** The single salvage test is "is this artefact *setup* or is it *output*?" Spec, tests, proven contracts, factual explorer findings carry; plan, partial implementation and the orchestrator transcript do not. The next run's orchestrator meets the failure "only through the run log — as a risk line in the new plan — never through inherited conversation."

4. **Three failure axes — context, verification, tooling — are the diagnostic vocabulary of the whole method.** Both the axis a failure *appeared on* and the axis it was *fixed on* are recorded; the "fixed on" column, over time, says where to invest. "'The model was not good enough' is not an axis." Ownership of the axes is delegated upward: the run-log page names the field review as their source.

5. **Iteration across runs is an attribution discipline.** One change per retry; same frozen spec, same kickoff except the edit; a spec that changes must be re-frozen at a new commit with every pointer updated, loudly. Three failures on the same axis means shelve; a task that never suited the orchestra means demote.

6. **Versioning is by pointer, and the fix travels with its reason.** Spec at a commit, kickoff at a version, run report committed at the run's final commit, run log entry committed alongside the setup change it caused, spec status updated to the landing commit at close.

7. **Provenance beats narrative.** Facts are recorded by hooks, checked by commands, reviewed by an independent critic; the orchestrator only assembles and is confined to one labelled "stated" section. The harness is judged by its recorded-to-stated ratio.

8. **The human owns judgement, and only judgement.** The machine records, checks, assembles; the human sets the abandon triggers, reads the ledger and open findings, decides acceptance, names the axis, the cause and the change, and reads the log before every kickoff. "The report carries every fact needed for the acceptance decision and does not make it."

9. **Findings should keep leaving the log.** Rules that recur graduate into CLAUDE.md, a hook, or the spec template, and stop being logged — the log stays short by design.

10. **Nothing lands unproven, and the ground is cleared afterwards.** Green units do not equal a green trunk; merge in wave order, integrate and rebase, re-prove end to end, let CI say it again. "The ground is clear for the next run — which is the real definition of finished."

Wayfinding note for the reader's purpose: both the endings guide and the run-log guide explicitly point *outward* for their foundations — "the **field review** for the economics underneath all of it" and "the **field review** for the abandon-and-improve economics and the three failure axes"; the planning guide owns abandon triggers and unit sizing, the verification guide owns the evidence display, the review guide owns the non-converging loop. The three pages read here are the *downstream* discipline; the field review, planning, verification and review guides are where the premises are actually stated.</result>

[ASSISTANT 💬]
The endings explorer has returned, and the endings guide answers the run folder question directly through one test: is an artefact setup or output. Setup survives runs by design. Output from a drifted run carries the drift.

The guide's salvage table, in its own words:

- **The spec: yes.** Setup, unless the spec was the failed axis, in which case the amended and re-frozen version carries instead.
- **Pre-written tests: yes.** Setup. They encode the spec, not the run. A failed test is fixed by the human at escalation, and the fix is a setup change.
- **Wave-zero contracts: if proven.** Contracts whose tests went green describe seams, not implementations. Carried as inputs to the next plan.
- **Explorer findings: if factual.** A fact about where code lives survives. Conclusions drawn for the failed approach do not.
- **The plan: no.** Per-run by design. The next plan is generated fresh with the failure as a risk line.
- **Partial implementation: no.** Output of a run you stopped trusting.
- **The orchestrator transcript: no.** The run log carries what it taught.

So the guide's answer to your residue question is the spec series, the tests, proven contracts and factual findings. Everything else is output and is cleared. The abandonment sequence ends with "clear the ground", and the merge sequence ends with evidence archived at the merge commit, branches deleted, and the spec's status pointed at the landing commit.

Two other things the pages state with conviction:

- **The run log carries the diagnosis, the report carries the facts.** The report is the factual body, assembled from recorded events with provenance on every line. The log entry is the human's judgement written afterwards from the report. The report can exist without the log. The log is worthless without the report. So the report is output that must survive long enough to be diagnosed, and the guide has it committed at the run's final commit.
- **Both pages point outward for their foundations.** The endings guide sends the reader to the field review for the economics underneath all of it, and the run-log guide sends them there for the three failure axes. The planning guide owns abandon triggers and unit sizing. The verification guide owns the evidence display.

The field review is likely the orchestrator-review page, which is in the fourth explorer's set. Three explorers are still running.

# 1. `~/Projects/flightdeck/library/source/orchestrator-pattern/spec-guide.html`

**Title:** "Writing a spec that three agents can act on" — subtitle "The document the four pillars stand on". Compiled August 2026. Parent document: "Orchestrating agent teams in Claude Code".

## 1. Purpose
The page teaches a developer how to take a task definition out of their head and write it as a file that an orchestrated run's three non-human readers can act on: "How to take the definition of a task out of a developer's head and put it into a document an orchestrator can decompose, a verifier can test, and a critic can hold the result against." It prescribes a nine-part anatomy, extraction methods, a Markdown template, a readiness checklist and drift rules.

## 2. Foundations

**Why a written spec at all:**
- "In turn-by-turn work the spec is the person. In orchestration it has to be a file, because the readers who need it most are not the person."
- "An orchestrated run has three readers who each need the definition of the task, none of whom can ask the developer a question mid-run."
- "If the three readers have different understandings, the run's own quality machinery is aligned on the wrong target. Tests pass, review approves, and the result is wrong. A shared spec is what makes verification and independent review mean anything."
- "time spent making the spec precise pays off more than time spent watching the implementation. That is the whole economic argument in one sentence."

**The three readers (verbatim role definitions):**
- "Reader one / The orchestrator / Reads the spec to decompose the work, fix interfaces, and decide what each subagent is accountable for."
- "Reader two / The verifier / Reads the spec to know what to test. Every behaviour it cannot find here becomes a behaviour that will not be checked."
- "Reader three / The critic / Reads the spec to know what counts as a gap. Without it, review collapses into style opinions and generic caution."

**Where the spec comes from / who owns it:**
- "Spec / What must be true. Outcomes, scope, constraints, behaviours, proof. **Written by the human with help. Frozen before the run.**"
- The template header carries an explicit owner field: `Status: draft | frozen        Owner: &lt;name&gt;        Kickoff: &lt;path to kickoff prompt&gt;`.
- "A spec answers *what must be true when this is done*. It is stable across implementations: two different teams could build from it and both results would satisfy it. **It is the input to planning, not the plan.** It describes outcomes and boundaries, not steps."

**Input to a run, not produced inside one:** unambiguous. The spec is "Frozen before the run", is "the input to planning", and the working sequence ends "Freeze it, commit it, and reference it from the kickoff." Under drift: "the spec changes before the code does… the run should stop at that finding rather than improvise, the developer updates the spec, and the run restarts against the new definition."

**What freezing means:**
- Status field moves `draft → frozen`.
- Precondition: "## Open questions / Must be empty before status becomes frozen." And: "An 'open questions' section is useful while the spec is being written and should be empty before the run starts. **A question left open is a decision delegated to whichever agent hits it first.**"
- Freezing is accompanied by commit-pinning: "Version the spec alongside the code and reference the commit it was frozen at from the run log."
- Freezing follows adversarial attack: "Attack it from a fresh context. Resolve every open question. Freeze it, commit it, and reference it from the kickoff."

**Checks / tests — what this page says:**
- Constraints "convert directly into checks": "Many of these convert directly into checks."
- Contracts: "each contract is a natural place for a contract test."
- The page does **not** define verdict classes; it treats verification as "checks that pass" plus commands with exit codes ("`npm test -- export` must exit 0", "Smoke script exits 0"). No pass/fail-vs-other-verdict taxonomy is given here — that is deferred to the verification guide.
- **Tests owned by the project vs checks written for the spec:** the page does not draw that distinction explicitly. It speaks of "the named tests", "test files and what they cover (map to B/E numbers)", and "Whether tests are pre-written and read-only." The ownership signal is the read-only/lock rule, not a project-vs-spec split.
- **Where check files live / who may edit them:** stated as spec content, by example and by template instruction. Example: "Unit and contract tests in `tests/export/` cover B1–B7 and E1–E3; they are written before implementation and are **read-only during the run**." Template: "If the tests are pre-written, name the files and state that they are not to be modified." Working sequence step 5: "If tests are pre-written, do that now and **lock them**."

**What the plan gates (per this page):** the plan is a separate document, not this page's artefact: "Plan / How it will be done. Files touched, approach, order, risks. **Written by the orchestrator, approved at a gate.**" And "Tasks / Who does what. Small, independently verifiable units with fixed interfaces. Derived from the plan; dispatched to workers."

**Separation from run mechanics:**
- "It is also not the kickoff prompt. The kickoff tells the orchestrator how to conduct the run: which tools, which agents, which gates, which display to maintain. The spec is referenced by the kickoff, and **it is the only one of the two that the verifier and critic should ever see.** Keeping them apart prevents run mechanics leaking into the definition of correctness."
- Checklist item: "Nothing in the spec describes how to conduct the run. Tools, agents, gates and displays belong in the kickoff."
- Not a PRD: "A PRD argues for why something should exist and for whom; it is a persuasion document with a business audience. A spec assumes the decision is made and pins down the behaviour precisely enough to test."
- Commonest failure: "a spec that is really a plan: it lists steps to take rather than conditions to satisfy. Steps cannot be tested, only followed, so the verifier has nothing to check and the critic has nothing to hold the result against."

## 3. Prescriptions

**The nine-part anatomy** (each with named primary readers; "Not every task needs every part at full weight, but a missing part should be a decision, not an oversight"):

| # | Section | Read by | Rule stated |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Intent | orchestrator · critic | "One or two sentences on the outcome and why it matters… what the critic uses to judge whether the work, even if every test passes, is the right work." |
| 2 | Scope | orchestrator · critic | "What is in, and explicitly what is out. Out-of-scope statements do more work than in-scope ones… The critic checks that nothing outside scope changed." |
| 3 | Constraints | orchestrator · verifier | "Non-negotiables about how the result may be built: dependencies allowed or forbidden, performance ceilings, compatibility targets, security rules, style rules that differ from defaults." |
| 4 | Interfaces and contracts | orchestrator · verifier | "The seams: function signatures, API shapes, file formats, schemas, CLI arguments, events. Fixing these in the spec is what allows parallel workers to build without each other's context." |
| 5 | Behaviours | verifier · critic | "each observable behaviour stated so that a test can be written from it without interpretation… the property that matters is that a second person could write the same test. **Number them so tests and review findings can refer to them.**" |
| 6 | Edge cases and failure modes | verifier · critic | "These are the behaviours most often narrowed silently by an implementer to make a test pass." |
| 7 | Prior decisions and non-goals | orchestrator · critic | "Things already decided elsewhere that the agents must not re-litigate, and tempting improvements that are deliberately not being made… stops the critic from flagging them as gaps." |
| 8 | Verification | orchestrator · verifier | "How the behaviours will be proven, and the single end-to-end step that demonstrates the whole feature works. Name the commands. If the tests are pre-written, name the files and state that they are not to be modified. **This section is what the run's stop condition is built from.**" |
| 9 | Definition of done | orchestrator · verifier · critic | "The short list that ends the run: which checks pass, what evidence is presented, what the reviewer has confirmed. Everything above feeds it; **nothing new should appear here.**" |

Plus a tenth, transient section: "## Open questions / Must be empty before status becomes frozen."

**Numbering conventions:** behaviours `B1.`, `B2.` …; edge cases `E1.`, `E2.` … Example DoD: "Reviewer reports no correctness gaps against B1–B7, E1–E3. Diff touches only `src/export/` and `tests/export/`."

**Four extraction methods:** (1) "Be interviewed" — "ask Claude to interview you using its question tool, with an instruction to skip the obvious and dig into edge cases, tradeoffs and the hard parts you might not have considered, then to write a complete spec to a file… When the spec is written, start a fresh session to execute it so the implementation context never sees the interview." (2) "Draft, then attack" — "have a fresh context read it with the reviewer's mandate: find every behaviour that could be implemented two different ways, every boundary that is not stated, every term that is used without definition." (3) "Write the tests first, and let the spec follow" — "Writing the tests exposes exactly what has not been decided, and the behaviours section can then be written by describing what the tests check." (4) "Mine the history" — "every correction is a behaviour or constraint that was never written down."

**The working sequence (six ordered steps, verbatim headings):**
1. "State the intent and the out-of-scope list first."
2. "Fix the interfaces." — "Decide the seams before the behaviours, because behaviours are expressed in terms of them."
3. "Enumerate behaviours as numbered, testable statements."
4. "Record prior decisions and non-goals."
5. "Write the verification section and the end-to-end proof." — "Name commands and files. If tests are pre-written, do that now and lock them."
6. "Attack it from a fresh context." — "Resolve every open question. Freeze it, commit it, and reference it from the kickoff."

**Readiness test:** "A spec is ready when a stranger with the repository could write the tests, and a second stranger with only the diff and the spec could say whether the work is done. Both strangers, in an orchestrated run, are agents."

**Nine-item pre-freeze checklist (verbatim):** every behaviour testable by a non-author; "The out-of-scope list names the most tempting expansions"; "Interfaces reuse existing names"; "Every edge case has a stated outcome, not a stated concern"; "The verification section names commands and files. A run's stop condition cannot be built from a paragraph"; "The end-to-end proof exercises the feature the way a user would"; "Nothing in the spec describes how to conduct the run"; "Open questions is empty"; "A fresh context has attacked it and the findings were resolved."

**Drift rules:** "the spec changes before the code does"; run stops at the finding; developer updates spec; run restarts. "Version the spec alongside the code and reference the commit it was frozen at from the run log."

**Constitution rule:** "Constraints and prior decisions that appear in spec after spec belong in `CLAUDE.md` or a rules file, where every session reads them once, and can then be deleted from individual specs. The reverse also holds: if `CLAUDE.md` is growing, some of it is probably spec-level detail that should live with the feature that needs it."

## 4. Vocabulary
- **Spec** — "What must be true. Outcomes, scope, constraints, behaviours, proof. Written by the human with help. Frozen before the run." / "A spec answers *what must be true when this is done*."
- **Plan** — "How it will be done. Files touched, approach, order, risks. Written by the orchestrator, approved at a gate."
- **Tasks** — "Who does what. Small, independently verifiable units with fixed interfaces. Derived from the plan; dispatched to workers."
- **Kickoff** — "The kickoff tells the orchestrator how to conduct the run: which tools, which agents, which gates, which display to maintain."
- **PRD (contrast)** — "a persuasion document with a business audience."
- **Intent / Scope / Constraints / Interfaces and contracts / Behaviours / Edge cases and failure modes / Prior decisions and non-goals / Verification / Definition of done** — as defined in the anatomy table above.
- **Open questions** — "Must be empty before status becomes frozen."

## 5. Cross-references
- Header context line: "Context: Orchestrating agent teams in Claude Code · Verification".
- On the kickoff: "The spec is referenced by the kickoff, and it is the only one of the two that the verifier and critic should ever see."
- Footer: "Compiled August 2026. Parent document: Orchestrating agent teams in Claude Code. Related: verification · the run log."
- Sources include Anthropic "Best practices for Claude Code", "Let Claude interview you" ("The interview-to-`SPEC.md` pattern"); Anthropic "Building verification loops in Claude Code with skills" — "Encoding checks so that every session applies them; spec validation as a verification loop"; Addy Osmani "How to write a good spec for AI agents" — "The spec as version-controlled source of truth; the spec → plan → tasks → implement sequence"; Augment Code "What is spec-driven development" — "the coordinator / implementer / verifier pattern".

## 6. Where artefacts live (per this page)
- The spec: "Markdown, kept in the repository beside the code it describes."
- Template filename convention implied by sources: `SPEC.md` ("The interview-to-`SPEC.md` pattern"). Planning guide later shows the concrete path form `docs/specs/export-html.md @ a1b2c3d`.
- Tests, by example: "`tests/export/`", commands `npm test -- export`, end-to-end script `scripts/export-smoke.sh`.
- Diff boundary, by example: "Diff touches only `src/export/` and `tests/export/`."
- Project-wide rules: `CLAUDE.md` or "a rules file".
- Kickoff prompt: referenced by path in the spec header (`Kickoff: &lt;path to kickoff prompt&gt;`).
- Spec version pinned in the run log: "reference the commit it was frozen at from the run log."

# 2. `~/Projects/flightdeck/library/source/orchestrator-pattern/verification-guide.html`

**Title:** "Verification: giving a run something better than 'looks done'" — "Pillar three, in depth". Strapline: "A check the agent can run beats a person who might notice."

## 1. Purpose
The page specifies how to build "an executable definition of done for orchestrated runs in Claude Code: what a good check looks like, the shapes it takes, how to write the target before the work, how hard it should gate the stop, and what evidence the human reads at the end." It exists because "Remove the developer and the loop has to be rebuilt out of things a machine can run."

## 2. Foundations

**Dependency and outputs (masthead, verbatim):**
- "Depends on: A spec with numbered behaviours"
- "Feeds: Independent review · the evidence display · the run log"

**Core premises:**
- "An agent stops when the work looks done. That is not a flaw to be prompted away; it is the only stop signal available in the absence of anything better. Every mistake then waits for a person to notice it, and in an orchestrated run the person is not there."
- "Official guidance puts it plainly: without a check the agent can run, you become the verification loop."
- "Give the agent something that produces a pass or fail it can read, and the loop closes without a human. Do the work, run the check, read the result, iterate until it passes. The developer's job moves from noticing mistakes to designing the thing that notices them."
- Relationship to review: "Independent review judges whether the work matches the spec's intent, but it can only do that well if the mechanical questions (does it compile, do the behaviours hold, did anything outside scope change) have already been answered by something deterministic. Review that has to do verification's job becomes vague and expensive."
- Evidence over narrative: the two-panel contrast "Narrative — not evidence… I have implemented the export feature and tested it thoroughly" vs "Evidence… `$ npm test -- export` … `exit 0`", with "The right panel is what a run's stop condition should be built from, and what the human reads at the final gate."

**What a check returns — verdicts:** the page is explicit that a check yields a machine-readable pass/fail signal, and enumerates the accepted signal forms rather than a verdict vocabulary:
- "Give the agent something that produces a **pass or fail** it can read".
- "Readable in the loop / Returns a signal the agent sees in the conversation: **an exit code, a test summary, a diff, a screenshot.** A check whose result only a human can interpret is observability, not verification."
- "Build exit code / **The bluntest possible pass/fail.** Its value is that it cannot be argued with."
- There is **no third verdict** ("skip", "warn", "n/a") defined as a legitimate outcome. Third states appear only as pathologies or as disclosure items: "checks that were skipped or marked pending" must appear on the evidence display under "what was not checked"; unmapped behaviours are "listed as unverified, deliberately"; flaky checks are quarantined "out of the gate immediately".

**Spec-owned vs project-owned:** the page does not create a two-class ownership split, but it does split *where the command is written down* by scope:
- "The command an agent runs to verify should be written down where it cannot be misremembered: **in `CLAUDE.md` for the project-wide ones, in the spec's verification section for the task-specific ones.** Official guidance recommends listing exact build and test commands so the agent never has to infer them."
- And a placement split for orchestrated runs: "hooks for structural checks and the diff boundary…; the spec's verification commands for behavioural and artefact checks (run at gates); and chained skills for the judgement-adjacent checks that sit just before review."

**Who may edit checks:**
- Property: "**Lockable** / The implementing agent cannot weaken it. **A check the agent can edit is a suggestion; a check it cannot edit is a target.**"
- "A check the implementer can edit will, under pressure, get edited."
- Checklist: "Test files are locked against the implementing agents. By hook, by default."
- Exception handling: "Pre-written tests can be wrong. When an implementer reports that a test contradicts the spec or cannot be satisfied, **that report should stop the run for a human decision rather than be resolved by the agent.** Silent resolution in either direction is how a locked target becomes a locked mistake."

**Where check files live:** by path-permission rather than by named directory — "putting tests in a path the implementing agent's worktree does not carry write permission for"; "a `PreToolUse` hook that blocks writes to the test directory for implementing agents". Concrete examples: `tests/export/behaviours.test.ts`, `tests/export/edges.test.ts`, `scripts/export-smoke.sh`.

**Baseline rule:** stated for artefact checks and for pre-run dry-running:
- "Golden output / fixture diff / Generate, diff against a checked-in reference, fail on any difference… **The reference is the target; updating it is a human decision.**"
- "The end-to-end proof exists and runs green on the reference fixture before any implementation begins. **Or fails in the expected way, if the feature does not exist yet.**"

## 3. Prescriptions

**Definition of a good check — six required properties (verbatim headings + rules):**
1. "Readable in the loop — Returns a signal the agent sees in the conversation: an exit code, a test summary, a diff, a screenshot. A check whose result only a human can interpret is observability, not verification."
2. "Terse on success, specific on failure — Silence or one line when it passes. On failure, the failing case and where. Screens of output invite a plausible summary instead of a fix."
3. "Deterministic — Same input, same result. A flaky check trains the agent to retry rather than investigate, and it will learn that lesson fast."
4. "Fast enough to run often — The loop runs the check many times. A check that takes minutes gets run once at the end, which is the same as not having it."
5. "Traceable to the spec — Each check maps to a numbered behaviour or edge case. Coverage of the spec becomes something that can be listed, not asserted."
6. "Lockable — The implementing agent cannot weaken it."

**The catalogue — five classes of check.** "A run usually needs at least one from each of the first three groups; the fourth and fifth are added as the codebase and the run log justify them."

- **Structural** — "Is the result at least coherent? Cheap, fast, and the first thing that should fail if an agent has drifted."
  - Type check — "Catches interface mismatches between parallel workers before any behaviour test runs. *Run after every edit via hook.*"
  - Build exit code — "The bluntest possible pass/fail… *Make it the floor of every gate.*"
  - Linter and formatter — "*Hook, never instruction.* A lint rule in `CLAUDE.md` is advisory; a lint hook is deterministic."
- **Behavioural** — "Does it do what the spec says? These are the checks that map one-to-one to numbered behaviours and edge cases."
  - Unit tests — "*Written from the spec before implementation* so they describe what was wanted rather than what was built."
  - Contract tests — "*The check that makes parallel decomposition safe:* each worker builds against the contract, and the contract test catches the drift."
  - End-to-end acceptance — "*The spec's final proof, and the only defence against the false green* where units pass and the feature is unusable. Often a small script rather than a test framework: run the thing, poke it, assert."
  - Reproduction test for bugs — "A failing test written first that captures the reported symptom, then made to pass… it prevents fixing a symptom instead of a cause."
- **Artefact** — "Does the output match a known-good thing? For work whose result is a file, a page, or a structure rather than a return value."
  - Golden output / fixture diff; Screenshot comparison ("*The check for visual work*"); Schema validation ("*The natural check at every handoff between agents* and every stage boundary in a workflow script").
- **Invariant** — "Do the properties that should always hold, hold? Broader than any enumerated case."
  - Property-based and fuzz tests; Assertions in code; Performance budget ("*Only worth automating for paths that matter*"); Static analysis and security scan ("Anything touching auth, input handling or the network earns one").
- **Project rules** — "Does it obey the things only this project cares about? The category most often left in a human's head."
  - Custom rule checks — "*Anything enforced by hand repeatedly qualifies.* Anthropic's guidance is to write the rule in plain English as if for a new teammate, then package it as a skill so every session applies it."
  - Diff boundary — "The change touches only the paths the spec allows. A trivial script over `git diff --name-only`, and one of the most effective scope fences available."
  - Spec validation — "A skill that checks each change against the spec in the repository and attempts to fix violations. This is where verification and review meet: mechanical where it can be, judgement where it must."

**Targets-before-work rules:**
- "A test written after describes what was built. A test written before describes what was wanted. The difference is exactly the set of defects that self-grading misses."
- Derivation: "Each numbered behaviour and edge case in the spec becomes at least one check, named so the mapping is visible: a test file or case that references `B4` is a test that someone can audit against the spec without reading the code. **Where the spec is not precise enough to write the check, that is a finding about the spec, and the right response is to fix the spec, not to guess.**"
- Writer/implementer separation: "one session write the tests from the spec and another write the code to pass them. **The two sessions must not share context**: a test-writer that has seen the implementation plan writes tests for the plan; a test-writer that has seen only the spec writes tests for the spec. In Claude Code this is two sessions in separate worktrees, or a test-writing subagent that runs to completion before the implementing agents start."

**The lock rule (three strengths, verbatim):** "Three ways to prevent it, in increasing strength: an instruction in the kickoff that test files are read-only during the run; a `PreToolUse` hook that blocks writes to the test directory for implementing agents; and putting tests in a path the implementing agent's worktree does not carry write permission for. **The hook is the practical default.**" Plus the escalation rule: a contradicting test "should stop the run for a human decision".

**The gating ladder (four rungs; "an unattended run needs at least the third"):**
1. "In the prompt — Ask the agent to run the check and iterate in the same message… Relies on the agent remembering, which under context pressure it may not."
2. "As a session goal — Set the check as a `/goal` condition. A separate evaluator re-checks it after every turn and the session keeps working until the goal resolves."
3. "As a deterministic gate — A `Stop` hook runs the check as a script and blocks the turn from ending until it passes. **Claude Code overrides the hook after eight consecutive blocks. Treat that override as a stall detector**: a run that hits it has a problem the check cannot fix, and the right response is to abandon and diagnose."
4. "By a second opinion — A verification subagent, or a dynamic workflow stage that checks its own findings, has a fresh model try to refute the result. This is the rung where verification hands over to independent review, and **it should be built on top of the deterministic gate, not instead of it.**"
- Floor: "**The floor for an unattended run is a deterministic gate on the spec's end-to-end proof.**"
- Workflow variant: "a schema check on every agent's output, a deterministic check at each phase boundary, and a refuting stage before results are merged."

**Placement rules — four placements ("The signal for moving right along the row is finding yourself invoking the check after every change: at that point it has earned a permanent home."):**
- "Invoked / Standalone — A skill you run deliberately after the artefact exists. Right for cross-cutting checks that do not apply every time: a security scan, an accessibility audit, a licence-header sweep."
- "Automatic / Embedded — The producing skill runs the check itself before reporting completion… Only possible on skills you control."
- "Sequenced / Chained — One skill invokes the next at its end: review, then simplify, then verify, then a design check if UI changed. A habit becomes a contract. Also the way to add a check to a skill you cannot edit."
- "Enforced / On every change — Hooks for anything that must happen with zero exceptions; CI for the same gates on every PR regardless of who authored it. Hold off until the chain is stable."
- Orchestrated-run split: "hooks for structural checks and the diff boundary…; the spec's verification commands for behavioural and artefact checks (run at gates); and chained skills for the judgement-adjacent checks that sit just before review."

**Evidence requirements (per check, verbatim):** "an evidence display for a run should carry, for each check: **the exact command, the exit code, the relevant lines of output (not a paraphrase), the commit it ran against, and which spec behaviours it covers.** Artefact checks include the artefact or the diff. Review findings sit alongside, in the same format." Two additions agents will not volunteer: "**what was not checked**: spec behaviours with no mapped test, checks that were skipped or marked pending, and any test file that changed during the run" and "**the cost**: agents spawned, iterations on the gate, tokens consumed."

**Eight anti-patterns (verbatim names):** "The weakened target" ("Lock the tests; put test-file changes on the evidence display"); "The suppressed error" ("address the root cause, do not suppress"); "The false green"; "Tests that describe the implementation" ("Write from the spec, before the code, in a separate context"); "The noisy check"; "The flaky check" ("a flaky gate is worse than no gate because it looks like one"); "The unmapped check" ("Number the behaviours; name the tests after them"); "Verification by narrative" ("No command, no output, no exit code. Not evidence, and not to be accepted as such at a gate").

**Pre-run checklist (eight items, verbatim):** every behaviour/edge maps to a named check with unmapped ones listed as deliberately unverified; e2e proof runs green on the reference fixture before implementation (or fails as expected); test files locked by hook; structural checks on every edit via hook; diff boundary knows allowed paths "Taken from the spec's scope section"; stop gated deterministically; exact commands written down "In `CLAUDE.md` or the spec, not in the orchestrator's memory"; evidence display shows "raw output, changed test files, unverified behaviours, and cost."

## 4. Vocabulary
- **Check (implicit definition, by properties):** something that "produces a pass or fail it can read" and "Returns a signal the agent sees in the conversation: an exit code, a test summary, a diff, a screenshot."
- **Observability (contrast):** "A check whose result only a human can interpret is observability, not verification."
- **Lockable:** "The implementing agent cannot weaken it."
- **Contract test:** "Two components agree on the seam between them. The check that makes parallel decomposition safe."
- **End-to-end acceptance:** "The feature works the way a user would exercise it. The spec's final proof."
- **Golden output / fixture diff:** "Generate, diff against a checked-in reference, fail on any difference."
- **Diff boundary:** "The change touches only the paths the spec allows."
- **Spec validation:** "A skill that checks each change against the spec in the repository and attempts to fix violations."
- **False green:** "Every unit test passes and the feature does not work."
- **Weakened target:** "The implementer edits a test, loosens an assertion, adds a skip, or mocks around the hard part."
- **Unmapped check:** "Tests exist but nobody can say which spec behaviour each covers."
- **Stall detector:** the eight-consecutive-block Stop-hook override — "Treat that override as a stall detector."
- **Deterministic gate:** "A `Stop` hook runs the check as a script and blocks the turn from ending until it passes."

## 5. Cross-references
- Masthead: "Depends on: A spec with numbered behaviours" / "Feeds: Independent review · the evidence display · the run log."
- On review's ownership: "Independent review judges whether the work matches the spec's intent, but it can only do that well if the mechanical questions… have already been answered by something deterministic."
- On the handover point: "This is the rung where verification hands over to independent review, and it should be built on top of the deterministic gate, not instead of it."
- On the spec's ownership: "The spec's final proof, and the only defence against the false green"; "Only an end-to-end acceptance check catches this, **which is why the spec must end with one.**"; "The diff boundary check knows the allowed paths. Taken from the spec's scope section."
- On the kickoff's ownership: "an instruction in the kickoff that test files are read-only during the run."
- On the observability pillar: "A display that shows intentions is a checkpoint tool. A display that shows check results is a verification tool… it is the form the observability pillar should converge on."
- Footer: "Parent document: Orchestrating agent teams in Claude Code. Related: the spec · the run log."
- Sources: Anthropic "Best practices for Claude Code" ("Give Claude a way to verify its work"), "Building verification loops in Claude Code with skills" (`/verify`, rubric graders, the four placements), "Orchestrate subagents at scale with dynamic workflows", "How Claude Code is used in practice".

## 6. Where artefacts live (per this page)
- Commands: "in `CLAUDE.md` for the project-wide ones, in the spec's verification section for the task-specific ones" — "not in the orchestrator's memory."
- Test files: in a locked/permission-denied path; "the test directory" guarded by a `PreToolUse` hook; example paths `tests/export/behaviours.test.ts`, `tests/export/edges.test.ts`, script `scripts/export-smoke.sh`.
- Golden references: "a checked-in reference".
- Test-writing sessions: "two sessions in separate worktrees".
- Structural checks and diff boundary: hooks; the same gates in CI "on every PR".
- Project rules: packaged "as a skill so every session applies it".
- Naming convention: "a test file or case that references `B4`"; "Number the behaviours; name the tests after them."

# 3. `~/Projects/flightdeck/library/source/orchestrator-pattern/planning-guide.html`

**Title:** "Planning a run: from spec to a shape worth paying for" — "Between the spec and the first dispatched agent". Strapline: "The plan is the cheapest place the run can fail."

## 1. Purpose
The page covers everything between a frozen spec and the first dispatched worker: "deciding whether the task deserves an orchestra at all, decomposing it into units with their own pass/fail, fixing the contracts, ordering the waves, setting the budgets, and producing the one-page plan the human approves before any worker spends a token." It prescribes the plan document's shape, the wave model, budgets, abandon triggers and the first-gate checklist.

## 2. Foundations

**Masthead (verbatim):**
- "Consumes: A frozen spec · explorer findings · the run log · the roster"
- "Produces: A plan approved at the first gate, then executed by the kickoff"

**The spec is an input, frozen, and not re-decided:**
- "**The frozen spec** supplies what must be true, the scope fence, the interfaces already decided, and the verification commands. **The plan never re-litigates it; a planning session that discovers a spec gap stops and sends the gap back**, because a plan built on an open question delegates that question to whichever agent hits it first."
- Anti-pattern "The plan that is a spec": "Behaviours and scope re-argued in the plan, drifting from the frozen document. **Now there are two sources of truth and the verifier follows one while the critic follows the other.**"
- First-gate check: "Nothing in the plan contradicts or re-decides the spec. Spec gaps went back as findings, not forward as improvisation."

**The plan is disposable; the spec is not:**
- "Unlike the spec, **the plan is disposable: regenerated for every run, and abandoned with it.**"
- Anti-pattern "The plan that survives its run": "A failed run patched by editing the plan mid-flight. **The plan dies with the run; the lesson moves to the run log and the setup, and the next plan is generated clean.**"

**Checks must pre-exist the plan (readiness premise):**
- "**Not yet when / The pillars are missing** — No frozen spec, no executable checks, or no reviewer path. Orchestrating without them buys speed toward an unverifiable result. Build the setup first; the run will still be there."
- "A task that decomposes beautifully but has no checks is not ready to orchestrate; it is ready to have its checks written."

**Whether to orchestrate at all:**
- "Orchestration is a deliberate complexity choice, not a default."
- "if you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan; and by extension, if one session could hold the whole task, skip the orchestra."
- "multi-agent systems consume tokens on roughly another order of magnitude, so the bar should be real."
- "Orchestrate when / It decomposes — The work splits into low-coupling units that can run in parallel against fixed contracts, **each with its own pass/fail**, and the volume exceeds one context."

**Planning context isolation:** "Do the planning in a context that will not implement. Plan mode makes the session read-only while exploring and planning… **What must not happen is planning inside an implementer's context, where the plan inherits the implementer's eagerness.**"

**What the plan gates:** three gates, verbatim from the plan template — "G1 this document · G2 contracts + green contract tests · G3 evidence display: checks, critic findings, diff boundary, cost." Described also as "Where the human looks (plan, interfaces, final evidence), what each gate shows". The wave diagram marks "GATE: interfaces" after Wave 0 and "GATE: evidence" after Wave 2: "The gate cells are where a human or a deterministic check must pass the run forward."

**What the human approves at gate one:** "The human approving it is checking four things: the approach is sane, the units are verifiable, the waves respect coupling, and the budgets and abandon triggers exist."

## 3. Prescriptions

**Four required inputs:** frozen spec; explorer findings ("Fan explorer subagents out over the planning questions… let their summaries land in the planning context instead of three hundred files. Read-only by construction, cheap by model, parallel by default"); the run log ("Known risks from the log go straight into the plan's risk section with their mitigations"); "The roster and the budget… Planning against an unbounded budget produces unbounded plans."

**Seven phases (verbatim headings and rules):**
1. "**Explore** — Dispatch explorers on the open questions. Collect summaries, not files."
2. "**Decompose** — Cut the work into units, each with its own pass/fail. Name them; **the names will thread through the plan, the checks, the branches and the evidence.**"
3. "**Fix the contracts** — Write down every seam between units — signatures, schemas, file formats — beyond what the spec already fixed. Contracts are what let wave two run in parallel; **each one gets a contract test.**"
4. "**Order the waves** — Group units by dependency… High-risk units run early and serial, so their failure is cheap; safe units run parallel."
5. "**Budget** — Cap workers, turns per agent, iterations per gate. Route models by stage. Write down the expected cost so the run log can compare it to the actual."
6. "**Set gates and abandon triggers** — Where the human looks (plan, interfaces, final evidence), what each gate shows, and — the pre-mortem — what observations mean stop: a named check failing N times, the stall override firing, a worker touching an out-of-scope path, cost passing its ceiling."
7. "**Pilot** — Run one or two representative units end-to-end before fanning out… **Also dry-run the checks: pre-written tests should fail in exactly the expected way against the unimplemented code, and the harness should go green on a known-good fixture.**"

**The three-wave shape:** "A run in three waves: contracts first, implementation in parallel, verification and review last."
- "Wave 0 · serial / Contracts — interfaces, schemas, contract tests — GATE: interfaces"
- "Wave 1 · parallel / Units — unit A, unit B, unit C, per-unit checks"
- "Wave 2 · serial / Proof — integrate + e2e, critic — GATE: evidence"

**Four decomposition rules:**
- "**Cut vertically** — A vertical unit crosses all the layers it needs — data, logic, surface — and delivers one testable behaviour end to end: the tracer-bullet shape… A horizontal unit ('all the models', 'all the endpoints') cannot pass an end-to-end check on its own, so its defects hide until integration, which is the most expensive moment to find them. **Vertical units also map cleanly onto spec behaviours, which keeps the unit-to-check-to-evidence thread unbroken.**"
- "**Size by verifiability** — A unit is too big when its pass/fail would need interpretation, and too small when its overhead (dispatch, context, review) outweighs its work. The practical test: **can this unit's done-ness be stated as one or two named checks, and would a competent agent finish it inside its turn budget?** Between those bounds, prefer smaller — abandoning a small unit is a discarded branch."
- "**Let coupling order the waves** — Anything two units share belongs in wave zero as a contract. After that, units that share nothing run in parallel; units with residual coupling run serial or get their seam promoted to a contract. Serialise the high-risk and the irreversible; parallelise the safe and the independent. **If the wave diagram needs more than a handful of waves, the coupling is telling you the decomposition is wrong** — or that this task wanted a single session after all."
- "**One unit, one owner, one branch** — Each unit is dispatched to one implementer in its own worktree, accountable vertically to the orchestrator. **Two agents sharing a unit is horizontal collaboration wearing a plan's clothing.**"

**The plan document — prescribed sections and header fields (verbatim template):**
```
# Plan: export-html · run 4
spec: docs/specs/export-html.md @ a1b2c3d   shape: workflow, 6 agents max
expected cost: ~medium · models: haiku (explore) / sonnet (units) / opus (critic)
## Approach            Three sentences. What the run does, in what shape, and the one judgement call being made
## Waves and units     W0 contracts … serial / W1 unit A … checks B1–B3 … budget 20 turns / W2 proof … serial
## Risks               From the run log and exploration: known failure modes, each with the planned reaction (mitigate, watch, or abandon trigger).
## Gates               G1 this document · G2 contracts + green contract tests · G3 evidence display: checks, critic findings, diff boundary, cost.
## Abandon triggers    e2e failing after 3 gate iterations · stall override fires · any write outside src/export/, tests locked dir · cost &gt; 1.5× expected.
```
Row shape in "Waves and units": wave · unit name · description · checks (mapped to spec behaviour numbers, e.g. "checks B4–B5, E2") · turn budget · serial/parallel.

**Two mechanical rules on the plan (verbatim):** "The units table is the source of truth the kickoff points workers at, so **unit names here must match branch names, check names and evidence sections.** And plans can be produced in variants when the approach is genuinely contested — ask the planner for two and choose at the gate, rather than letting the contest resurface mid-run."

**Scope rules for the plan's content:** "The plan answers *how, in what pieces, in what order, at what cost* — and nothing the spec already answers. … Everything in it should be scannable; prose belongs in the approach paragraph and nowhere else." Length: "The plan fits on a page."

**Five budget rules (verbatim headings):**
- "Cap the fan-out. — A hard maximum on concurrent workers, enforced by the workflow script or the dispatch instruction, not by hope."
- "Budget per agent, per gate, per run. — `maxTurns` on each role, an iteration cap on each deterministic gate (**the Stop-hook override at eight consecutive blocks is a built-in ceiling**), and a run-level cost ceiling in the abandon triggers."
- "Tier models by wave. — Exploration and formatting on cheap models, units on the mid tier, critic and orchestration on the strongest. Workflow scripts route per stage; `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL` caps a whole session."
- "Record expected cost. — One line in the plan. The run log compares it to actual."
- "Make 'stop' observable. — **Every abandon trigger must be something the evidence display or a hook can actually see. A trigger nobody can observe is a wish.**"
- Rationale: "Budgets are not pessimism; they are what makes abandoning cheap."

**Eight anti-patterns (verbatim):** "The plan that is a spec"; "The horizontal cut"; "Big-bang fan-out" ("Twelve workers dispatched with no pilot"); "The unbudgeted plan"; "Planning inside the doer" ("Plan read-only; approve; then execute"); "The transcript plan" ("Ten pages of reasoning where one page of decisions should be. The human cannot gate what they cannot scan, so the gate becomes a rubber stamp"); "Dependency by conversation" ("Units that 'coordinate as needed' instead of through a wave-zero contract"); "The plan that survives its run".

**First-gate checklist (eight items, verbatim):** nothing contradicts/re-decides the spec; "Every unit names its checks and its budget. Unit names match what branches, checks and evidence will use"; "Every seam between units is a wave-zero contract with a test"; "High-risk work runs early and serial; parallel units share nothing"; "Fan-out is capped, models are tiered, expected cost is written down"; "Abandon triggers are observable, and the run-log's known failures each have a line in the risks"; "A pilot unit is identified, and the checks dry-run in the expected state"; "The plan fits on a page."

## 4. Vocabulary
- **Plan** — answers "*how, in what pieces, in what order, at what cost* — and nothing the spec already answers"; "disposable: regenerated for every run, and abandoned with it."
- **Vertical unit** — "crosses all the layers it needs — data, logic, surface — and delivers one testable behaviour end to end: the tracer-bullet shape."
- **Horizontal unit** — "('all the models', 'all the endpoints') cannot pass an end-to-end check on its own."
- **Wave 0 / Contracts** — "interfaces, schemas, contract tests", serial, gated on interfaces.
- **Wave 1 / Units** — parallel implementation with per-unit checks.
- **Wave 2 / Proof** — "integrate + e2e, critic", serial, gated on evidence.
- **Gate** — "The gate cells are where a human or a deterministic check must pass the run forward."
- **Abandon trigger** — "what observations mean stop: a named check failing N times, the stall override firing, a worker touching an out-of-scope path, cost passing its ceiling."
- **Pilot** — "Run one or two representative units end-to-end before fanning out."
- **Explorer findings** — "what the codebase actually looks like… Read-only by construction, cheap by model, parallel by default."
- **Stall override** — "the Stop-hook override at eight consecutive blocks is a built-in ceiling."

## 5. Cross-references
- Masthead: "Consumes: A frozen spec · explorer findings · the run log · the roster" / "Produces: A plan approved at the first gate, then executed by the kickoff."

- Other sources: Anthropic "Best practices for Claude Code" ("Explore–plan–implement–commit; plan mode as read-only planning with direct plan editing; 'if you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan'"); "Orchestrate subagents at scale with dynamic workflows" ("the script as a re-runnable plan"); "Building Effective Agents" ("Orchestrator-workers as a deliberate complexity choice… the permissive-plan cost-spike failure mode"); "Multi-agent orchestration patterns" ("multi-agent token costs roughly an order of magnitude above single-agent; the supervisor as bottleneck").

- Plan title/naming: `# Plan: export-html · run 4` — named per feature and per run number.
- Implementation isolation: "Each unit is dispatched to one implementer in its own worktree."

# Cross-page synthesis relevant to your problem documents

- **Spec provenance and ownership is unambiguous across all three pages:** human-written, human-owned, frozen and commit-pinned *before* a run, referenced by the kickoff, never produced inside a run and never re-decided by the plan. Any built system where the spec is generated or amended inside the run inverts three explicit rules ("Written by the human with help. Frozen before the run.", "The plan never re-litigates it", "the spec changes before the code does").
- **Freezing = open questions empty + attacked by a fresh context + committed + referenced from kickoff/run log.** No page defines freezing as merely a status flag.
- **A check returns a machine-readable pass/fail signal (exit code, test summary, diff, screenshot).** No page authorises a third verdict; "skipped", "pending" and "unverified" exist only as *disclosure* items on the evidence display, and flaky checks are removed from the gate rather than given a soft verdict.
- **No page draws a project-tests vs spec-checks ownership split.** The split the guides actually draw is (a) *where the command is written* — `CLAUDE.md` for project-wide, spec verification section for task-specific — and (b) *placement* — hooks for structural + diff boundary, spec commands for behavioural + artefact at gates, chained skills for judgement-adjacent.
- **Check location is defined by write-permission, not by a canonical directory:** a locked test directory guarded by a `PreToolUse` hook, or a path outside the implementer worktree's write permission; the planning guide calls it "tests locked dir". Only humans update golden references; only humans resolve a test-vs-spec contradiction.
- **The plan gates three things:** G1 the plan itself, G2 contracts plus green contract tests, G3 the evidence display (checks, critic findings, diff boundary, cost) — plus abandon triggers that must be observable.</result>
