## 2. `~/Projects/flightdeck/library/source/orchestrator-pattern/piecing-it-together.html`
Title: **"From idea to accepted run: how the pieces fit"**; nav label **"The map · Claude Code orchestration"**.

### 2.1 Purpose
This is the master map: "One pass through a single orchestrated run, from the idea in your head to a merged result, with every session, agent, document, gate and tool placed where it belongs in the sequence, and the loops that take you back when a run has to be abandoned." It is written "For a developer arriving with an idea and leaving with an accepted run" and is the only page that gives the complete stage 1–10 sequence, the exit/re-entry table, the full session roster and the folder layout.

### 2.2 Foundations
**The Foundation layer (pre-run, per-project):**

&gt; "Built once per project, before the first run. Everything here is reused by every run and improved by every abandoned one."

&gt; "Two kinds of things live here. The **harness** is the Claude Code configuration that makes agents deterministic: hooks, skills, agent definitions, permissions. The **orchestration folder** is the git-tracked home for the documents a run consumes and produces: spec template, kickoff library, specs, plans, reports, the log. The harness enforces; the folder remembers."

**Legend (the four markers used throughout):** "**Human** you, at a gate or authoring a document · **Agent** a Claude session or subagent · **Checked** a deterministic result · **Exit** a place the run can be abandoned."

**Shape of the journey:** "Numbered circles are stages. Square markers are human gates. Red markers are exits, where the run stops and a loop begins. Each stage names who acts, what goes in, what comes out, and what it leaves in the folder."

**When a run ends / what is kept:** the run ends at stage 9 (report assembled) → Gate 3 → stage 10 (Accepted: merge, log, promote), and: "**Loop out.** The next idea enters at stage 1 with a better template, a better library, and a log that already knows this codebase's failure modes."

**Exit doctrine:**

&gt; "Any red marker above stops the run. What happens next is the same every time, and the only question is where the loop re-enters."

&gt; "On exit: the report is assembled anyway (an abandoned run's report is the most useful kind), the branch is left as it is, and the human reads the failures section and writes the run log diagnosis: symptom, axis seen on, cause, axis fixed on, the single change made, what to watch. The change is made to the artefact the axis points at. Then the run restarts clean at the stage that artefact feeds. Nothing is patched in place."

&gt; "Exits before stage 6 are cheap and should be taken freely. Exits after stage 6 have spent parallel tokens, which is why gates 1 and 2 exist: they are the last two places a wrong assumption can be caught before it is multiplied by the number of workers."

&gt; "A worker reporting that a test contradicts the spec is an exit, not a bug for the worker to resolve. Either the test or the spec is wrong, and only a human can say which."

**Exit / re-entry table** (fixed-on → change made to → re-enter at):
| Fixed on | Change made to | Re-enter at |
|---|---|---|
| Context — spec | "The spec (a behaviour, boundary, interface or decision); the spec template if the gap is structural" | "Stage 1, then 2 if behaviours changed, then 3" |
| Context — run conduct | "The kickoff (roles, gates, ceilings, display, paths); the kickoff library" | "Stage 3" |
| Context — project | "`CLAUDE.md`, a skill, an agent definition" | "Stage 3 (foundation changed; run restarts)" |
| Verification | "A missing or unmapped check, an unlocked test, the acceptance script, a flaky or noisy check, the gate" | "Stage 2" |
| Tooling | "A hook, a permission, worktree isolation, a return schema, the workflow script's stage boundaries" | "Foundation, then stage 3" |

**Human-owned vs agent-owned, stated as the page's one-sentence reduction:**

&gt; "you write the spec and the kickoff, agents write the tests, the plan and the code, checks and a critic judge the result, hooks record what happened, and you decide at three gates using evidence rather than narrative."

**Session roster ("Sees" / "Must not see" — the visibility law):**
| Role | Stage | Sees | Must not see | Form |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Interviewer | 1 | "the idea, the spec template, the run log" | — | "interactive session" |
| Spec attacker | 1 | "the draft spec, the reviewer mandate" | "the interview" | "fresh session" |
| Test writer | 2 | "the frozen spec, the fixture, the codebase" | "any plan or implementation" | "fresh session or subagent" |
| Orchestrator | 4–9 | "kickoff, spec, test mapping, constitution, prior reports, worker returns" | "worker transcripts, the interview, the reviewer's reasoning" | "fresh session; plan mode at 4" |
| Explorer | 4 | "the codebase" | — | "subagent, read-only tools, small model" |
| Worker | 5–6 | "one unit, its interfaces, its checks, the worker template" | "other units, the plan as a whole, test files as writable" | "subagent, worktree-isolated, tiered model, structured return" |
| Verifier | 7 | "the merged branch, the check results" | "the implementer's reasoning" | "optional subagent asked to refute" |
| Reviewer | 8 | "spec, diff, reviewer mandate" | "the orchestrator's context, worker transcripts" | "subagent, fresh, strong model" |
| Assembler | 9 | "events, checks, plan, findings" | — | "skill invoked by hook or final step" |
| You | "1, 2, 3, G1, G2, G3, 10" | "the display, then the report" | "the transcripts, until something needs diagnosing" | — |

Note the roster gives the Worker as 5–6, i.e. one worker may build the seams at stage 5.

### 2.3 Prescriptions (ordered)

**Foundation (before stage 1), six blocks:**
1. *Constitution* — "`CLAUDE.md` — build and test commands, conventions that differ from defaults, protected paths, where the orchestration folder is and what to read from it"; "**Rules that must fire** live in hooks, not here; this file stays short".
2. *Hooks* — "**On edit** — type check, lint, format (structural checks)"; "**Block writes** to the test directory and protected interfaces for implementing agents"; "**Stop gate** — runs the spec's acceptance command; blocks the turn until green; eight blocks means abandon"; "**Event log** — subagent start/stop, task created/completed, tool failures, permission denials, compactions, worktree lifecycle → `events.jsonl`"; "**Session end** — assemble the run report".
3. *Skills* — "**Verification loops** — project rules no linter knows, written in plain English, one skill each"; "**Check wrapper** — runs a named check, captures command, exit, output to the run directory"; "**Diff boundary** — files touched versus allowed paths"; "**Report assembler** — reads events, checks, plan, review; renders the report".
4. *Agent definitions* — "`.claude/agents/*.md` — one file per role, narrow tools, chosen model, worktree isolation on anything that writes code"; "**Worker return shape** — every worker ends by returning unit, spec refs, artefacts, status".
5. *Permissions and budgets* — "**Allowlist** known-safe commands; sandbox filesystem and network"; "`--allowedTools` on non-interactive runs"; "**Ceilings** — max agents, max gate iterations, spend cap, stall rule; per-stage model tiering"; "**CLI tools** installed: `gh` at minimum".
6. *Orchestration folder* — "**Templates** — spec (nine parts), kickoff variants, worker prompt, reviewer mandate"; "**Per-spec** — the frozen spec, plan, reports"; "`RUNLOG.md` — diagnosis entries, newest first".

**The journey (10 stages + 3 gates):**

1. **Stage 1 — Idea → spec / "The spec-building session."** Human+Agent: "Start a session with the idea in one paragraph and ask to be interviewed: skip the obvious, dig into edge cases, tradeoffs and failure modes, then write the spec to a file in the nine-part shape. Answer questions; do not draft." Then: "a second, fresh session attacks the draft with the reviewer's mandate: every behaviour that could be built two ways, every unstated boundary, every undefined term. Rewrite against the findings until open questions is empty." Then: "Freeze it. Commit it. The commit hash is the spec's identity for the rest of the run." Sessions: "interview session · attack session (fresh)". In: "the idea · spec template · `RUNLOG.md` (read for known failure modes)". Out: "`specs/&lt;name&gt;/spec.md @ commit`, status frozen". Gate: "**Human** readiness checklist passed".
2. **Stage 2 — Spec → targets / "The test-writing session."** "A fresh session, or a test-writer subagent, that has seen only the spec. It derives one named check per numbered behaviour and edge case, writes the end-to-end acceptance script, and records the mapping. It never sees a plan or an implementation." Baseline: "Run everything once on the reference fixture to establish the baseline: structural checks green, behaviour checks failing in the expected way, acceptance script failing because the feature does not exist. Commit the tests. From here they are read-only to implementing agents (the block-writes hook enforces it)." Also: "The diff boundary check is configured from the spec's scope section at the same time." Out: "tests mapped to B/E numbers · acceptance script · diff boundary paths · baseline check results". Gate: "**Human** every behaviour mapped or listed as deliberately unverified".
3. **Stage 3 — Targets → kickoff / "Assembling the kickoff."** Human-authored. "The kickoff is how the run will be conducted, not what it must produce. Pull from the library, not the whole library: which agent roles and how many, worktree isolation on, the gates and what each requires, the budget ceilings, the model per stage, the display to maintain, the acceptance command the Stop gate runs, and the paths to the spec, tests, report directory and previous reports for this spec." Then: "Create the run branch and the run directory. Note the kickoff version in the run's header." Out: "`runs/&lt;id&gt;/kickoff.md` · branch `run/&lt;spec&gt;-&lt;n&gt;` · empty `runs/&lt;id&gt;/`". "**Not in it** anything that belongs in the spec".
4. **Stage 4 — The run begins / "The orchestrator session, plan phase."** "A fresh session started from the kickoff, in plan mode. The orchestrator reads the spec, the test mapping, the constitution and prior reports, and produces the plan: units of work, each with its spec refs and its mapped checks, the interfaces between units, the order, and the agent assigned to each. Investigation of the codebase goes to explorer subagents so the orchestrator's context stays clean." And: "Nothing has been built and no worker has been spawned. This is the cheapest moment to be wrong." Out: "`runs/&lt;id&gt;/plan.md` · intent page on the display".
5. **Gate 1 — plan.** "Read the plan against the spec. Does every behaviour have a unit? Is anything planned that the spec did not ask for? Are units small enough to pass or fail on their own? Edit the plan directly if needed, then approve. The orchestrator leaves plan mode." Decides: "approve · edit and approve · **Exit** back to spec".
6. **Stage 5 — Interfaces phase / "Fixing the contracts."** "Before parallel work, the orchestrator (or a single worker) writes the seams the plan named: types, signatures, schemas, file formats, reusing existing names as the spec requires. **Checked** The contract tests from stage 2 run against the stubs; structural checks pass; the diff boundary passes." Sessions: "orchestrator · one worker at most". Gate: "Stop hook on the contract checks".
7. **Gate 2 — interfaces.** "The last look before tokens are spent in parallel. Do the contracts match the spec's interfaces section? Are they the ones the workers will build against? Approve, or **exit** if the seams are wrong, because every worker will inherit the error."
8. **Stage 6 — Implement phase / "Workers, in parallel, in isolation."** "The orchestrator dispatches one worker per unit, each in its own worktree with the unit's spec refs, interface files and mapped checks, and nothing else. Workers build, the on-edit hooks fire, the block-writes hook keeps tests untouched, and each worker iterates against its own checks until green, then commits atomically and returns its structured result. Handoffs are files and schema-validated returns; workers do not talk to each other." And: "As units land, the orchestrator merges worktrees into the run branch and the display shows check results per unit, unverified behaviours, and cost so far. A worker that cannot satisfy a test, or that finds the test contradicts the spec, stops and reports rather than resolving it; that report is an **exit** for a human decision." And: "At scale, this phase is a dynamic workflow: the script holds the loop and the stage results, only the merged outcome reaches the orchestrator's context."
9. **Stage 7 — Verify phase / "The run's stop condition."** "On the merged branch: every check the spec names, through the wrapper, output captured verbatim; the acceptance script; the diff boundary; the test-file change list. The Stop gate holds the turn open until the acceptance command is green. If it blocks eight times, the run has a problem checks cannot fix: **exit**." Out: "`runs/&lt;id&gt;/checks/` · evidence page".
10. **Stage 8 — Review phase / "The critic."** "A reviewer subagent in a fresh context, given the spec, the diff and the reviewer mandate: report correctness and requirement gaps only, assume something is wrong, no style. Findings return to the orchestrator, which fixes and re-runs stage 7 once. Findings are not filtered; disputed ones are marked disputed." Out: "findings with severity and state · `/code-review` output if used".
11. **Stage 9 — Run ends / "The report is assembled."** "The session-end hook or a final orchestrator step runs the assembler: events, checks, plan and findings become the run report, every section marked recorded, checked, reviewed or stated. The ledger reconciles plan against outcome: landed, not landed, unplanned, discarded. A PR is opened from the run branch with the report linked. The evidence page is frozen as the report's HTML twin." Out: "`runs/&lt;id&gt;/report.md` · PR · frozen evidence page".
12. **Gate 3 — final review.** "Read the ledger first, then the open findings, then the verification section's three volunteered-by-nobody lines: unverified behaviours, test-file changes, files outside the boundary. Do not read the orchestrator notes first. The report carries the facts and does not make the decision; you do." Decides: "accept · accept with reservations · **Exit** abandon".
13. **Stage 10 — Accepted / "Merge, log, promote."** "Merge the PR. Write the short run log entry: spec, kickoff, outcome, cost, what worked, any reservation. Prune the worktrees. Then the promotion pass: anything the run confirmed as a rule graduates into the constitution, a hook or the spec template, and any kickoff variant that proved itself is saved to the library." Out: "merged commit · `RUNLOG.md` entry · promoted rules".

**"What tends to be missed" — nine rules stated as corrections:**
- "**The kickoff and the plan are different documents.** The kickoff is written by you before the run and says how it will be conducted. The plan is written by the orchestrator at stage 4 and approved by you at gate 1. Neither is the spec."
- "**The test-writing session comes before the run, in its own context.** Tests derived after seeing a plan describe the plan. The baseline run at stage 2, where the acceptance script fails for the right reason, is what proves the target is real."
- "**The spec attack session.** A fresh context with the reviewer's mandate, applied to the spec before anything is built. Cheapest exit in the whole process."
- "**Three visibility documents, not one.** The evidence display during the run, the run report frozen at the end, the run log entry written by you afterwards. Intentions on the display are a gate 1 tool; results on the display are what let you leave."
- "**Budgets and the stall rule** belong in the kickoff and the harness, or an unattended run has no ceiling. The Stop hook's eight-block cap is a stall detector, not an inconvenience."
- "**Permissions are part of tooling.** Allowlists, sandbox, `--allowedTools`, protected paths. A worker that cannot write to the test directory does not need to be told not to."
- "**Structured returns from workers.** Without a fixed return shape, the report's agents table and ledger are recalled rather than assembled."
- "**The promotion pass at stage 10.** Rules confirmed by runs graduate out of the log into the constitution, hooks or templates, and stop being logged. This is how the setup improves without the log growing."
- "**Worktree pruning.** Stale worktrees are the usual reason the isolation pattern gets abandoned. Part of stage 10."

### 2.4 Vocabulary defined here
- **Harness** — "the Claude Code configuration that makes agents deterministic: hooks, skills, agent definitions, permissions."
- **Orchestration folder** — "the git-tracked home for the documents a run consumes and produces: spec template, kickoff library, specs, plans, reports, the log." With: "The harness enforces; the folder remembers."
- **Kickoff** — "how the run will be conducted, not what it must produce."
- **Plan** — "written by the orchestrator at stage 4 and approved by you at gate 1."
- **Fresh** — "'Fresh' means started with no memory of the sessions before it."
- **Exit** — "a place the run can be abandoned"; also "Red markers are exits, where the run stops and a loop begins."
- **Checked** — "a deterministic result."
- **Ledger** — "The ledger reconciles plan against outcome: landed, not landed, unplanned, discarded."
- **Run log diagnosis entry** — "symptom, axis seen on, cause, axis fixed on, the single change made, what to watch."
- **Promotion pass** — "anything the run confirmed as a rule graduates into the constitution, a hook or the spec template, and any kickoff variant that proved itself is saved to the library."

### 2.5 Cross-references
Footer: "Reference pages: **the field review** · **the spec** · **verification** · **the run report** · **the run log**." Inline: "See **the folder** below" (self-reference from the Foundation block). The page is the index; it does not restate what each companion owns beyond naming them, but stage-by-stage the artefacts it hands off correspond exactly (spec → the spec guide, stage-2 targets → verification, stage 9 → the run report, stage 10 → the run log, pillars → the field review).

&gt;   CLAUDE.md                    constitution; points at orchestration/

## 3. `~/Projects/flightdeck/library/source/orchestrator-pattern/core-stages-4-7.html`
Title: **"Setting up an orchestration run — the core (stages 4 to 7)"**; nav label **"Setting up an orchestration run · part two"**.

### 3.1 Purpose
This is the deep internals page for the agent-owned middle of a run: "Stages 4 to 7 of an orchestrated run in Claude Code: from a fresh orchestrator session reading a frozen spec, through the plan, the seams, the parallel workers, and the whole-feature verification that decides when the run stops." It is explicitly part two of a three-part series and covers "The part of the process that is almost entirely agents, with the human at two gates."

### 3.2 Foundations
**The three-part division (its own statement of the whole-run shape):**

&gt; "**Part one · setup** Spec, targets, kickoff. The human is the main character."
&gt; "**Part two · the core** Plan, interfaces, workers, verify. The orchestrator is the main character."
&gt; "**Part three · finishing** Review, report, gate 3, log, promote, re-enter. Hardening and showing."

**The governing idea:**

&gt; "Everything in the core follows from one idea inherited from human-in-the-loop work: build the earlier structure before the dependent one. The core writes that ordering down and enforces it."

**What must be frozen on entry:**

&gt; "Entering the core, three things exist and are frozen: `spec.json` at a commit, the tests derived from it (read-only to anything that writes code), and the kickoff that says how this run is conducted. The orchestrator is a fresh session started from the kickoff. It has never seen the interview that produced the spec and never will."

**The core's shape and where the human appears:**

&gt; "The core goes green in predetermined phases. Interfaces first, so every unit can test its seams. Then waves of parallel workers, each accountable for a slice of the spec, each fenced to its own paths, each unable to edit the tests or the seams it builds against. Then the whole feature, on the merged branch, against the acceptance script. At each phase the stop condition is a check result, and the human appears exactly twice, at the two moments where a wrong assumption is about to be multiplied by the number of workers."

**When the run ends (stop condition):**

&gt; "The Stop hook runs the acceptance command and refuses to let the orchestrator's turn end until it exits zero. … The orchestrator cannot declare done; only the command can."

&gt; "After eight consecutive blocks Claude Code overrides the hook and ends the turn. Eight is Anthropic's number, a runtime safeguard so a broken check cannot trap a session forever; it is not chosen, it is exploited. A tighter ceiling is the hook script counting its own blocks, writing a stalled event on the fourth or fifth and exiting zero to end the turn cleanly, with the built-in cap as backstop. Either way the number is a stall detector."

**What the orchestrator may and may not do:**
- Stage 4, plan mode: "Plan mode restricts the session to read-only tools. The orchestrator can explore the codebase, read the spec and tests, spawn explorer subagents, and write a plan; it cannot edit files. Three consequences matter. The plan phase cannot leak into implementation no matter how confident the orchestrator is. The orchestrator's context stays small… And approving the plan is the act that takes the session out of plan mode, so gate 1 is a switch rather than a convention." Also: "**Only approve leaves plan mode.**"
- Prompting workers: "The orchestrator does not tell the worker how. It tells the worker what it is accountable for, what proves it, and where the fence is; the decomposition, the ordering and the fences are the orchestrator's contribution, all upstream of the prompt."
- On blocks: "stop dispatching, do not resolve the contract yourself, write the block to the run directory, ask the user."
- On findings: "Findings go to the orchestrator, never straight to the worker whose context is the thing being challenged. … The orchestrator does not adjudicate: a finding the fix-worker disputes stays open and reaches the report marked disputed."
- On done: "The orchestrator cannot declare done; only the command can."

**What the worker may and may not do (the three wiring encounters):**
&gt; "Tries to edit a locked file — The block-writes hook refuses the write before it happens and the worker sees why. Nothing goes red because nothing changed."
&gt; "Breaks a contract in a shared file — The contract test goes red in the worker's own check run. It cannot edit the test, so the only way back to green is to undo its change. The worker fixes its own mistake."
&gt; "Discovers the wiring is wrong for its unit — It must not route around the contract; that produces code that satisfies the tests while not doing what the spec meant. It stops, returns `status: blocked` with the contract it needs changed and the spec entity that requires it. **Exit** Either the spec's interfaces section or the plan's reading of it was wrong, and only a human says which."

**Model tiering doctrine:**
&gt; "a smaller model iterating against a deterministic check converges on tasks it would fail if asked to get right in one pass, because the check loop is doing work that raw capability would otherwise do. The default is a smaller tier for workers, with escalation driven by the plan's flags: size L, a risk mark, or a unit with entries in `decisions` gets the stronger model… A useful kickoff rule is escalation on failure: a worker that hits its iteration ceiling is retried once on the stronger tier before returning blocked. Everything upstream of the workers stays on the strongest model: the orchestrator, the test-writer, the reviewer."

**One-sentence reduction:**
&gt; "the orchestrator decomposes and orders, the seams are built and locked before anyone builds against them, cheap workers iterate against checks they cannot edit inside fences they cannot cross, and a hook that only a passing command can satisfy decides when the run is done."

### 3.3 Prescriptions (ordered)

**Stage numbers and names as this page states them:**
- **Stage 4 · Plan** — "Main character: orchestrator, in plan mode. Sees: kickoff · spec · test map · constitution · prior reports. Produces: `runs/&lt;id&gt;/plan.json`. Ends at: gate 1."
- **Gate 1 · Plan approval**
- **Stage 5 · Interfaces** — "Main character: orchestrator, or one worker in sequence. Sees: the plan's interfaces list · the spec's interfaces section · the contract checks. Produces: one commit on the run branch · the protected path set. Ends at: gate 2."
- **Gate 2 · Interfaces approval**
- **Stage 6 · Workers** — "Main character: the workers; the orchestrator dispatches and merges. Each worker sees: its rendered prompt only. Produces: per-unit commits · structured returns · `events.jsonl` filling. Ceilings: agents · iterations per unit · spend."
- **Stage 7 · Verify** — "Main character: the Stop hook; the orchestrator merges and re-dispatches. Runs: the full check set on the merged branch. Produces: `runs/&lt;id&gt;/checks/` · the evidence display in its final form. Ends by: acceptance green, or the stall cap."

**Stages 1–3 as referenced here (not numbered by name, but stated):** part one is "Spec, targets, kickoff. The human is the main character." Stage 1 is the spec — "A plan that cannot be fixed by editing units is a spec problem. The run stops here and re-enters at stage 1." Stage 2 is the tests/targets — "the stage-2 tests do"; "the list of test files changed since stage 2, which should be empty"; "the run re-enters at stage 2 with one test changed"; "for the first time the acceptance script from stage 2". Stage 3 (kickoff) is referenced as the frozen third input: "the kickoff that says how this run is conducted."

**Stage 8 onward as referenced here:** part three is "Review, report, gate 3, log, promote, re-enter." Also: "the whole-diff review after the core covers the rest"; "Everything after the core, the whole-diff review, the report, gate 3, is judgement and record laid on top of these facts, and none of it should run if stage 7 is not green."

**Ordered prescriptions:**
1. **Write the plan to a file.** "The kickoff must say to write the plan to a file. Plan mode's default output is conversational; the plan is consumed later by dispatch and by the report's ledger, and both need `runs/&lt;id&gt;/plan.json`."
2. **The plan is data, not prose.** "A plan for an orchestrated run is read three times, by the orchestrator to dispatch, by the assembler to reconcile plan against outcome, and by the human to scan for gaps. All three want rows. Each unit is a pointer into things that already carry the detail, spec entity IDs, interface IDs, check names, paths, and the plan restates none of it."
3. **The plan unit schema** — verbatim: `id`, `name`, `spec_refs` ("what this unit is accountable for"), `owns` ("the only paths it may write — its diff boundary"), `needs` ("interfaces it consumes"), `produces` ("interfaces it defines (stubbed at stage 5)"), `checks` ("its stop condition, from the test map"), `worker`, `model`, `group` ("wave id"), `size` ("S|M|L"), `flags` (`produces-interface`, `modifies-existing`, `risk`, `human-decision`), `decisions` ("a call made where the spec was silent"). Top level: `"spec": "&lt;path&gt;@&lt;commit&gt;"`, `interfaces: [{id, name, reuse|new, check}]`, `"order": [["wave-1 groups"], ["wave-2 groups"]]`. Rules: "Interfaces are first-class objects at the top of the plan, each with its own contract check; that list is the entire input to stage 5. `order` is explicit waves, the dispatch schedule for stage 6. `decisions` is where a human-decision flag points… Status is not on the plan; that is the report's job."
4. **Schema location rule.** "Without a template the orchestrator writes prose, because that is what plans look like in its training. A `plan` schema in `orchestration/schemas/`, named by the kickoff, is what makes the plan parseable rather than interpreted."
5. **Gate 1 is a page with a mechanical half.** "The gate is a local page that opens the run directory, reads `plan.json`, resolves every reference against `spec.json`, and derives the checks a person would otherwise do by eye: every behaviour and edge in exactly one unit, and the uncovered ones listed; every `needs` matched by a `produces` or an existing interface; no two units owning the same path; every named check present in the test map; spec version of the plan equal to spec version of the tests. Those appear as flags at the top. What remains for the human is judgement: unit size, decomposition, and each entry in `decisions`."
6. **Gate 1's three outcomes, each a file.** "**Approve** writes an approval block into the plan (`approved: {at, spec_version, plan_hash}`) so the orchestrator and the assembler can verify they are working from the plan the human saw. **Edit** writes a new plan revision; the kickoff tells the orchestrator the plan file is the source of truth and to re-read it after the gate, so edits win without a conversation. **Comment** writes `comments.json` keyed by unit ID, and the page renders the comments as a revise-plan prompt to paste into the orchestrator session; it re-plans, the page reloads. Only approve leaves plan mode." Mechanism: "In Chrome the File System Access API lets the page read and write the run directory in place, so there is no export and import step. The same page family, with a different lens, serves the spec freeze before the core and the report after it."
7. **Stage 5 — the three kinds of interface.** "An interface marked reuse gets nothing created; the existing type or contract is confirmed to be where the spec says and the contract check references it. An interface that is its own implementation, a type, a schema, a migration, a route, an association, a permitted-params list, is written in full, because there is nothing to defer. An interface that has behaviour behind it, a function or an action, is written as a signature whose body raises a not-implemented error carrying the unit ID that will implement it. If units own module files that do not exist yet, those are created with their exports declared, so every import a worker will write already resolves."
8. **The stub rule.** "The stub raises; it never returns. A stub that returns plausible data, an empty result or a fake redirect, lets a behaviour test pass falsely and lets a worker build against fake behaviour. A raise with the unit ID means every failure in the next phase names the unit that has not been done yet."
9. **Stage 5's stop condition.** "The stubs do not produce a signal; the stage-2 tests do, and what stage 5 changes is the reason they fail. … The stop condition for the phase is that specific pattern in the output, green structure and contracts, red behaviour for the right reason, and the Stop hook holds the turn open for it."
10. **Commit and lock.** "One commit, `interfaces: comments`, on the run branch. It does two things: every worker's worktree will inherit the seams, and the interface paths join the protected set, so the block-writes hook now stops workers from changing them. … Without it two workers sharing a type each invent their own; with it the shared vocabulary is fixed before anyone speaks, and a worker that needs a seam to change has to stop and report."
11. **The lock-by-path limit and its fallback.** "The lock is by path, so it is clean where a file is pure interface … and awkward where interface and implementation share a file … For those files the contract test is the lock. The association spec lives in the read-only test directory; a worker that changes the association breaks a test it cannot edit. **Lock the file when you can; where you cannot, make sure a contract test covers the seam.**"
12. **Gate 2's one question.** "The gate 2 page shows the interfaces commit as a diff with the contract check results beside each interface, and the modifies-existing and risk flags highlighted. One question: are these the seams the spec's interfaces section described, and are they the ones every worker should build against." Exit rule: "If the seams are wrong the fix is upstream, in the spec's interfaces section or the plan's reading of it, never in the code. The branch is left as it is and the run restarts where the fix lands." After approval: "Approval writes the approval block, the interface paths are confirmed in the protected set, and the seams become canon. From here the wiring is verified three times: it was verified when built, it is verified continuously because every worker's check set includes the contract checks, and it is verified again on the merged branch at stage 7."
13. **The wave rule.** "Within a wave, units depend on each other's interfaces and never on each other's implementation; that is what lets them run in parallel. Where a unit genuinely needs another's finished behaviour, the plan puts it in a later wave, and the later wave's check set includes the earlier wave's behaviour tests as well as the contracts. Wave two cannot go green by breaking wave one, because wave one's tests are in wave two's stop condition and wave two cannot edit them. Regression protection grows wave by wave, from the plan's `order` field and the check-set rule, not from anything a worker decides."
14. **The three prompt layers** (table): *Agent definition* — lives in `.claude/agents/worker.md`, carries "Role, tools allowed and denied, model tier, worktree isolation, the return shape", varies "never". *Worker template* — lives in `orchestration/templates/worker.md`, carries "The sections, the rules, the order; the place the 'must not see' boundary is implemented, because what is not a slot cannot reach the worker", varies "per project". *The fill* — "`plan.json` resolved against `spec.json`", carries "The unit's spec entities verbatim, interface signatures, paths, check names and command", varies "per unit". Rule: "Not the plan. The plan unit is data; the prompt is rendered from it at dispatch time."
15. **Worker prompt slots** — verbatim: "`&lt;unit id and name&gt;` / `&lt;spec entities, verbatim: the behaviours and edges this unit is accountable for&gt;` / `&lt;interfaces consumed: signatures, marked read-only&gt;` / `&lt;interfaces produced: already stubbed, to be implemented&gt;` / `&lt;paths this unit may write&gt;` / `&lt;checks that must be green, and the exact command&gt;` / `&lt;rules: tests and interfaces are read-only · outside "owns" is out of bounds · on a contradiction between a test and the spec, stop and return blocked&gt;` / `&lt;iteration ceiling&gt;` / `&lt;return shape: unit · spec refs · artefacts written · status · blocked-on&gt;`" — under the header comment "nothing else reaches the worker".
16. **Deterministic rendering.** "Render the prompt deterministically, with a small skill or script over the two JSON files, rather than having the orchestrator compose it freehand. Freehand composition is where orchestrator context leaks into workers and where a slot is quietly dropped under context pressure. It also makes the report's agents table honest: the task a worker was given becomes a recorded file rather than a stated recollection."
17. **How a block reaches the human, interactive shape.** "What makes this deterministic is a `PostToolUse` hook on the subagent tool that reads the returned result, appends a blocked event to `events.jsonl` on a match, and injects a line into the orchestrator's context saying dispatch must halt; a notification hook pings the human at the same time."
18. **Workflow shape and the interactive/script boundary.** "In the workflow shape, dynamic workflows do not accept user input during execution, only a permission prompt can pause one, and the script has no filesystem access of its own. A block there is a stop condition the script handles: skip dependents, finish or stop the wave, return the block as the final result to the session, which then asks. A block almost always means a spec or plan change, which means a new run. This is why the core runs interactively through gate 2 and only the parallel waves of stage 6 are candidates for a workflow: the stages with gates need a session that can stop and ask; the stage where the human has already chosen not to be present is where a script that cannot ask is the right tool."
19. **Optional per-unit adversary.** "A finding is resolved when the fix-worker's checks are green and, if the kickoff asks, the reviewer re-checks once. … Per-unit review is usually reserved for risk-flagged units; the whole-diff review after the core covers the rest."
20. **Stage 7's full check set.** "The orchestrator merges the wave worktrees onto the run branch and the full set runs through the check wrapper, every result captured verbatim: structural checks, every contract and behaviour test, and for the first time the acceptance script from stage 2, plus the diff boundary over the run's entire diff, the list of spec behaviours with no green check, and the list of test files changed since stage 2, which should be empty." Rationale: "Units interact in ways their own checks cannot see: two changes pass separately and fail together, a shared factory is satisfied by one unit and broken by another, a count is right in the model spec and wrong on the page. The acceptance script is the only check that exercises the feature the way a user would."
21. **The fix loop at 7.** "On failure the orchestrator reads the output, identifies the unit from the failing check's spec mapping, dispatches a fix-worker with that check as its target, on the stronger tier if the kickoff says so, re-merges, and the hook runs again."
22. **Verification subagent.** "A verification subagent, if the kickoff asks for one, runs here: given the merged branch and the check results and told to try to refute them. It is a refinement on top of the deterministic gate, not a substitute for it."
23. **The display flip.** "Through gate 2 it showed intentions, the plan and the seams. From here it shows results: commands, exit codes, output lines, spec coverage, what was not verified, test files touched, cost per unit and per phase. This is the flip from an approval tool to a verification tool."

**Summary table (verbatim columns: Stage / Main character / Sees / Produces / Stops on / Exit means):**
| Stage | Main character | Sees | Produces | Stops on | Exit means |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 Plan | orchestrator, plan mode | kickoff · spec · test map · constitution · prior reports | `plan.json` · intent page | gate 1 approval block | spec problem → stage 1 |
| 5 Interfaces | orchestrator or one worker | plan interfaces · spec interfaces · contract checks | interfaces commit · protected paths | green shape, red behaviour for the right reason; gate 2 | seam problem → spec or plan |
| 6 Workers | workers, in worktrees | rendered prompt only | unit commits · structured returns · events | each unit's checks green, or ceiling | blocked → human picks spec or plan |
| 7 Verify | the Stop hook | merged branch · full check set | `checks/` · evidence display | acceptance exits 0 | stall cap → which check kept failing |

### 3.4 Vocabulary defined here
- **Plan mode** — "restricts the session to read-only tools. The orchestrator can explore the codebase, read the spec and tests, spawn explorer subagents, and write a plan; it cannot edit files."
- **`owns`** — "the only paths it may write — its diff boundary."
- **`spec_refs`** — "what this unit is accountable for."
- **`needs`** — "interfaces it consumes." **`produces`** — "interfaces it defines (stubbed at stage 5)."
- **`checks`** — "its stop condition, from the test map."
- **`order`** — "explicit waves, the dispatch schedule for stage 6."
- **`decisions`** — "a call made where the spec was silent."
- **Approval block** — `approved: {at, spec_version, plan_hash}`.
- **Wave** — "Within a wave, units depend on each other's interfaces and never on each other's implementation; that is what lets them run in parallel."
- **Seams** — "everything a worker will import from another worker, declared and not implemented, checked, committed, and locked."
- **Stub** — "a signature whose body raises a not-implemented error carrying the unit ID that will implement it"; "The stub raises; it never returns."
- **The eight-block cap** — "Eight is Anthropic's number, a runtime safeguard so a broken check cannot trap a session forever; it is not chosen, it is exploited. … the number is a stall detector."
- **Escalation on failure** — "a worker that hits its iteration ceiling is retried once on the stronger tier before returning blocked."

### 3.5 Cross-references

### 3.6 Where artefacts live according to this page
- `specs/&lt;name&gt;/spec.json` (worked example: `specs/comments/spec.json`) — frozen at a commit; referenced in the plan as `"spec": "&lt;path&gt;@&lt;commit&gt;"`.

- `runs/&lt;id&gt;/events.jsonl` — implied; "`events.jsonl` filling", blocked events appended.

- Branch `run/&lt;spec&gt;-&lt;n&gt;` (example `run/comments-1`); interfaces commit named `interfaces: &lt;spec&gt;` (example `interfaces: comments`).
- Tests in the project's test directory (example `spec/`), read-only.

So the run folder contains six things: the kickoff version used, the plan, the events, the check outputs, the review findings, and the report. All of them are output. None is setup. The spec and tests map live in a per-spec folder outside every run, one folder per spec holding its version series. The run is named spec plus a number.

**This is what flightcrew built.** The specs folder outside the runs, the byte-identical pins inside, the spec-dash-number default name, and the run branch pattern all come from this page. The one place the built system departed is copying the spec into each launch, where the guide only points at it by commit. The original run-problems file called this layout improvised. It was not. It was followed.

**Your vision departs from the guides on one point.** You want the spec series inside the run's folder, adjacent to the run assets it drives. The guides want the spec series outside, in the memory, with runs pointing at it by commit. Both satisfy the endings guide's salvage test, because in both the spec survives and the plan, partial implementation and transcript do not. The difference is where the surviving thing sits. That is a decision, and now it is a decision made knowingly against the source rather than one made for you by an agent.

**Two other things settled by the twelve pages:**

- **The three visibility documents.** The evidence display during the run, the run report frozen at the end and committed, the run log entry written by the human afterwards. The report is output that must survive because the log is written from it. The guides commit it. Your overwrite model needs to decide whether the report of an abandoned instance is kept or whether its content is considered absorbed by the log entry.
- **The guides disagree with themselves on the branch.** The map says on exit "the branch is left as it is". The endings guide's final abandonment step says "delete the run's branches, remove its worktrees, prune." Both cannot hold. Flightcrew inherited the ambiguity and resolved it by creating no run branch at all.

One more discrepancy the explorer flagged: the core-stages page uses JSON artefacts and a schemas directory, the map uses markdown and none. Flightcrew chose JSON. The map is the only page with the folder listing, so the two never had to agree on it.

Mostly yes, and the misses are instructive. Taking the thirteen run-problems against your layout:

**Dissolved by the model itself**
- 1, 2, 4, 5: one work in three locations, no attempt concept, the backpointer, the hoisted series. Under the guides' setup-and-output split these were never defects. The mission folder is the investment, each launch is one attempt, and the number in the launch name is the attempt order. The only tooling change is that launch.json should carry the mission name and the attempt number as fields, replacing a previous-launch link computed from file modification time.
- 3: the runner refusing to reuse a directory is correct behaviour. A launch is one attempt and is never reopened.
- 10: two log entries for two attempts is correct. The heading should carry mission and attempt number so lineage reads without following pointers.

**Resolved only if the documents follow**
- 6, 8, 11: the launch README, the design contract's one-off instruction and STRUCTURE.md describe shapes that never existed. The layout fixes nothing here until those three documents are rewritten to describe it.
- 9: the branch convention. The guides say run slash mission dash n. The runner only records a branch name and never creates or checks it. That stays a tooling defect under any layout.

**Given a home but not an owner**
- 12, 13: the mission folder is exactly where the idea, the interview and the draft spec belong. That is the guides' stage one, and it now has an address. Nothing yet creates that folder, dispatches the interviewer, or produces the frozen spec. The stage has a home and still no tooling.

**Not touched**
- 7: the three incompatible shapes across branches. Other branches grew specs inside run folders. Those folders would need to become mission folders, and that is a per-branch migration, not a layout decision.

**Two things I'd flag before you commit to names.**
- **Mission collides with an existing folder.** The deck already has a missions directory holding idea documents like the crew adviser and the library shape. Since a mission is where an idea becomes a spec, your new folder may simply be that existing one, with one subfolder per named mission. That is elegant, but that directory is currently user-facing and off limits to agents. Making it the spec home makes it agent-facing at least for the interview stage.
- **Drop the copies.** The guides point at the spec by commit and never copy it. Flightcrew copies the spec and map into each launch and locks the copies. With versioned immutable files in the mission folder, the copies are redundant, and removing them removes the byte-identical triplication.

**On rearranging the two completed launches post hoc.** You can move the files with git, but you cannot make the record agree with the move. Both frozen tests maps carry locked-path globs naming the old specs folder. Both launch.json files point at paths inside their own folder. The runner hardcodes the old specs path when it locks. The bin-runlog suite asserts the file is named RUNLOG.md, and that suite is locked, so renaming the log to FLIGHTLOG.md fails a frozen check. Fixing any of that means editing frozen artefacts, which is the quiet spec shift the endings guide names as an anti-pattern.

My advice is to leave the two launches exactly as they are. They are the evidence of two attempts and the pins inside them are true for the commits they name. Apply the layout as a context-axis change in the log, absorbed into the next spec and map version, and let the next mission be the first one built in the new shape. The move then happens in tooling under a new frozen spec, not by hand against a closed record. That is the guides' own rule applied to the guides' own folder.

p='structure-problems.md'
t=open(p).read()
head,body=t.split('# Structure problems\n',1)

def sect(marker, prose):
    global body
    # insert prose after the last comment line following marker heading block
    i=body.index(marker)
    # find end of the comment block after marker
    j=i+len(marker)
    lines=body[j:].split('\n')
    k=0
    while k<len(lines) and (lines[k].startswith('<!--') or lines[k]==''):
        # stop at first blank after at least one comment when next non-blank is a heading
        if lines[k]=='' and k+1<len(lines) and lines[k+1].startswith('#'):
            break
        k+=1
    ins='\n'.join(lines[:k])
    rest='\n'.join(lines[k:])
    body=body[:j]+ins+'\n'+prose.rstrip('\n')+'\n'+rest

sect('# Structure problems\n', """
This document describes the structure problems of the flightcrew orchestration system: how a piece of work, its spec, its attempts and its record are named and laid out on disk. It is one of a set of problem documents, each covering one domain, written to inform the plan of a later launch that will address them. It diagnoses. It proposes no remediation.

Every observation was verified on branch `flightcrew-buildout` at commit `75b2b42`. Paths and line numbers refer to that revision. The working tree may be checked out on another branch, so read evidence with `git show flightcrew-buildout:<path>` rather than from disk. Where a claim concerns another branch, the branch is named.
""")

sect('## Agent Invariants\n', """
- The launch is the unit of work. The run is the unit of attempt. Neither is interchangeable with the other.
- A spec exists once, in one place, and is referenced from everywhere else by version and commit. No launch, run or tool holds a copy.
- The reader has none of the conversation that produced this document. Every claim here stands on the cited evidence alone.
