[USER]    💭: none
oh sorry continue

------------------------------------------------------------

[ASSISTANT 💬]
- **A ratio.** Run the same scenario many times, count how often the behaviour happened, and compare that against a threshold you wrote down before running. Seven passes out of ten against a threshold of six is a pass. This exists because an agent's output varies between runs, so one run proves nothing.
- **A verdict sheet.** A fresh model reads the output against a written rubric and fills in a fixed set of questions with yes or no and a quotation for each. This is for qualities no script can measure, like whether an explanation landed or a tone held.

Now the gap in what was built. There are two files that define what a check can say about itself. The tests map file, where each check is listed, has no place to write a threshold, a sample size, a rubric path or anything else the second and third kinds need. The check result file, where the runner records what happened, allows exactly four words: pass, fail, error, skipped. Nowhere in either can a ratio or a sheet be written down. So even if a test-builder wanted to build a statistical or judged check, the two documents the runner reads and writes have no slot for it, and the runner would reduce it to a pass or fail from the exit code anyway.

Where the knowledge sits instead: the kickoff part for agent-shaped work describes what each kind needs, but it is read by the orchestrator at plan time, after the checks are already frozen. The spec-builder is told to tag each behaviour with its kind when the product is agent-shaped, but nothing checks that it did. The test-builder, the role that would build the ratio or the sheet, is taught one shape of check, the exit-code kind, and never sees the other two described.

So "the built system carries one verdict where the manuals define three" means this: the manuals promise three kinds of answer, and the files, the runner and the builder that were built against those manuals can only produce, record or understand the first kind.

def sect(marker, prose):
    global body
    i=body.index(marker); j=i+len(marker)
    lines=body[j:].split('\n'); k=0
    while k<len(lines) and (lines[k].startswith('<!--') or lines[k]==''):
        if lines[k]=='' and k+1<len(lines) and lines[k+1].startswith('#'): break
        k+=1

Every problem below is measured against four positions a testing artefact can occupy:

|---|---|---|---|

A **check** is a wrapper the tests map names. It runs something, whether a project test, a script or a scenario, reads the result, and returns a verdict a gate can read. A **test** is a project's own assertion. It is owned by the project, may predate any spec and outlive every run, and is invoked by a check but never written by a run. A **target** is the status a check holds once it exists before the work and is locked against it; it is not a separate kind of artefact.

Because verification is one of the three failure axes, checks change between runs: a run may find a check wrong or missing, the log records it, and the next run's test-builder writes the corrected set. That is why checks belong to the run and not to the spec. It is also why the run folder must exist before the test-builder is dispatched.

P['### 1. The vocabulary has no rail\n']="""
**What.** The words the system uses for testing are defined in five places and do not agree. `library/terms.md:2` defines a check as any executable verification, test or otherwise, that returns pass or fail. `flightdeck/manuals/testing/testing-conventions.md:3` says the same. `flightdeck/manuals/testing/testing-description.md:9` says every check returns one of three verdicts. `terms.md:5` defines `class` as one of the many kinds of check, distinguished by what it proves, and `terms.md:10` defines `check class` as the declared method by which a behaviour will be falsified, two different axes under near-identical names. `flightdeck/flightcrew/schemas/tests-map.schema.json:76-80` carries both axes as fields on every check: `kind`, required, with the seven values of the description manual, and `class`, optional, with four values from the spec verification addendum. **Why it matters.** The product flightcrew builds is often agent-shaped: crew definitions, skills, prompts, workflows. P['### 4. Checks have no home of their own\n']="""

The testing manuals themselves never say where a check's files live. `testing-description.md:5` announces that the placements answer where a check lives, and the placements section at `:107-113` then defines four ways a check is caused to run: standalone, embedded, chained, enforced. None is a directory. The one sentence that states a filesystem rule is `testing-conventions.md:7`, that a check's files live in a directory named for its spec, and it is not repeated anywhere.

**Why it matters.** The rail gives checks a home: the run folder. Every current document points somewhere else, and the documents that promise to say where checks live say something else instead. A reader following the description manual's own map arrives at a section about invocation and leaves with no answer. A reader following the conventions arrives at a spec folder that no command creates. A reader following the builder's precedence arrives at the project's own tests.

**Effect on the system.** The placement rule that decides whether a check is a run artefact or a project artefact, the most consequential structural fact about a check, is one line in one document and is contradicted by three others. The folder named checks under flightcrew holds no checks and will confuse any reader who takes the name literally. Under the rail, all four documents and the folder name need to change together or the rail is not readable from the repository.
"""
P['### 5. The lock defends paths the model will move\n']="""
**What.** `flightdeck/flightcrew/hooks/lock-guard.mjs:6-13` denies edits to paths under the launch's locked list. It intercepts three tools, Edit, Write and NotebookEdit, per `hooks/lib.mjs:15`; a shell command that rewrites a file is not intercepted. It returns without checking anything during the targets phase. The locked list is empty and boundary enforcement is off from `fc launch new` until `fc launch pin tests-map`, per `bin/cmd/launch.mjs:291` and `hooks/boundary-guard.mjs:23`. At pin, `launch.mjs:441-445` adds the map's own locked paths plus two globs: the run's `specs/` subfolder and the canonical spec folder. `bin/cmd/boundary.mjs:42-46` treats everything under the run folder as inside the boundary unconditionally.

Every one of the thirty suites under `flightdeck/testbench/suites/` imports `../../lib/suite-lib.mjs`, outside its own directory. That library is locked because the map lists `flightdeck/testbench/lib/**`. No field in the map declares that a check depends on it. The map's only statement of what a check touches is its `command` string.

**Why it matters.** Under the rail, checks move into the run folder. The lock as built covers the run's `specs/` subfolder and nothing else inside the run, and the boundary check counts the whole run folder as inside bounds. A run-local `checks/` folder would therefore be protected by neither guard. The lock also guarantees only what it can see: an implementer that edits a check through the shell, or edits a helper the check imports that the map does not list, is not stopped. The guides' principle is that a check the agent can edit is a suggestion and a check it cannot edit is a target. Today the target is held by the accident that every assertion sits inside a listed path.

**Effect on the system.** The two guards, the pin command and six locked suites that assert the current glob composition all encode the old layout. Moving checks into the run changes what the lock must cover and what the boundary must exclude, and the map needs a way to declare a check's dependencies so that locking the check locks what decides its verdict.
"""
P['### 6. The map series and the run disagree about where the map lives\n']="""
**What.** The tests map is versioned like the spec. `flightdeck/manuals/versioning/tests-map-versioning.md:7-13` places the series beside the spec, one folder holding `tests-map.v1.json`, `tests-map.v2.json` and so on, and `:135` revises by copying the latest file to the next number in the same folder. `tests-map.schema.json:34-49` requires each `previous_versions` entry to name the earlier file, and `flightdeck/flightcrew/checks/validators/validate-tests-map.mjs:97-98` resolves the pinned spec by looking for `spec.v<n>.json` beside the map.

**Why it matters.** The rail puts checks in the run folder because they change between runs. The map is the document that names the checks, and it is also a versioned series whose versions absorb the log's decisions. Those two facts pull in different directions. If the map lives with the checks in the run, the series is split across run folders and every sibling reference above breaks. If the map lives with the spec series in the launch's `specs/` folder, it describes checks that sit in a different folder, and a map version and the run whose checks it names have to be tied together some other way.

**Effect on the system.** Nothing in the current system can hold either arrangement, since it knows only the canonical spec folder. The decision is open and is listed below. Until it is made, the test-builder's destination, the pin command's copy target, the lock's globs and the validator's resolution rule cannot be specified.
"""
P['### 7. Rules live where the builder does not read\n']="""
**What.** `flightdeck/testbench/tests.keep` states the harness rule in four lines: harnesses are reusable across branches, the folder is merge-protected, launch results never go there, and `runs/` holds local output. No file under `flightdeck/flightcrew/crew/` mentions `testbench` or the keep file. The conventions tell the builder to report untestable entries; the schema has no such field, and the field it does have is marked as a human's decision. The description of what a statistical or judged check owes sits in a kickoff part read by the orchestrator after the map is frozen, not in the builder's role file or in the manuals the role file names.

**Why it matters.** The guides' principle is that each role reads its own tailored context and nothing else, and that a rule an agent should follow is one it will eventually break unless it is in front of it or enforced. Three rules that govern what the test-builder writes are in places the test-builder is never sent. The role file's own instruction that auto-loaded project instructions do not apply to it closes the last route by which it might have found them.

**Effect on the system.** A test-builder following its role file to the letter produces checks that ignore the harness rule, uses a word the map cannot hold, and never learns what a varying-class check needs. The rules exist. They are not addressed to the role that needs them.
"""
P['## Decisions the rail forces\n']="""
- Where the tests map lives: with the spec series in the launch's `specs/` folder, or with the checks it names in the run folder. The version series as built assumes one folder.
- What a statistical check and a judged check look like on disk: what command produces each, what file the ratio or the sheet lands in, and how a gate reads it. Nothing can be built for the two missing verdicts until this is fixed.
- Whether a run-local check wrapper is a script of its own or only a command string in the map, given that the runner already turns any command's exit code into a verdict.
- Whether `flightdeck/flightcrew/checks/` keeps its name, given that it holds no checks in the map's sense.
"""

## B. Every mention of a CLI, command-line tool, bin script or "command" as a built thing

### (i) Tools the project already has, which agents call

- "CLI tools installed: `gh` at minimum" — `piecing-it-together.html`, Foundation → Permissions and budgets.
- "Hooks make tool use non-optional… CLI tools (`gh`, cloud CLIs) are the most context-efficient way to reach external services." — `orchestrator-review.html`
- "Implemented with the project's test runner, invoked by the single command recorded in the project instruction file." — `orchestration-tooling.md`
- "token usage from the CLI's JSON output" — `run-report-guide.html` (Claude Code's own CLI).
- "Non-interactive runs (`claude -p`) can emit streaming JSON that a small local page or script can render." — `orchestrator-review.html`
- "CLI availability" listed as a *tooling-axis* failure item — `run-log-guide.html` line 45: "Hooks, allowlists, worktree isolation, schema at handoffs, CLI availability, the workflow script's stage boundaries." Note this is availability of third-party CLIs, in a list of harness mechanisms — not a CLI the method builds.
- "CLI arguments" / "CLI shapes" appear twice in `spec-guide.html`, but only as a category of *interface the spec'd feature under construction* might have: "The seams: function signatures, API shapes, file formats, schemas, CLI arguments, events." and "Signatures, schemas, formats, CLI shapes, events. Reuse existing types by name." These are about the product being built by a run, not about the orchestration system.

That is the complete set of `CLI` / `command-line` occurrences across all fifteen source documents. I grepped the raw HTML for `bin/`, `npx`, `package.json`, `Makefile`, `command-line`, `command line`: **zero hits for `bin/`, `npx`, `package.json`, `Makefile`, and zero for "command-line"/"command line" anywhere.** The word "CLI" appears exactly 6 times, all listed above.

### (ii) Scripts the method says to write

- Hook scripts — "Implemented as PreToolUse, PostToolUse and Stop hooks in the project settings, invoking scripts kept in the repository." (`orchestration-tooling.md`)
- Event-log script — "A small script appended to `SubagentStart`, `SubagentStop`, `TaskCreated`, `TaskCompleted`, `PostToolUseFailure`, `PermissionDenied`, `Stop`, `PreCompact`, `WorktreeCreate` and `WorktreeRemove` writes each event, timestamped, to `runs/&lt;id&gt;/events.jsonl`." (`run-report-guide.html`)
- Check wrapper — "The verification commands the spec names run through a wrapper that writes command, exit code and output to `runs/&lt;id&gt;/checks/`. The diff boundary check and the test-file change list are two more commands in the same wrapper. The Stop hook that gates the run is the natural place to call it." (`run-report-guide.html`)
- Diff boundary — "Diff boundary The change touches only the paths the spec allows. A trivial script over `git diff --name-only`, and one of the most effective scope fences available." (`verification-guide.html`); "Did anything outside scope change? Diff-boundary script Deterministic, at gates" (`review-guide.html`)
- End-to-end acceptance script — "Often a small script rather than a test framework: run the thing, poke it, assert." (`verification-guide.html`); example: "`scripts/export-smoke.sh` exports the reference fixture…" (`spec-guide.html`)
- Prompt renderer — "Render the prompt deterministically, with a small skill or script over the two JSON files, rather than having the orchestrator compose it freehand." (`core-stages-4-7.html`); "a brief is rendered from them by a script, never composed freehand by the orchestrator" (`orchestration-principles.md`)
- Report assembler — a **skill**: "Report assembler — reads events, checks, plan, review; renders the report" (`piecing-it-together.html`)
- Stop-hook stall counter — "A tighter ceiling is the hook script counting its own blocks, writing a stalled event on the fourth or fifth and exiting zero…" (`core-stages-4-7.html`)
- The workflow script — "The orchestration is a script, saved and rerun, not a sequence of decisions remembered from last time." (`orchestration-principles.md`); "A run's script is saved and runs as a named command. The same orchestration runs the same way every time it is invoked." (`orchestration-tooling.md`) — this is a Claude Code *dynamic workflow*, "saved under the project's workflows directory and invoked by name", explicitly constrained: "The script itself has no filesystem or shell access."

Every one of these is a **leaf script**: single-purpose, invoked by a hook, a skill or a workflow stage. None is described as a parent that others hang off.

### (iii) Any central runner or command suite

**No. It does not appear anywhere in any of the fifteen sources.**

There is no `bin/`, no named executable, no command suite, no subcommand table, no installer, no "the runner" as an actor. The closest three things, and why none of them is one:

1. "Implemented as a saved prompt or command in the repository, invoked with the spec as its argument." (`orchestration-tooling.md`, Liftoff prompt) — this is a Claude Code slash command / saved prompt file, sitting alongside "saved prompt"; the whole entry describes a *prompt* ("the rich starting prompt handed to the orchestrator at liftoff"), and the worked example in `kickoff-guide.html` is a markdown document (`# Kickoff: parallel feature build`) that the human assembles from a library.
2. "A run's script is saved and runs as a named command." (`orchestration-tooling.md`, Dynamic workflows) — the harness's own workflow feature, invoked through `/workflows`, and expressly denied shell and filesystem access.
3. "the goal command" (`orchestration-tooling.md`) — Claude Code's built-in `/goal`.

All three are Claude Code's own invocation surfaces, which your question excludes.

## C. "Deterministic tools" and "writing tools for agents", as stated

`orchestration-principles.md`, section **Deterministic tools**:

&gt; "An unsupervised agent is only guaranteed to behave when it cannot do otherwise… Every guarantee a run relies on must therefore be enforced by something deterministic, a script or a permission rule that does not consult the agent, and every tool an agent uses must return output terse and unambiguous enough that there is no room for interpretation."

Its four bullets:

&gt; "- Enforce with hooks, not instructions. A check that must run, runs from a hook; a file that must not change is blocked by a rule.
&gt; - Keep the toolset minimal and non-overlapping. Under attended work a wrong tool choice was corrected at the next prompt; in a run it is repeated by every agent that faces the same choice, and nobody is there to notice.
&gt; - Return terse, unambiguous output, paginated or truncated where large, with errors that say what to do next. A worker that misreads a verbose result or an internal error has no one to ask, so the tool has to carry the correction itself.
&gt; - Reach external services through command-line tools rather than raw API calls. Their output is compact and their behaviour is already well understood, which matters most when many agents pay the context cost at once and none can be watched."

Note the fourth bullet's scope: CLI-over-raw-API is about **reaching external services**, i.e. `gh` and cloud CLIs, not about the orchestration system's own shape.

`orchestrator-review.html`, "Tooling → Deterministic tools":

&gt; "Agents do well with tools that give terse, unambiguous output and badly with tools that need interpretation. A test runner that prints one line per failure and exits non-zero keeps an agent focused and accountable; one that prints three screens of noise invites a plausible summary instead of a fix."
&gt; "Hooks make tool use non-optional. Unlike instructions in `CLAUDE.md`, which are advisory, a hook that runs the linter after every edit or blocks writes to a protected directory is deterministic and cannot be forgotten. CLI tools (`gh`, cloud CLIs) are the most context-efficient way to reach external services."

`verification-guide.html`, anti-pattern:

&gt; "The noisy check Pages of output per run. The agent summarises instead of reading and the summary is optimistic. Make checks terse; pipe through a filter if the tool cannot be quiet."

`orchestration-tooling.md`, Test harness, on the single command:

&gt; "- One command runs the whole harness and returns one exit code. A subset runs the checks mapped to one unit.
&gt; - Output is terse enough to be read in an agent's context and unambiguous about which check failed and why.
&gt; - The same command works identically whether an agent, a hook or a human invokes it."

And the simplicity rule, `agentic-principles.md`:

&gt; "- The simplest arrangement that could work is tried first: one agent before several, a prompt before a script."
&gt; "- Choose the simplest arrangement first. One agent before several; a plain prompt before a scripted workflow. Add structure only when the simpler shape has failed."

## E. How state is held during a run

State is distributed: **each file is written by its own producer**, and no document names a single state file that one process maintains.

- Events, by hooks: "Event log — subagent start/stop, task created/completed, tool failures, permission denials, compactions, worktree lifecycle → `events.jsonl`" (`piecing-it-together.html`); "`events.jsonl` recorded by hooks" (folder listing); "A small script appended to `SubagentStart`… writes each event, timestamped, to `runs/&lt;id&gt;/events.jsonl`." (`run-report-guide.html`)
- Plan, by the orchestrator in plan mode: "Produces `runs/&lt;id&gt;/plan.json`" (`core-stages-4-7.html`); "The kickoff must say to write the plan to a file. Plan mode's default output is conversational; the plan is consumed later by dispatch and by the report's ledger, and both need `runs/&lt;id&gt;/plan.json`."
- Plan is references, not copies: "// `plan.json` — one unit; every value is a reference, never a copy"; "Each unit is a pointer into things that already carry the detail, spec entity IDs, interface IDs, check names, paths, and the plan restates none of it."
- **Status is explicitly excluded from the plan**: "Status is not on the plan; that is the report's job." (`core-stages-4-7.html`) — this is the sources' direct answer to the launch.json question: run status is not held in a mutable state file, it is *reconstructed at the end* from events + checks + plan.
- Approval, written by the gate page into the plan: "Approve writes an approval block into the plan (`approved: {at, spec_version, plan_hash}`) so the orchestrator and the assembler can verify they are working from the plan the human saw."
- Human comments, their own file: "Comment writes `comments.json` keyed by unit ID."
- Check results, by the wrapper: "`checks/` command · exit · output, per check"; "run through a wrapper that writes command, exit code and output to `runs/&lt;id&gt;/checks/`."
- Worker results, by the worker: "Return structured results from workers. Each subagent definition ends with an instruction to return a result in a fixed shape (unit, spec refs, artefacts written, status), validated by a schema check at the handoff." (`run-report-guide.html`)
- Workflow stage results, by the runtime: "Dynamic workflow runtimes hold stage results outside the model's context; the script writes them to the run directory as stages complete."
- Blocks, by a hook: "a PostToolUse hook on the subagent tool that reads the returned result, appends a blocked event to `events.jsonl` on a match, and injects a line into the orchestrator's context saying dispatch must halt" (`core-stages-4-7.html`)
- The report is a late join, not a live state: "reads the events file, the checks directory, the reviewer's return and the plan, and renders the report" (`run-report-guide.html`)

The governing principle, from `orchestration-tooling.md`: "Agents communicate through files. There is no shared memory and no reading of another agent's transcript." And on run outputs: "Implemented as a per-run directory in the repository, **written to by hooks, agents and the workflow runtime**" — three writers, no single owner.

**There is no `launch.json`, no run-state file, no session record maintained by one process. The word "launch" does not appear in the sources; the constitution's term is "liftoff", and it names a moment, not a file: "Liftoff is the moment that replacement begins".**

---

## F. How the human interacts during a run

- Three gates only: "the human appears exactly twice" in the core (`core-stages-4-7.html`); across the whole journey, "You 1, 2, 3, G1, G2, G3, 10 the display, then the report" (`piecing-it-together.html` roles table).
- Gate 1 is a **local page**, not a prompt: "A page, not a reading exercise. The mechanical half of the gate runs before the human looks at anything." / "The gate is a local page that opens the run directory, reads `plan.json`… In Chrome the File System Access API lets the page read and write the run directory in place, so there is no export and import step. The same page family, with a different lens, serves the spec freeze before the core and the report after it." (`core-stages-4-7.html`)
- The three human actions at that gate are all file writes, not commands: "Three outcomes, each a file. Approve writes an approval block into the plan… Edit writes a new plan revision… Comment writes `comments.json` keyed by unit ID, and the page renders the comments as a revise-plan prompt to paste into the orchestrator session; it re-plans, the page reloads. Only approve leaves plan mode."
- Plan-mode approval is the phase-advance mechanism: "approving the plan is the act that takes the session out of plan mode, so gate 1 is a switch rather than a convention."
- Editing the plan directly: "Edit the plan directly if needed, then approve. The orchestrator leaves plan mode." (`piecing-it-together.html`); "a plan produced this way can be edited directly before approval" (`planning-guide.html`)
- The kickoff instructs the orchestrator to halt and wait: "HALT — Gate 1: present PLAN.md; wait for approval." / "HALT — Gate 2: present contracts + green/red dry-run; wait." / "HALT — Gate 3: present the evidence display; wait." (`kickoff-guide.html`) — the human's act is a reply in the session, and the run halts on its own.
- What halting is: "An interactive session waits whenever it ends its turn with a question." (`core-stages-4-7.html`)
- Reading is the primary interaction: "Human Read the ledger first, then the open findings, then the verification section's three volunteered-by-nobody lines… Do not read the orchestrator notes first." (`piecing-it-together.html`)
- The display is what lets the human be absent: "A display that shows intentions is a checkpoint tool. A display that shows check results is a verification tool. The second is what allows the human to leave the room." (`verification-guide.html`)
- Hooks handle the involuntary interactions: "a notification hook pings the human at the same time." (`core-stages-4-7.html`)
- Human-only invocation, where it exists, is a **skill**: "Any workflow with side effects outside the repository disables invocation by the model. Only a human can trigger it, by name." (`orchestration-tooling.md`); "Workflows with side effects outside the repository are invoked by a human only" (`orchestration-principles.md`)

**Nowhere do the sources describe the human typing a command to advance a phase.** The advance mechanisms named are: leaving plan mode by approving, writing an approval block from the gate page, replying in the halted session, and editing the plan file. The one place a human types anything is pasting a revise-plan prompt the gate page renders for them — a prompt, into a session, not a command into a shell.

---

## Closing statement

The sources prescribe a tooling shape made entirely of Claude Code harness primitives plus flat files, with no program sitting above them. Every "Implemented as…" line in `orchestration-tooling.md` resolves to one of eight things — a markdown file (spec, CLAUDE.md, plan, kickoff, run log, report), a subagent definition with YAML frontmatter, a SKILL.md, a hook wired in `settings.json`, the project's existing test runner behind one command, a git worktree/branch convention, a dynamic workflow script saved under the workflows directory and invoked by name, or a per-run directory of artefacts written independently by hooks, agents and the workflow runtime. The scripts the method tells you to write are all leaves called by something else: hook scripts, a check wrapper, a diff-boundary one-liner over `git diff --name-only`, an acceptance smoke script, a prompt renderer, a report assembler packaged as a skill. Run state is deliberately not centralised — `plan.json` holds references and no status ("Status is not on the plan; that is the report's job"), `events.jsonl` is appended by hooks, `checks/` is written by the wrapper, and the report is a late join of all of them — and the human's interface is a local HTML gate page with File System Access plus a halted session, never a shell. The only CLIs the sources ever name are `gh` and cloud CLIs, as the context-efficient way for agents to reach *external services*, and Claude Code's own `claude -p`, `/goal` and `/workflows`. **A central command-line runner for the method itself appears nowhere in any of the fifteen documents — no `bin/`, no command suite, no named executable, and no folder slot for one in the map page's layout. The `fc` CLI is the builder's decision, not a prescription of the sources**; if anything the sources push the other way, with `agentic-principles.md`'s "one agent before several, a prompt before a script" and the map page's harness/memory split that leaves no room for a third top-level thing.</result>

[ASSISTANT 💬]
The sources explorer confirms your read, and sharply.

- **No runner anywhere.** Across the three constitution documents and twelve guides, the word CLI appears six times, every one about tools the project already has or Claude Code's own commands. Zero mentions of a bin directory, a command suite or a named executable. The map page's folder listing has hooks, skills, agents, templates, specs, runs and the log. No slot for a third thing.
- **Every script the method asks for is a leaf.** Hook scripts, a check wrapper, a diff-boundary one-liner, a smoke script, a prompt renderer, a report assembler packaged as a skill. Each is called by a hook, a skill or a workflow stage. None is a parent that others hang off.
- **State is deliberately not centralised.** Events written by hooks, the plan written by the orchestrator with references and no status, checks written by the wrapper, returns written by workers, the report a late join of all of them. The core-stages page says it directly: status is not on the plan, that is the report's job. There is no run-state file maintained by one process, and the word launch does not appear in the sources at all. The constitution's word is liftoff, and it names a moment.
- **The human never types a command to advance anything.** The named mechanisms are leaving plan mode by approving, a gate page writing an approval block into the plan, replying in a halted session, and editing the plan file. The one thing a human types is a revise-plan prompt the gate page renders for them.
- **The principles lean against it.** Keep the toolset minimal and non-overlapping. One agent before several, a prompt before a script. The CLI-over-API bullet is about reaching external services.

So the shape the sources prescribe is harness primitives plus flat files, with a page for the human. The built system inverted that: a runner that owns a state file the human advances by command, with hooks that read that file to know what to enforce. The other two explorers will tell us how deep the inversion goes and where the choice was made.

**Introduced, not argued.** The runner appears in the document's own preamble as an already-settled part of the contract (line 3): the document "fixes the directory map, file ownership, **CLI surface**, file formats, hook behaviour, crew roster, and the run journey."

**Section 6, "The `fc` CLI"** (line 189) is the interface statement, not a rationale:

&gt; Entry `flightcrew/bin/fc &lt;command&gt; [sub] [args] [--launch &lt;name&gt;] [--json]`. One line on success except commands whose purpose is a document or listing (`launch status`, `events summary`, `runlog show`, `worker render`, `critic render`, `verifier render`, `distribute` without `--apply`, `validate all`, `doctor`). Exit `0 | 1 | 2`.

**The only recorded justification in the design document** is one bullet in §11 "Decisions already made (do not reopen)" (line 284):

&gt; - Single `fc` entry with per-command modules, invoked by path; no install.

**What it replaces / what the runner does instead of other mechanisms.** The design records the division of labour rather than a comparison. Hooks are *not* an alternative to the runner — they are a parallel enforcement layer that calls back into it: hooks "run in place from `flightcrew/hooks/`" (line 19), and the SessionEnd hook does "best-effort `fc evidence` and `fc report`" (line 257). Workflow scripts are a third layer, explicitly forbidden from doing the runner's work (line 303): "Scripts only dispatch agents and return payloads … no file or shell access. … After a workflow completes, the orchestrator persists every payload with `fc return`." And the orchestrator agent is given no write tools at all (line 294):

&gt; - The orchestrator holds no Write or Edit; it writes through `fc plan write`, `fc launch note`, `fc return`.

Also (line 295): "No scribe role; report assembly is a command and a hook."

**Alternatives considered: none are recorded.** Grepping the design and the spec for `alternative`, `considered`, `rejected`, `instead of`, `skill` returns nothing about the runner choice. The word "skill" appears in design.md only once, in the forbidden-paths line (line 9), referring to the dev-workspace skill as an out-of-scope directory. The CLI decision is filed under "do not reopen" without a stated comparison.

**Section 0 (byte-unchanged files, line 15):**

&gt; Byte-unchanged in this build: `manuals/spec/**`, `manuals/testing/**`, `manuals/versioning/**`, `manuals/rubrics/**`, `testbench/benches/rubrics/**`, `flightcrew/schemas/spec.schema.json`, `flightcrew/templates/spec.template.json`, `flightcrew/crew/spec-judge.md`, `flightcrew/crew/spec-attacker.md`. `flightcrew/crew/spec-builder.md` changes on exactly the lines section 7.1 names.

**What pre-existed.** The design treats the validators and the worker renderer as pre-existing but *not* protected — they are absorbed into the new structure. §11 (line 288) lists only the spec-stage assets as preserved: "The existing spec-stage agents, spec schema and template, rubric and bench, and existing manuals are kept byte-unchanged except the spec-builder lines in 7.1; their historical `dev/` paths are recorded as such in `manuals/README.md`." The old validator suite is explicitly relocated (§9 UT targets, line 265): "including moving `testbench/benches/validator-suite/` to `testbench/suites/validate-spec/` with cases and goldens kept and the runner's validator path fixed". Line 314 records why one check is exempt from the "everything fails at baseline" rule: "T23 (`suites/run-all`) is a world-state check whose baseline passes before implementation, because the runner is a targets-stage deliverable" — this is the *suite* runner, not `fc`.

## 2. `spec.v1.json` — I1 and the nodes that fix the runner

**I1** is the runner's existence, name, path, resolution order and exit codes:

&gt; `flightdeck/flightcrew/bin/fc &lt;command&gt; [sub] [args] [--launch &lt;name&gt;] [--json]; exit 0 | 1 | 2. fc resolves its assets from its own location and the launch root as $FLIGHTCREW_ROOT, else $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR, else the git toplevel of cwd, else the repository containing fc; launches live at &lt;root&gt;/flightdeck/launch/. Commands and flags: launch new &lt;spec-path&gt; … launch activate &lt;N&gt; [--allow-draft]; launch status; launch phase &lt;p&gt; [--force]; launch gate &lt;G1|G2|G3&gt; &lt;approve|exit&gt; …; launch end &lt;accepted|accepted-with-reservations|abandoned|partial&gt; …`

**Scope nodes that fix it:**

- **SC1**: "flightdeck/flightcrew/: **the fc command-line runner and its command modules**, the universal check harnesses (libraries, validators, gates), the crew definitions, the hook scripts and settings fragment, the schemas, the templates and kickoff library, the dynamic workflow scripts, and MANIFEST.txt."
- **SC2**: "… this build's own launch folder flightcrew-buildout **produced by the fc commands as the first run**."
- **SC8** (an out-of-scope node): "Installing anything: no global commands, no package.json, no symlinks into the home directory; **fc is invoked by path**."
- **SC5**: "… fc distribute writes into a target directory only when a human passes --apply."

**The justification node, D2** — the single sentence in the whole spec that says *why* a CLI:

&gt; **D2**: One fc entry point with a module per command, invoked by path, **because a single user needs one surface to remember and nothing to install**.

Supporting: **D1**: "Node ES modules with zero dependencies and no package.json, because the harness must run identically on any machine with Node 22 and git; hooks are Node too so one test harness covers scripts and hooks." **D15**: "The orchestrator holds no Write or Edit tool and writes only through fc plan write, fc launch note and fc return, because the agents guide makes the orchestrator touch nothing." **D16**: "There is no scribe role: report and evidence assembly are commands and a SessionEnd hook, because a second way to produce the same file is drift."

**The output-shape and exit-code constraint, C3** (the node later violated — see §3):

&gt; **C3**: Every script exits 0 on success, 1 on a usage or environment error, and 2 on a failed check or a blocking decision; **on success it prints at most one line**, except commands whose purpose is a document or listing (launch status, events summary, runlog show, worker render, critic render, verifier render, distribute without --apply, validate all, doctor, and every suite run.mjs), and except when --json is passed.

Also **C2**: "No script or hook writes outside the four in-scope directories, os.tmpdir(), and (for fc distribute --apply only) the target directory given on the command line."

**ACC** names the runner twice: "launch/flightcrew-buildout/ holds launch.json, kickoff.md, plan.json, plan.md, evidence/summary.json, report.md and evidence.html **produced by fc** … **fc locked** reports no change under the paths the buildout tests map locks."

**Counts.** The spec has 54 behaviours and 24 edges (78 B/E total).

| | B (54) | E (24) | B+E |
|---|---|---|---|
| Text begins `fc …` — the node *is* a runner command's behaviour | **28** (B2, B3, B12, B14–B17, B19–B21, B27–B30, B32, B35, B36, B41, B43–B51, B54) | **12** (E7, E10–E12, E15, E17–E20, E22–E24) | **40** |
| Mentions `fc` but the subject is another actor (hook, validator, journey, report) | 9 (B1, B13, B18, B31, B34, B37, B40, B42, B52) | 8 (E1–E4, E6, E8, E13, E21) | 17 |
| No mention of `fc` — hooks, validators, suites, orchestration | 17 (B4–B11, B22–B26, B33, B38, B39, B53) | 4 (E5, E9, E14, E16) | 21 |

So **57 of 78 B/E nodes (73%) name `fc`**, and 40 are direct statements about a runner command. Of 14 interfaces, **I1 is the runner itself**; I14 embeds it in the permission fragment ("`Bash(node flightdeck/flightcrew/bin/fc *)`, `Bash(flightdeck/flightcrew/bin/fc *)`, `Bash(./flightdeck/flightcrew/bin/fc *)`" — three invocation forms because nothing is installed). Of 9 constraints, **C3 and C2** bind the runner's output and write surface. Of 18 decisions, **D2** is the runner's charter; D1, D15, D16 support it. Of 9 scope nodes, SC1, SC2, SC5 and SC8 name it.

The distribution is itself the answer to "how central": the runner is not one component among many, it is the surface almost every provable behaviour is expressed through.

**Blast radius.** Pass 1, F10, observation, `bin/cmd/distribute.mjs:105`, resolved: "fc distribute --apply without --target defaults to &lt;root&gt;/.claude, whereas C2 permits writes under --apply only into 'the target directory given on the command line' and SC5 lists .claude/ as never written."

**The C3 conflict / stall message do not appear as review findings** — they were carried by the human/orchestrator into the run log (see §4). No finding in either pass mentions the size of the runner or its line count.

## 6. Pre-build state

`flightdeck/STRUCTURE.md` does not exist at `078c446` (`fatal: path 'flightdeck/STRUCTURE.md' does not exist in '078c446'`). On `main` it does. The tree block (line 26) shows `bin/` already reserved for exactly this purpose:

&gt; ```
&gt; ├── flightcrew/                        orchestration — orchestrated agentic building
&gt; │   ├── bin/                           runners — runnable scripts needed for every launch
&gt; │   │   └── worker/
&gt; ```

`git show main:flightdeck/flightcrew/bin/runners.keep` is one line:

&gt; ```
&gt; Runnable scripts needed for every launch.
&gt; ```

STRUCTURE.md explains what these files are (lines 62–64):

&gt; Each folder that needs describing holds a `&lt;task&gt;.keep` file — `archive.keep`, `orchestration.keep`, **`runners.keep`**, `checks.keep`, `agents.keep`, `workspace.keep`, `runs.keep`, `documentation.keep`, `ideas.keep`, `visuals.keep`, `tests.keep`. The filename names the default task the folder serves, and the body describes it in a line or two.
&gt; Unlike a conventional `.keep`, these are not disposable markers for an empty directory. They persist alongside real contents … Read them first when working in an unfamiliar folder…

`git ls-tree -r main flightdeck/flightcrew/` shows `bin/` held exactly two entries before the build:

- `flightdeck/flightcrew/bin/runners.keep`
- `flightdeck/flightcrew/bin/worker/render-worker-prompt.mjs`

alongside the pre-existing validators (`checks/spec-readiness-lint.mjs`, `checks/validators/{schema-lib,validate-all,validate-md,validate-plan,validate-spec,validate-tests-map}.mjs`) and schemas (`spec`, `plan`, `tests-map`). Both `bin/` files arrived in the same commit, `a9bd004 Add validators, worker renderer, docspecs and worker template`.

**So the scaffold anticipated a runner *directory* — "runners — runnable scripts needed for every launch" — but not a single-entry command suite.** What pre-existed was one loose script per job (`render-worker-prompt.mjs`, six validators), each invoked directly. The v1 build's move was to keep the directory's stated purpose and collapse the loose scripts behind one entry: `fc.mjs` plus 19 `cmd/*.mjs` modules, with the validators retained as independently runnable programs (design line 311) and `bin/worker/` surviving as an internal library (`bin/worker/render.mjs`, cited in pass-2 F10).

[ASSISTANT 💬]
The rationale explorer is back, and the provenance is now exact.

- **The runner was never proposed, only assumed.** The transcript has no message where the agent weighs a CLI against hooks or skills. By the time the word is spoken in prose, the spec is frozen and 29 suites are locked. The design contract introduces it in its preamble as a settled part of the deal and files it under decisions not to reopen, with one bullet and no alternatives recorded.
- **The only justification is one sentence in the spec.** Decision D2: one entry point with a module per command, because a single user needs one surface to remember and nothing to install. That is the whole argument.
- **The scaffold invited a directory, not a suite.** Before the build, the bin folder held a keep file reading "runnable scripts needed for every launch" and one loose script. The build kept the directory's purpose and collapsed everything behind one entry.
- **The spec is mostly about the runner.** Of 78 behaviours and edges, 57 name fc and 40 are direct statements about a runner command. The interface node I1 is the runner itself. The orchestrator was given no write tools and writes only through fc, and the scribe role was removed because report assembly is a command.
- **The critics never questioned it.** Both review passes fault the runner's fidelity to its own spec, one-line output violations, a render command that refuses the phase the kickoff dispatches in, a flag silently discarded, an error defaulted away. No finding asks whether a CLI should exist, what it should be named, or how large it is. The name flowed through the critique pass unchallenged.
- **Your objection is on record and was deferred.** You asked what fc was, then asked for it to be called flightcrew. The agent admitted the name was its own choice that nothing you said asked for, quoted 900 occurrences, and offered a rename after landing. You said finish the run. The rename never happened.

One more thing worth holding. The run log's own "kept" line credits the runner with the thing the build was proudest of: the run's record produced by the commands, not by hand. The sources get that same property from hooks writing events, a wrapper writing checks and an assembler joining them. So the benefit the runner is credited with is one the prescribed shape already delivers without a runner.

`launch status`, `check`, `verify`, `budget`, `boundary`, `locked`, `worker`, `return`, `plan`, `report`, `evidence` never write launch.json.

### events.jsonl
Written through `launch-lib.appendEvent` (`checks/lib/launch-lib.mjs:203-221`), which fills `ts`, `launch`, `phase` (read out of launch.json), `source:'fc'`, `detail:{}`. Callers:
- `cmd/launch.mjs:577` (`phase`), `:641` (`gate`), `:643` (`phase` on gate-move), `:664` (`escalation`), `:832` (`launch_end`)
- `cmd/budget.mjs:142` (`trigger` when a ceiling is passed)
- `cmd/events.mjs:88, :101` (`append`, `usage`)
- `cmd/worker.mjs:186` (`unit_merged`)
- `bin/worker/return.mjs:108` (`return`)
- `hooks/lib.mjs:8` imports the same function — hooks write with `source: hook`, bypassing fc.

### escalation.json
`launch-lib.mjs:317-340` — `writeEscalation` / `readEscalation` / `clearEscalation`. Written only by `fc launch escalate` (`launch.mjs:663`); cleared by `fc launch phase` (`:578`), `fc launch gate` (`:645`), `fc launch end` (`:833`). Read by `hooks/stop-gate.mjs` (its presence releases the gate) and `hooks/lib.mjs:8`.

### Evidence files
`evidence/T&lt;n&gt;.json` one per check (`cmd/check.mjs`), `evidence/summary.json`, `evidence/boundary.json` (`cmd/boundary.mjs`), `evidence/locked.json` (`cmd/locked.mjs:17-21, :33`), `evidence/budget.json` (`cmd/budget.mjs`). `evidence.html` is re-rendered best-effort by nearly every mutating command via `bestEffortRender` (`launch-lib.mjs:352-372`), which swallows all errors and never changes an exit code.

### FLIGHTCREW_LAUNCH
- Set as output: `fc launch new` prints `export FLIGHTCREW_LAUNCH=&lt;name&gt;` as its one success line (`launch.mjs:310`).
- Consumed by `resolveLaunch` (`launch-lib.mjs:158-183`): a non-empty value names one launch whatever its status; the literal `none` means "no launch".
- `--launch &lt;name&gt;` is implemented by writing into a copied env (`fc.mjs:322`), so the flag and the variable are the same mechanism.
- Propagated to children by `childEnv` (`fc.mjs:174-183`), which also sets `FLIGHTCREW_ROOT`.

### Active-launch resolution (`checks/lib/launch-lib.mjs`)
Root: `FLIGHTCREW_ROOT` → `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` → git toplevel of cwd → the repository holding the script (`ROOT_SOURCES`, `:31`); "The first source that names a root is final; a root without flightdeck/launch/ is NoRoot, never a reason to fall through" (`:14-16`, enforced `:96-110`).
Launch: `FLIGHTCREW_LAUNCH`, else the unique `launch.json` with `status: 'active'` (`:158-183`). `launchesIn` scans only subdirectories carrying `launch.json`, skipping `specs` (`:135-155`). Errors: `NoRoot, NoLaunch, TwoActive, MissingLaunch, Unreadable`.
Commands that skip resolution: `WITHOUT_LAUNCH = {validate, lint, distribute, doctor}` (`fc.mjs:32`), plus per-module overrides — `launch new|activate` (`launch.mjs:39`), `check --baseline` (`check.mjs:29`), `runlog show` (`runlog.mjs:20`).

### Is launch.json the single source of run state?
Largely yes, with three carve-outs: (a) `events.jsonl` is an independent append-only log — the fired-trigger state (`fired()`, `launch-lib.mjs:265-273`), the budget counters and the stop-block counts live there, not in launch.json; (b) `escalation.json` is a separate presence-flag file; (c) `review/resolutions.json` overrides finding state in the pass files (`launch.mjs:~740`).

### What breaks if launch.json is hand-edited or absent
- **Absent / unparsable:** `readLaunch` throws `LaunchError('Unreadable')` (`launch-lib.mjs:118-131`); `resolveLaunch` rethrows it; `fc.mjs:344-351` turns it into exit 1 for every launch-needing command. `launchesIn` records `json:null, error` and skips the folder as a candidate. Hooks: the guards print an `ask` decision, `event-log` and `session-end` stay silent (`hooks/README.md`, "The no-op rule").
- **Hand-edited:** nothing detects it at write time; `fc validate launch` (`checks/validators/validate-launch.mjs`, 209 lines) is the only checker and must be run deliberately. Because `writeLaunch` rewrites the whole object read at command start, an edit made between two fc commands survives only until the next mutating command reads-and-rewrites. Derived artefacts (`kickoff.md`, `plan.md`, `evidence.html`, `report.md`) are re-rendered and any hand edit to them is overwritten — stated as policy in `templates/constitution-fragment.md:7` and `cmd/plan.mjs:5` ("plan.json is the source of truth and plan.md is rendered from it, never hand-edited (spec D5)").
- **Two active launches:** every launch-needing command exits 1 (`fc.mjs:220-222`) and `fc launch activate` refuses (`launch.mjs:325-328`).

- `flightdeck/flightcrew/workflows/{fc-explore,fc-implement,fc-review}.js` — **zero fc invocations.** Every mention of fc is in a header comment or an inlined schema `description` (`fc-explore.js:2`, `fc-implement.js:2, :17`, `fc-review.js:2, :18, :131`). See §10.

They name fc by absolute path in agent briefs: `flightcrew-build.js:63` (gates call `node ${FD}/flightcrew/bin/fc.mjs check T1`), `:64` (unit U2a owns `bin/fc`, `bin/fc.mjs`, `bin/cmd/{launch,events,budget,runlog,plan,validate,lint}.mjs`), `:72` (session-end best-effort), `:119` (verifier runs `fc doctor` and `fc distribute`), `flightcrew-targets.js:23` (defines constants `FC = FD + '/flightcrew/bin/fc'`, `FC_MJS`), `:68` ("fc will fail because bin/fc is absent: it must return a result, not throw").

### (d) Kickoff templates — `templates/kickoff/`
`base.md` (27 ln, `version: 3`) is the densest fc consumer in the system: its 7-step **Conduct** section names `fc launch status, fc return explorer, fc plan write, fc launch gate G1 approve|exit, fc worker render, fc return worker, fc worker merge, fc launch gate G2, fc launch phase verify, fc verify, fc verifier render, fc return verifier, fc launch phase review, fc critic render, fc return critic, fc return critic --resolve, fc launch phase report, fc launch end`, plus `fc launch escalate` in **Escalate**, `fc locked`/`fc boundary` in **Never**, and `fc return`/`fc worker merge` in **Outputs**.
`shape-session.md` names `fc worker render, fc return, fc events summary, fc launch escalate halt`. `shape-workflow.md` names `fc distribute --apply, fc worker render, fc critic render, fc return, fc worker merge, fc launch escalate`. `task-feature.md` names `fc launch escalate spec-gap`.

## 4. HUMAN COMMANDS

From `manuals/launch/launch-anatomy.md:93-102` (commands-by-phase, human column) and `manuals/orchestration/journey.md:18-31`, in run order:

| Phase | Command | Advances state? |
|---|---|---|
| before | `fc distribute --apply --target .claude` | installs (writes `.claude`, not run state) |
| before | `fc lint spec &lt;path&gt; --repo $REPO` | read |
| before | `fc validate spec &lt;path&gt; --for-freeze` | read |
| targets | `fc launch new &lt;spec&gt; [--name] [--kickoff] [--branch]` | **advance** (creates launch.json, base_commit, kickoff) |
| targets | `fc launch activate &lt;L&gt; [--allow-draft]` | **advance** (`status: active`) |
| targets | `fc check all --baseline &lt;map&gt;` | writes the draft map's `baseline.observed`; no launch state |
| targets | `fc launch pin tests-map &lt;map&gt;` | **advance** (`tests_map`, `paths`, `lock_commit`, kickoff re-render) |
| targets | `fc launch phase plan` | **advance** (`phase`) |
| plan | `fc plan render` (after editing plan.json) | renders plan.md |
| G1 | `fc launch gate G1 approve` \| `exit` | **advance** (`gates.G1`, phase → contracts) |
| G2 | `fc launch gate G2 approve` \| `exit` | **advance** (`gates.G2`, phase → implement) |
| implement | `fc launch status` | read |
| report/G3 | `fc launch end &lt;accepted\|accepted-with-reservations\|abandoned\|partial&gt; [--at] [--units]` | **advance** (`outcome, status, ended, phase:'ended'`; also renders report + evidence + RUNLOG stub) |
| after | `fc launch land --commit &lt;sha&gt; --pr &lt;url&gt;` | **advance** (`landed`) |
| after | `fc runlog show --spec S` | read |
| any | `fc launch status`, `fc events summary`, `fc report`, `fc evidence`, `fc budget`, `fc validate all`, `fc doctor` | read (7 forms) |

**Counts:** 15 commands in the ordered spine (3 pre-launch + 5 targets + 1 plan + 2 gates + 1 status + 1 end + 2 after), plus 7 read-any commands. **8 advance state** (`launch new, launch activate, launch pin tests-map, launch phase plan, launch gate G1, launch gate G2, launch end, launch land`) — 7 of the 8 are `fc launch` sub-commands. The remaining ~14 read or render.

Note the phase-move asymmetry: `launch-anatomy.md:98-100` puts `fc launch phase verify`, `fc launch phase review` and `fc launch phase report` in the **agent** column, while `journey.md:30, :46` requires a human decision (G3) between `fc launch phase report` and `fc launch end`.

Refusal preconditions the human meets (`launch-anatomy.md:115-119`): `phase plan` refused until pins frozen/`allow_draft` + baseline agrees + launch and kickoff validate; `phase review` and `critic render` refused while `summary.json` is older than HEAD; `launch end` (accepted family) refused unless `summary.json.commit == HEAD` and the tree is clean; `launch land` refused unless evidence at the landing commit has zero fail/error.

## 5. COUPLING

### Cannot work without fc
- **The evidence page** — `bin/cmd/evidence.mjs` is the only renderer; `launch-lib.bestEffortRender` reaches it by relative URL `../../bin/cmd/evidence.mjs` (`launch-lib.mjs:362`) and returns `false` if the file is absent.
- **The run report** — `bin/cmd/report.mjs`; `journey.md:87`: "`fc launch end`, `fc report`, `fc evidence` and the SessionEnd hook assemble the report and the evidence page; no agent writes either."
- **The run-log stub** — `writeStub` inside `cmd/runlog.mjs`, called from `launch end` (`launch.mjs:~845`).
- **Kickoff render** — `renderKickoff`/`writeKickoff` in `cmd/launch.mjs`; `templates/kickoff/README.md:7`: "`fc launch new` and `fc launch kickoff` render `flightdeck/launch/&lt;L&gt;/kickoff.md`".
- **Worker/critic/verifier dispatch render** — `bin/worker/render.mjs` (397 ln), reached only through `cmd/worker.mjs`, `cmd/critic.mjs`, `cmd/verifier.mjs`.
- **The stop gate** — via the gate modules, which spawn `fc.mjs check`.
- **Storing any agent return** — `bin/worker/return.mjs` + `cmd/return.mjs` are the only writers of `returns/*.json` and `review/pass-*.json`.
- **Every phase/gate/pin/end transition** — no other module calls `writeLaunch`.

### Does not go through fc
- **`lock-guard`, `boundary-guard`, `event-log`, `structural-check`** — pure hooks reading `launch.json` and `events.jsonl` through `checks/lib/launch-lib.mjs` and `glob-lib.mjs`. They work on a checkout with `bin/` deleted.
- **The validators** — `checks/validators/*.mjs` are programs in their own right; `cmd/validate.mjs:5-7` says fc "adds nothing to their output: it resolves the document, hands the remaining arguments through unchanged, and returns their exit code". Same for `cmd/lint.mjs:5-6`. They can be, and in the testbench are, run directly.
- **`structural-gate.mjs`** — runs the launch's structural command through `/bin/sh -c` with no fc reference (unlike the other two gates).
- **The testbench** — `run-all.mjs` and 8 of 30 suites never spawn fc.
- **The workflow scripts** — zero fc calls by construction (§10).
- **`hooks/settings.fragment.json`** — a static file; fc only prints it (`distribute`).
- **`git`** — all git work goes through `checks/lib/git-lib.mjs` (259 ln), importable without fc.

## 8. NAME

- **`design.md:19`** introduces it without argument: "`flightcrew/` — … Global assets used by every launch: the `fc` runner and its command modules (`bin/`)". No justification passage exists; the abbreviation is asserted.
- **`design.md:31-34`** fixes the files: "`fc` bash shim: exec node `"$(dirname "$0")/fc.mjs"` `"$@"`" and "`fc.mjs` entry; parses `--launch/--json`; imports `cmd/&lt;command&gt;.mjs` exporting `run(args, ctx)` and `help`".
- **Spec `I1` (`launch/specs/flightcrew-v1/spec.v1.json:118-125`)** is the entry that fixes the name: `"id": "I1", "status": "ok", "name": "fc"`, whose `text` is the entire CLI surface — `flightdeck/flightcrew/bin/fc &lt;command&gt; [sub] [args] [--launch &lt;name&gt;] [--json]; exit 0 | 1 | 2` followed by every command and flag. It also fixes the root resolution order and the statement "launches live at `&lt;root&gt;/flightdeck/launch/`".
- Repeatedly stated as **not a PATH command**: `hooks/README.md:5` ("nothing installs it on PATH"), `workflows/README.md:5`, `templates/kickoff/README.md:7`, `templates/constitution-fragment.md:4` ("`fc` below is shorthand for that path, not a command on PATH"), `crew/spec-builder.md:17`, `crew/test-builder.md:17`, `testbench/README.md`. The only sanctioned shorthand is a per-shell alias: `launch-anatomy.md:3` — "Optional, per shell, not an install: `alias fc="$PWD/flightdeck/flightcrew/bin/fc"`".
- **Occurrences of the token `fc`** (`git grep -c "\bfc\b"`, lines containing it): **1,660 lines across 164 files** under `flightdeck/`. By directory: `testbench/` 458 · `flightcrew/` 362 · `manuals/` 274 · `launch/specs/` 151; the balance is in the two committed launch folders (`evidence.html`, pinned specs, returns).
- Lines matching the literal `flightdeck/flightcrew/bin/fc`: 48 files, led by `manuals/harness/permissions.md` (4), `crew/{verifier,test-builder,spec-builder}.md` (3 each), `templates/constitution-fragment.md` (3), `hooks/settings.fragment.json` (3).

## 9. OUTPUT SHAPE

`checks/lib/output.mjs` (112 ln) is "the one place every fc command, validator, gate and hook writes a line" (`:1`). It exports `EXIT`, `setJson`/`isJson`, `print`, `ok`, `warn`, `errorLine`/`errorLines`, `fail`, `json`, `exitOk`/`exitUsage`/`exitBlocked`/`exitWith`.

- **Success:** `ok(line)` — one stdout line, silent in JSON mode (`:57-62`).
- **Failure:** `fail(text)` — lines on **stderr, in every mode**, including JSON mode (`:79-83`).
- **Warnings:** `warn` prints `warn:  &lt;message&gt;` with two spaces, silent in JSON (`:65-69`).
- **Validator errors:** `errorLine(message, rule)` → `error: &lt;message&gt; — [&lt;rule&gt;]` per design 5.12 (`:72-74`).
- **JSON mode:** `--json` sets a module-global; `ok` and `warn` fall silent and the command prints one document with `json()` (`:19-28`, `:86-88`).
- **Write mechanism:** every write goes through a synchronous `writeAll` on the raw fd, retrying `EAGAIN` and swallowing `EPIPE` — "a pipe on macOS can be asynchronous, and a process that calls `process.exit` straight after `console.log` can lose the line" (`:8-9`, `:32-46`).

**Designed for an agent.** Evidence: the success line is one line by rule (`design.md:12`); every failure line is a next action, not a diagnosis — `fc.mjs:263` "two launches are active: &lt;names&gt;; pass --launch &lt;name&gt; or set FLIGHTCREW_LAUNCH"; `launch.mjs:648` `gate &lt;id&gt; exited; now run: fc launch end abandoned --at &lt;id&gt;`; `lock-guard.mjs:12` "…is locked for launch &lt;L&gt;; report a wrong or unsatisfiable check instead of editing it"; `launch.mjs:~810` "no evidence: evidence/summary.json is absent, HEAD is &lt;sha&gt;; run fc verify". Exit codes are the primary channel and `--json` gives a machine-readable body for `check`, `verify`, `boundary`, `locked`, `budget`, `events`, `return`.

**Commands with long output:** `fc worker render` prints the entire sealed dispatch prompt (`worker.mjs:101`); `fc launch status` prints ≈8+ lines including a counts-and-ceilings block (`launch.mjs:540-547`); `fc launch pin tests-map` prints one `Bash(&lt;command&gt;)` line per check in the map (`:580-582`); `fc distribute` prints the full copy plan and the settings fragment (14 `print` sites); `fc doctor` prints one line per condition; `fc events summary` prints a by-event/by-agent listing; `fc runlog show` prints the whole log; `fc launch end` prints the cleanup lines plus the report path. `fc evidence` and `fc report` write files and print one line — the long artefact is the file, not the stream.

---

## 10. WORKFLOW TENSION

**The three workflow scripts call fc zero times.** `fc-explore.js` (165 ln), `fc-implement.js` (278 ln), `fc-review.js` (497 ln) contain no `spawn`, no `Bash`, no shell, no file read; every occurrence of the token `fc` inside them is in a header comment (`fc-explore.js:2`, `fc-implement.js:2`, `fc-review.js:2`) or inside an inlined JSON schema `description` string (`fc-implement.js:17`, `fc-review.js:18, :131`).

`workflows/README.md` states the constraint and the resolution verbatim:

&gt; "A script here only dispatches agents and returns payloads. It reads no file, runs no command, touches no git state and stamps no time: `Date.now()`, `new Date()` and `Math.random()` are unavailable in the workflow runtime, so a timestamp arrives through `args`. **After a workflow completes, the orchestrator writes each returned payload to a file and stores it with the `fc return` command for its kind — `fc return worker &lt;file&gt; --unit &lt;id&gt;`, `fc return critic &lt;file&gt; --pass &lt;n&gt;`, `fc return verifier &lt;file&gt; --pass &lt;n&gt;`, `fc return explorer &lt;file&gt; --id X&lt;n&gt;` — then lands each green unit with `fc worker merge &lt;unit&gt;` in wave order** — nothing a script returns is stored until the orchestrator stores it, and nothing a script did counts as evidence until a check has run."

The kickoff part states the same division:

&gt; `templates/kickoff/shape-workflow.md`: "The orchestrator session keeps the three gates, every fc command and every stored return; only the dispatch mechanism moves into the script. … The scripts replace only the dispatching in conduct steps 1, 4 and 6; every fc command in those steps stays with the orchestrator, and after a workflow completes the orchestrator persists every payload with `fc return` and lands units with `fc worker merge`."
&gt; And on display: "while a script runs, its phase lines in the `/workflows` view are the display and never evidence; progress is the returns stored with `fc return` and the evidence page once the workflow completes."

**So: fc state is not updated during a workflow-shaped run.** It is updated (a) by the *agents the workflow spawns*, which are real Claude Code sessions with Bash and which run `fc check` in their own worktrees (`crew/implementer.md:22`, `templates/worker-dispatch.template.md:27`); (b) by the *hooks* firing inside those spawned sessions, which append to `events.jsonl` directly through `launch-lib`; and (c) by the orchestrator session, after the script returns, running `fc return` / `fc worker merge` / `fc launch escalate` on the returned payloads.

Two consequences the files record: `fc worker render &lt;unit&gt;` must be run **and its output committed** before `/fc-implement` is invoked, "because a subagent worktree branches from HEAD and an uncommitted launch-folder file is invisible to the worker" (`workflows/README.md`, fc-implement section; repeated in `shape-workflow.md`); and gates "are never inside a script — the script ends and the session halts at the gate" (`shape-workflow.md`).

---

## Factual tensions observed

1. **The one-line rule versus the command set.** `design.md:12` states "Success prints one line", and `output.mjs:57-62` implements `ok()` to that rule — but 8 commands print multi-line success output through `print()`: `distribute` (14 sites, 0 `ok`), `launch status`/`pin`/`gate exit`/`end` (16 `print` sites in `launch.mjs`), `doctor` (3, 0 `ok`), `events summary` (8), `runlog show`/`stub` (4), `worker render` (whole prompt). `cmd/events.mjs:5-6` concedes the exception in prose ("The summary is a listing, so it prints more than one line") rather than the rule being amended.

2. **The workflow scripts are named `fc-*` but cannot call fc.** `workflows/fc-{explore,implement,review}.js` carry the runner's name while the runtime forbids reading a file, running a command or stamping a time (`workflows/README.md`). During a `shape-workflow` wave, `launch.json`, `events.jsonl` and `evidence.html` receive no fc write at all; the state catch-up is deferred to the orchestrator afterwards.

3. **"The evidence page is never behind the state" versus best-effort rendering.** `cmd/launch.mjs:6-7` states every state change "re-renders the evidence page best-effort so the page is never behind the state", but `bestEffortRender` (`launch-lib.mjs:352-372`) catches every error, returns `false`, and "never changes a caller's exit code" — a failed render is silent, so the page can be behind the state with no signal.

4. **Two different strings for the same TwoActive condition.** `launch-lib.mjs:177` throws `` `two or more launches are active: ${names}` `` while `fc.mjs:262` rewrites it as `` `two launches are active: ${names}; pass --launch &lt;name&gt; or set FLIGHTCREW_LAUNCH` ``. A caller importing the library (a hook, a gate) sees a different message than a caller of fc.

5. **`fc doctor`'s exit code for ambiguous launches is contested inside the testbench itself.** `suites/bin-doctor/run.mjs:3-4`: "One reading is assumed. B30 makes 'at most one launch is active' one of doctor's own conditions, and a failed condition is exit 2 (C3); the exit 1 that two active…". Two spec nodes point at different codes for one situation and the suite picks a side.

6. **The `node`-on-PATH hole the runner warns about applies to the runner.** `hooks/README.md` Troubleshooting puts "`node: command not found`" first and says Claude Code gives hooks a minimal PATH, prescribing an absolute interpreter path, which `fc distribute --apply` substitutes into the fragment. But `bin/fc` itself is `exec node …` with a bare `node` (`bin/fc:4`), and `settings.fragment.json:69-71` allows `Bash(flightdeck/flightcrew/bin/fc *)` and `Bash(./flightdeck/flightcrew/bin/fc *)` — the shim forms with the same dependency.

7. **`fc distribute` never distributes fc.** It copies "the crew definitions and the workflow scripts, never a hook" (`cmd/distribute.mjs:1`), while `crew/implementer.md:22` and `templates/worker-dispatch.template.md:27` require `./flightdeck/flightcrew/bin/fc` to exist *inside the worker's worktree*. That copy arrives only because `flightcrew/` is committed in the run branch, not through any distribution step; `hooks/README.md` similarly notes hooks "run in place … via `$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR`".

8. **The guards do not use fc, but the guards' documented backstop is an fc command.** `lock-guard.mjs` and `boundary-guard.mjs` read `launch.json` directly (no fc), yet `hooks/README.md` "The hole the guards do not cover" names `fc locked` — "It runs inside `fc verify`, so a shell write is caught before a run can be accepted" — as the third backstop. The guards are fc-independent; their completeness is not.

9. **Phase moves are attributed to different actors in two manuals.** `launch-anatomy.md:98-100` places `fc launch phase verify|review|report` in the agent column, while `journey.md:30, :46` requires the human at G3 between `fc launch phase report` and `fc launch end`; `crew/orchestrator.md` (lines 18, 23, 24, 25) has the orchestrator running `fc launch phase` four times.

10. **The runner outweighs everything it coordinates.** `bin/` + `checks/` is 8,596 of 12,879 lines (66.7 %) of `flightdeck/flightcrew/`; the crew it dispatches is 523 lines (4.1 %) and the hooks that enforce the same launch.json are 604 lines of code (4.7 %). `bin/cmd/launch.mjs` alone (887 lines) is longer than the entire crew roster plus the entire hook set.</result>

</task-notification>

[ASSISTANT 💬]
The third explorer is back, and the size of the inversion is now measured.

**How much of the system the runner is**
- The runner and its libraries are two thirds of the flightcrew folder by line count. The crew it dispatches is four percent. The hooks that enforce the same state are five percent. One command module, the launch commands, is longer than the entire crew roster and the entire hook set together.
- 44 distinct command forms across 19 commands. The orchestrator role file alone is told to run fc 29 times.
- Eleven of the 29 locked suites test fc subcommands directly. Twenty-two of 29 spawn it. Over a third of the system's own verification verifies the CLI.

**What the runner owns**
- Every transition of a run. Eight commands write the launch state file and nothing else does. Phase, gate, pin, end and land are all runner writes.
- Every rendered artefact: kickoff, plan, dispatch prompts, evidence page, report, run log stub. None can be produced without it.
- The active launch is resolved from an environment variable or a scan for the one active state file. Two active launches make every command fail.

**Where the human sits**
- Fifteen commands in the ordered spine a human types across a run, eight of which advance state. Seven of those eight are launch subcommands. The sources have the human typing none.

**What does not go through it**
- The two guards read the state file directly and would work with the runner deleted. The validators are programs in their own right. The workflow scripts call fc zero times because the runtime forbids shell, so during a workflow-shaped wave the state file, the events and the evidence page receive no runner write at all, and the orchestrator catches up afterwards by hand.

**Tensions the built system carries against itself**
- The one-line success rule is broken by eight commands, and the spec's own constraint on it was carried into the log as a conflict for version two.
- The workflow scripts are named after a runner they cannot call.
- The evidence page is promised never behind the state, but its render swallows every error silently.
- The runner is invoked by a shim that depends on node being on the path, the exact hole the hooks README warns about.
- Distribute never distributes the runner, yet workers are told to invoke it inside their worktrees.
- Two manuals attribute the same phase moves to different actors.

Against the sources this is one problem with several faces rather than several problems. The prescribed shape is harness primitives writing flat files, with a page for the human and no program above them. The built shape is a program above them that owns the state, renders every artefact, advances every phase, and is what the human, the orchestrator, the gates and the tests all talk to. The four questions I put to you earlier are what decide how the document frames it. The sharpest is the second: whether the human was ever meant to be at a terminal. If not, the runner's spine of fifteen commands is not a usability problem, it is the wrong interface.

[ASSISTANT 💬]
No, and I moved too fast. Your answers settled the shape, the origin and the two decisions. They did not settle how the shape actually runs, and the scaffold's problems lean on that. The open ones:

- **How a hook knows which run it is in.** Today the lock guard and boundary guard read the active launch's state file to learn the locked paths. Under document gating there is no state file. The tests map carries the locked paths itself, but something has to tell a hook which map, and which run folder, applies to the session it is firing in. Branch name, run folder as working directory, an environment variable set at liftoff, or the kickoff. This one decides whether the guards survive.
- **Who writes a freeze or an approval into a document, and what checks it.** The spec already has a frozen status and a commit header written by the human. The plan has no approval block today. Under your model the human writes the approval into the plan and the orchestrator reads it. What refuses to proceed if it is absent, and is that a validator the next role runs or a hook?
- **Where the ceilings live.** Budgets, model tiers and abandon triggers sit in the launch state file today. The guides put them in the kickoff and the plan. That is a small move but it changes what the budget script reads.
- **Whether events stay.** The sources want an append-only event log written by hooks. That is not state in your sense, since nothing gates on it, but it is a per-run file a hook must find.

Now your two questions.

**Which commands are worth keeping as leaf scripts.** Judged by one test: does the command take its inputs as paths and arguments, write one artefact, and hold nothing between calls? Yes for these.

- **check.** Run one command, capture exit and output, write one evidence file. This is the guides' check wrapper almost exactly, once it takes the map path as an argument instead of resolving a pin.
- **boundary and locked.** A diff since a base commit against allowed and locked globs. The guides call this a trivial script over git diff. Fold the two into one.
- **worker, critic and verifier render.** Deterministic prompt rendering from the plan and the spec into a sealed dispatch. The core-stages guide asks for exactly this script, and it is your pre-build prompt injector idea. The strongest candidate.
- **evidence and report render, and the run log stub.** The guides' assembler. Reads events, checks, plan and returns from a run folder and writes the page, the report, the stub. Fits a session-end hook or a skill.
- **plan render.** Plan markdown from plan JSON. Trivial leaf.
- **return.** Validate an agent's return against its schema and write it to the run folder. The guides want schema-validated handoffs. It stays a leaf if the destination is an argument.
- **validate and lint.** Already standalone programs. The runner adds nothing to them by its own comment.
- **budget.** Count events against ceilings. Leaf once the ceilings come from the plan or kickoff.
- **worker merge.** A git merge of a unit branch into the run branch. Leaf, and arguably just git.

Not recyclable, because their whole job is owning state: launch new, activate, status, phase, gate, pin, end, land, escalate, note, kickoff. Eleven subcommands, the 887-line module, and the reason the human types fifteen commands. Distribute and doctor are installation, not run, and belong to the foundation if anywhere.

**Can a leaf be absorbed into a larger surface later.** Yes, and that is the natural order, provided the leaves are built to a discipline. Each takes explicit paths and arguments and never resolves a global active run. Each writes one artefact and touches nothing else. Each returns the three exit codes and one line. Then a surface like your flight can wrap them as subcommands, call them from a web server, or add discovery and convenience, and the system underneath runs identically whether the surface exists or not. The failure mode to design against is the one the runner fell into: the surface grows logic of its own, roles start calling the surface instead of the leaves, and the leaves stop being usable alone. The guides' one-agent-before-several rule applies to scripts too.

Do you want to settle the four open questions before I revise the scaffold, or leave them in the document as decisions the shape forces?
