[ASSISTANT 💬]
It lands, with one seam to close before it becomes a spec decision.

**What lands.** A runner as deterministic tooling is what the principle actually asks for, and you're right that the principle pushed the builder toward it. Budget counting, rendering, scaffolding a launch or a run, wrapping a check: these are exactly the things a script does better than an agent remembering to. The mistake was not the runner, it was making the runner the thing every role and the human talk to, and the thing that owns the state. Your version puts the web page in front of the human, leaves the runner behind the page and the hooks, and keeps the gate flips in a document. The gate page in the core-stages guide writes an approval block into the run directory through the browser's file access, so a live launch.json a page can read and write is the guides' own mechanism. And a control-center file holding the active launch directory answers the open question about how a hook knows which run it is in. It is the environment variable made durable, which is better than the variable.

**The seam.** You've now got two candidate places for a gate to live, and they cannot both be the gate. One is launch.json, where a page flips a gate. The other is the document itself, a frozen header on the spec and an approval block on the plan, which is what you said gates the next agent. If launch.json holds the gate, then the runner or the page writing it is the thing maintaining state, and the fc problem returns one level up with a nicer interface. If the document holds the gate, launch.json is an index: it points at the current spec version, the current run and the hook configuration, and it mirrors state rather than owning it. The second is the one that keeps your decision intact. The test is simple: if launch.json were deleted, could the next role still tell whether it may proceed by reading the artefact it was handed? If yes, launch.json is an index and you're safe.

**Launch level versus run level.** Your instinct to put launch.json at the launch level is right, and it forces the same discipline. It can hold what spans runs: the spec series, the map series, which run is current, the hook settings, the ceilings. It should not hold each run's phase, gate results and outcome, or it becomes the run-state file again with an array in it. Those belong in the run's own documents: the plan's approval block, the evidence summary, the report. Then a new run is a new folder and a pointer flip, which is exactly what your run new command does.

**The runner's shape.** One entry with leaf commands is fine as a namespace. The constraint that keeps it honest: every command takes paths and arguments, writes one artefact, reads launch.json only as an index, and works when called alone. The moment a command can only be called after another command has set something up, you've got the old runner. Init and run new are the exceptions, since scaffolding is their whole job.

**The control-center file.** Two things to decide early. It is mutable state outside git, so it should be ignored by git and nothing gated should depend on it. And it is per repository, so parallel worktrees either inherit it or need their own, and workers in worktrees are the case where hooks most need to know the run.

**For the spec version.** The 57 of 78 count gives you the constraint directly: a behaviour is stated about an artefact or a role, and the runner is how it is implemented. A node that starts with the runner's name is a node about the implementation. If the next spec holds that line, the runner behaviours fall to a handful about scaffolding and rendering, and the space that opens is the orchestration behaviour the first spec was light on.

So the trade-off is right. The one decision to make before I revise the runner document is whether launch.json is the gate or the index. Everything else in your description follows from that answer.

[ASSISTANT 💬]
That dissolves the seam. Two states, two homes, two mechanisms:

- **Freeze state** lives in the document. A file whose status field reads frozen is immutable, and a hook enforces it by reading the file it is about to edit, not by consulting any run. That covers spec, map and plan alike, needs no environment variable, no active-run resolution and no locked-paths list computed at pin time. It is the deterministic-tools principle at its purest: the rule is in the artefact and the hook cannot be talked out of it.
- **Phase state** lives in launch.json. Gates, current phase, current run. A page writes it, a human reads it, the runner reads it or takes paths. Naming the current run in launch.json removes the whole active-launch problem: there is no scan for the one active state file, no two-active refusal, no environment variable to set per shell. A failed run is closed by pointing the launch at a new run folder, and only the named run is runnable.

That also reframes what went wrong. The built runner fused the two states into one file. Freeze was enforced through the launch's locked-paths list, which is why the lock is off during targets, why it needed pin to populate it, why a hand edit to a pinned copy went unreported, and why the guards need to resolve an active launch before they can decide anything. Separate the states and each of those disappears without a fix of its own.

**The spec seam, applied.** A node earns its place if it states something about an artefact's state, a hook's enforcement, a role's inputs and outputs, or what a rendering must contain. A node whose subject is the runner's argument parsing, its root resolution order, its output format, its exit codes, or which subcommand does what is a statement about an implementation. Those either move into a small spec of their own for the runner, or become constraints on scripts in general rather than behaviours of the system. Under that seam my expectation is that the 40 command-shaped nodes shrink to a handful about scaffolding and rendering, the 17 that mention fc incidentally get reworded around their real subject, and the 21 that never mention it stay. The space that opens is where the orchestration behaviours the first spec was light on go: what the orchestrator does at each gate, what a worker receives and returns, what the test-builder writes and where, how a run ends.

- **Revise the runner scaffold** to the two-state model. Problem 3 becomes one file holding two kinds of state, with the fused lock as its evidence. p='fc-problems.md'; body=open(p).read()
def sect(marker, prose):
    global body
    i=body.index(marker); j=i+len(marker)
    lines=body[j:].split('\n'); k=0
    while k<len(lines) and (lines[k].startswith('<!--') or lines[k]==''):
        if lines[k]=='' and k+1<len(lines) and lines[k+1].startswith('#'): break
        k+=1
    body=body[:j]+'\n'.join(lines[:k])+'\n'+prose.strip('\n')+'\n'+'\n'.join(lines[k:])

P['# Runner problems\n']="""
This document describes the problems of the flightcrew v1 runner, the command-line program at `flightdeck/flightcrew/bin/fc` that the built system drives every run through. It is one of a set of problem documents, each covering one domain, written to inform the plan of a later launch and the next version of the spec. It diagnoses. It proposes no remediation. The run folder model is defined in the structure problems document and the check placement model in the testing problems document; neither is restated here.

Every observation was verified on branch `flightcrew-buildout` at commit `75b2b42`. Paths and line numbers refer to that revision. The working tree may be on another branch, so read evidence with `git show flightcrew-buildout:<path>`. Only what was built counts as evidence: the two recorded runs were driven by Claude Code workflows, not by flightcrew, so their results say nothing about the system. One fact about origin is stated once here and applies throughout. The constitution documents that describe the method's tooling were deliberately withheld from the build so as not to spoil its context and to see what it would produce on its own. What it produced followed the deterministic-tools principle further than the principle asks, not in a different direction.
"""
P['## Agent Invariants\n']="""
- A document's freeze is written in the document and enforced by a hook that reads the file it is about to edit. Phase state is held in `launch.json` at the launch level. The two are never fused.
- The runner is tooling behind pages and hooks. It is not what a human uses to advance a run.
- The foundation runs without any interface layered over it.
- If `launch.json` were deleted, the next role must still be able to tell from the artefact it holds whether it may proceed. `launch.json` indexes phase state; it is not the freeze.
- The reader has none of the conversation that produced this document. Every claim stands on the cited evidence alone.
"""
P['## The target shape\n']="""
The tooling the method's sources prescribe is made of the harness's own primitives and flat files: hooks wired in the project settings, skills, one agent definition per role, dynamic workflow scripts, templates, schemas, and a per-run directory of artefacts each written by the thing that produced it. Roles chain by handing documents forward. The spec-builder receives an idea and produces a spec. The test-builder receives the spec and produces the tests map and the checks. The orchestrator receives the spec, the tests and the kickoff. Nothing sits above the roles holding state on their behalf. A `bin/` folder holds a few scripts a launch needs, such as the worker prompt renderer that was an idea before the build.

The system has two kinds of state and they have different homes. **Freeze state** is whether a document is immutable. It is written in the document's own status field, and a hook enforces it by reading the file an agent is about to edit: if the file says frozen, the edit is refused. This applies to the spec, the tests map and the plan alike, and needs no knowledge of which run is active. **Phase state** is where a launch is: which run is current, which phase it is in, which gates have been passed. It is written in `launch.json` at the launch level, one file per launch, and a local web page reads and writes it live. Because `launch.json` names the current run, that run is the only runnable one, and a failed run is closed by pointing the launch at a new run folder.

A **runner** is intended, as deterministic tooling: a program of **leaf commands** that scaffold a launch or a run, render a dispatch or a report, count a budget, or wrap a check. A leaf command takes paths and arguments or reads `launch.json`, writes one artefact, and works when called alone. The runner may grow as far as the built one eventually. What it is not is the **control surface**: the thing a human uses to read and advance a run. That is a local web page writing to `launch.json` or to a document.

A control-center file under `flightdeck/` holds active configuration such as the launch directory, and later other configuration. It is mutable state outside git, so nothing gated may depend on it, and parallel worktrees either inherit it or need their own.
"""
P['### 1. The runner became the control surface\n']="""
**What.** Across the three constitution documents and the twelve source guides, no central runner, `bin/` directory, command suite or named executable appears. The word CLI appears six times, every one about tools the project already has or Claude Code's own commands. The pre-build scaffold on `main` held `flightdeck/flightcrew/bin/runners.keep`, reading "Runnable scripts needed for every launch", and one loose script. The build collapsed everything behind one entry. The build transcript contains no message proposing a runner or weighing it against hooks or skills; the runner appears in the design contract's preamble, `flightdeck/launch/specs/flightcrew-v1/design.md:3`, as a settled part of the deal, and is filed at `design.md:284` under decisions not to reopen with one bullet. The spec's only justification is decision `D2`: one entry point with a module per command, because a single user needs one surface to remember and nothing to install. Under `flightdeck/manuals/launch/launch-anatomy.md:93-102` the human types fifteen commands across a run, eight of which advance state, and seven of those eight are `fc launch` subcommands. The sources have the human advance a run by leaving plan mode, by a gate page writing an approval block into the plan, by replying in a halted session, or by editing the plan file, and never by typing a command. Both critic passes in `flightdeck/launch/flightcrew-buildout-2/review/` fault the runner's fidelity to its own spec and never question its existence, name or size.

**Why it matters.** The runner as tooling is what the deterministic-tools principle asks for. The runner as the surface a human remembers and types into is the opposite of what the method describes, where the human reads a display and approves at gates. A single surface to remember is a convenience for a person at a terminal. The method is built so that the person is not at the terminal.

**Effect on the system.** Every manual, every kickoff part and the orchestrator's own role file are written as sequences of runner commands. The human's fifteen-command spine is the run's user interface, and a page that later layers over the top has to reproduce that spine rather than replace it. The decision was never examined by the critics because it sat inside the spec they were judging against.
"""
P['### 2. One file holds two kinds of state\n']="""
**What.** `launch.json` holds both the freeze and the phase. Eight subcommands write it and nothing else does, `flightdeck/flightcrew/bin/cmd/launch.mjs:309, 352, 451, 465, 576, 640, 702, 831`: every phase, gate, pin, end and land is a runner write. Freeze is not enforced from the documents. It is enforced through the launch's locked-paths list, which `fc launch pin tests-map` populates from the map at `launch.mjs:439-447`. `flightdeck/flightcrew/hooks/lock-guard.mjs:6-13` therefore reads `launch.json` to decide, is off during the targets phase, and matches nothing until a map is pinned. A hand edit to a pinned spec copy is never reported, as the second run's critic recorded in pass 1 finding F6. To read `launch.json` at all, the guards and every command must first resolve an active launch: an environment variable, else the single launch whose status is active, per `flightdeck/flightcrew/checks/lib/launch-lib.mjs:158-183`. Two active launches make every command fail.

The sources distribute state by producer: events written by hooks, the plan written by the orchestrator with references and no status, checks written by a wrapper, returns written by workers, and the report assembled from all of them. The core-stages guide says it directly: status is not on the plan, that is the report's job.

**Why it matters.** Freeze and phase are different kinds of fact. A frozen spec is frozen whether or not any run exists, and a hook can know that by reading the spec. A gate result belongs to one launch and changes as the launch proceeds. Fusing them means the immutability of a document depends on a run's state file being present, populated and resolvable, so the strongest guarantee the system offers rests on its most fragile mechanism. Separating them removes the pin as the moment locking begins, removes the active-launch resolution from the guards, and removes the two-active refusal entirely.

**Effect on the system.** The lock has a window at the start of every run in which nothing is locked. The guards cannot decide without a state file and an environment. Every command carries the resolution logic and its error cases. The pin command exists largely to carry freeze into phase state, and the locked-paths glob it adds for the run's own spec copies is what the critic found unenforced. Under the target shape each of these disappears without a fix of its own.
"""
P['### 3. The spec describes the runner, not the orchestration\n']="""
**What.** The frozen spec `flightdeck/launch/specs/flightcrew-v1/spec.v1.json` has 54 behaviours and 24 edges. Fifty-seven of the 78 name the runner, and 40 open with a runner command as their subject. Interface `I1` is the runner itself, its full command surface and its root resolution order. Decision `D15` gives the orchestrator no write tools and has it write only through three runner commands. Decision `D16` removes the scribe role because report assembly is a command. Eleven of the 29 locked suites test runner subcommands directly and 22 spawn it. What remains once the runner nodes are set aside is 21 behaviours and edges about hooks, validators, suites and orchestration.

**Why it matters.** A spec fixes what must be true of the result. The method's sources say it describes outcomes, not steps, and that two teams could build from it and both results would satisfy it. A spec whose behaviours are the argument lists, exit codes and output shapes of one program's subcommands fixes an implementation and leaves the outcome it serves largely unstated. The orchestration behaviours the system exists for, what the orchestrator does at each gate, what a worker receives and returns, how a run ends, are where the first spec is thin.

**Effect on the system.** The tests derived from the spec test the runner, so the system's own verification is mostly verification of the CLI. The critics judged against the spec, so they judged the runner's fidelity to itself. For the next version the seam is this: a node about an artefact's state, a hook's enforcement, a role's inputs and outputs, or what a rendering must contain is a behaviour of the system and stays. A node about the runner's arguments, resolution order, output format, exit codes or which subcommand does what is a statement about an implementation, and either moves into a small spec of the runner's own or becomes a constraint on scripts in general.
"""
P['### 4. Every role and every artefact goes through the runner\n']="""
**What.** The runner renders every artefact a run produces: the kickoff, the plan markdown, the sealed dispatch prompts for worker, critic and verifier, the evidence page, the report and the run log stub. None can be produced without it. It offers 19 commands in 44 invocable forms. `flightdeck/flightcrew/crew/orchestrator.md` tells the orchestrator to run it 29 times. The runner and its libraries are two thirds of `flightdeck/flightcrew/` by line count; the crew it dispatches is four percent and the hooks are five. The launch command module alone, at 887 lines, is longer than the entire crew roster and the entire hook set together. The run log's entry for the second run credits the runner with the run's record being produced by commands and not by hand.

Three parts of the system do not go through it. The two guards read `launch.json` directly and would work with the runner deleted. The validators are programs in their own right, and the runner's own comment at `bin/cmd/validate.mjs:5-7` says it adds nothing to their output. The three workflow scripts under `flightdeck/flightcrew/workflows/` call the runner zero times, because the workflow runtime forbids shell, so during a workflow-shaped wave no state is written and the orchestrator catches up afterwards by hand.

**Why it matters.** The property the runner is credited with, a record produced by commands rather than recollection, is one the sources obtain from hooks writing events, a wrapper writing check output and an assembler joining them, each a leaf. Routing every artefact through one program buys nothing those leaves do not, and costs the ability to call any of them alone. The three things that bypass the runner are the three that most resemble what the sources prescribe, and they are the three that still work.

**Effect on the system.** The runner is the largest thing in the system and the hardest to replace, because every role file, template and manual addresses it. Of the built commands, most are already leaf-shaped and worth keeping in that form: `check`, `boundary` and `locked` folded together, the three `render` commands, `evidence`, `report` and the run log stub, `plan render`, `return`, `validate` and `lint`, `budget` once its ceilings come from the plan or kickoff, and `worker merge`. The eleven `launch` subcommands are the state owner and are not leaves. `distribute` and `doctor` are installation, not run.
"""
P['### 5. The runner breaks its own output rule\n']="""
**What.** `design.md:12` and constraint `C3` require one line of output on success. Eight commands print more: `distribute`, `launch status`, `launch pin`, `launch gate exit`, `launch end`, `doctor`, `events summary` and `worker render`. The second run's critic found the pin and phase commands exceeding the rule in pass 1 finding F8 and again in pass 2 finding F2, noting that the constraints suite samples nine other commands so neither is caught. The conflict was carried into the run log as a spec conflict for the next version. The evidence page is promised never to fall behind the state at `bin/cmd/launch.mjs:6-7`, and the render that keeps that promise, `launch-lib.mjs:352-372`, swallows every error and never changes an exit code. The shim at `bin/fc:4` invokes a bare `node`, the exact hole the hooks README warns about for hook scripts.

**Why it matters.** Terse, unambiguous output with errors that say what to do next is the deterministic-tools principle's own definition of a good tool, and the reason a runner is worth having. A rule the runner's own commands break, a promise kept by a function that hides its failures, and an interpreter dependency the system elsewhere calls a trap are small in themselves and carry into every leaf command that survives.

**Effect on the system.** Any leaf kept from the built runner inherits its output library and its shim. The one-line rule needs restating as a rule about leaf commands with its exceptions named, and the best-effort render needs to either report or not promise.
"""

## 1. HOOKS INVENTORY

Six scripts plus a shared library and the fragment, at `flightdeck/flightcrew/hooks/`.

| file | event(s) | reads | decides / writes | exit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `event-log.mjs` | SessionStart, SessionEnd, SubagentStart, SubagentStop, TaskCreated, TaskCompleted, PostToolUseFailure, PermissionDenied, PreCompact, PostCompact, Stop, WorktreeRemove (`event-log.mjs:7-10`) | envelope; `launch.json` via context | one `events.jsonl` line, `source: hook`, detail keys whitelisted per event (`:31-46`); `systemMessage` on SessionStart (`:70-72`) | always 0 |
| `lock-guard.mjs` | PreToolUse, matcher `Edit\|Write\|NotebookEdit` | `launch.json` `phase`, `paths.locked` | `deny` decision on stdout + `lock_denied` event (`lock-guard.mjs:11-12`) | always 0 |
| `boundary-guard.mjs` | same event/matcher | `paths.enforce_boundary`, `paths.allowed`, `paths.locked`, `spec.name`, `phase` | `deny` + `boundary_denied` (`boundary-guard.mjs:26-27`) | always 0 |
| `structural-check.mjs` | PostToolUse, matcher `Edit\|Write` | `launch.json.structural[&lt;ext&gt;]` (`:24-26`) | runs `/bin/sh -c` at git toplevel; writes last 20 lines to stderr | 0 sound / no command; **2** on failure (`:35,39`) |
| `stop-gate.mjs` | Stop, `timeout: 600` | `escalation.json`, `launch.tests_map` pin, pinned map file, `plan.json`, `launch.ceilings.stop_blocks`, `events.jsonl` | `check_run` / `stop_block` / `stall` + `trigger` / `stop_release` events; stderr block lines | 0 green/released/stalled; **2** blocking (`:144`) |
| `session-end.mjs` | SessionEnd | `../bin/fc.mjs` existence | spawns `fc evidence`, `fc report` under a 1500 ms budget (`:11,23-35`) | always 0 |
| `lib.mjs` | — (shared) | stdin, `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR`, launch resolution | `decide()`, `record()`, `log()`, `runGuard()` | wrapper forces 0 unless handler returns 2 (`lib.mjs:226`) |

README no-op rule, verbatim (`hooks/README.md:20-32`):

&gt; ## The no-op rule
&gt; A hook is a silent no-op — exit 0, empty stdout, nothing said to the session and no event appended, though a `hooks.log` line is always permitted — whenever it cannot be sure it is speaking for a run:
&gt; - `$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` is unset, or the directory it names has no `flightdeck/launch/`.
&gt; - No launch has status `active`, or `FLIGHTCREW_LAUNCH=none`.
&gt; - Stdin is not a JSON object. When a launch does resolve, this one adds a single line to `hooks.log` and still says nothing to the session.
&gt; Two launches are active at once, or the resolved `launch.json` will not parse: the guards print an `ask` decision naming the cause, and the recording hooks, `event-log` and `session-end`, stay silent. `stop-gate` writes one `hooks.log` line and exits 0 whenever its gate cannot run at all — no map pinned, the map file missing, the gate script absent.
&gt; Every error inside a hook is caught, written to `hooks.log` if a launch is known, and turned into exit 0. A hook never crashes a session. Two mechanisms are distinct: the guards refuse a single tool call by printing a `deny` decision on stdout and still exiting 0, while `structural-check` and `stop-gate` hold the turn itself by exiting 2. No hook does anything else.

Fragment wiring (`hooks/settings.fragment.json`): eleven single-hook event entries, all with command string
`"node \"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/flightdeck/flightcrew/hooks/event-log.mjs"` — SessionStart `:4-6`, SubagentStart `:15-17`, SubagentStop `:18-20`, TaskCreated `:21-23`, TaskCompleted `:24-26`, PostToolUseFailure `:27-29`, PermissionDenied `:30-32`, PreCompact `:33-35`, PostCompact `:36-38`, WorktreeRemove `:39-41`; SessionEnd `:7-14` runs `event-log.mjs` then `session-end.mjs`. No matcher on any of these.

```json
"PreToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Edit|Write|NotebookEdit",
  "hooks": [ {"type":"command","command":"node \"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/flightdeck/flightcrew/hooks/lock-guard.mjs"},
             {"type":"command","command":"node \"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/flightdeck/flightcrew/hooks/boundary-guard.mjs"} ] } ]   // :42-50
"PostToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Edit|Write",
  "hooks": [ {"type":"command","command":"node \"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/flightdeck/flightcrew/hooks/structural-check.mjs"} ] } ]  // :51-56
"Stop": [ { "hooks": [
  {"type":"command","command":"node \"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/flightdeck/flightcrew/hooks/event-log.mjs"},
  {"type":"command","command":"node \"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/flightdeck/flightcrew/hooks/stop-gate.mjs","timeout":600} ] } ]      // :57-64
```

## 2. WHAT THE HOOKS NEED TO WORK

Every hook goes through `runHook` → `resolveContext` (`lib.mjs:94-135, 213-235`). Shared requirements: `node` on PATH (fragment commands start with bare `node`, `settings.fragment.json:5` etc.); `$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` set and naming a directory containing `flightdeck/launch/` — it is the *only* root source: `resolveRoot({ env, cwd, sources: ['CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR'] })` (`lib.mjs:98`), and a throw returns `null` → `process.exit(0)` (`lib.mjs:99-101, 218`). Stdin must parse to a JSON object or the hook logs `'stdin was not a JSON object; no action taken'` and exits 0 (`lib.mjs:219-223`). `FLIGHTCREW_LAUNCH=none` throws `NoLaunch` (`checks/lib/launch-lib.mjs:175`) → `resolveContext` returns null.

Per hook, beyond the shared set:

- **event-log**: needs a resolved launch (`if (!ctx.launch) return 0;` `event-log.mjs:63`) and a recorded event name (`:65`). No `launch.json` field required beyond `phase` for the announcement, which defaults to `'unknown'` (`:71`).
- **lock-guard**: launch resolved (`lib.mjs:253`); ambiguity → `ask` (`lib.mjs:249-252`); fired abandon trigger → blanket `deny` (`lib.mjs:254-259`); needs `paths.locked` — absent means `[]` and no denial (`lock-guard.mjs:9-10`); no-ops in phase `targets` (`:8`).
- **boundary-guard**: additionally requires `paths.enforce_boundary` truthy, else exit 0 with no decision (`boundary-guard.mjs:23`); `permitted()` returns `null` for any phase not in `BOUNDARY_PHASES` and not `targets`, which is also a pass-through (`:17-19, 25`).
- **structural-check**: launch resolved (`:20`), an edit target (`:21-22`), and a `structural` map entry for the extension; absent/blank template → exit 0 silently (`:24-26`). Needs `/bin/sh`; a spawn error is exit 2 (`:32-35`). Does *not* need a tests map or plan.
- **stop-gate**: launch resolved (`:64-67`); phase in `GATE_FOR` (`:11, 70-71`); no open `escalation.json` (`:73-76`); **a pinned tests map** — `launch.tests_map.path` non-blank (`:78-82`) and the file readable (`:83-88`); the gate module present and exporting `run` (`:43-54, 90-94`). Each missing precondition writes one `hooks.log` line and returns 0. `plan.json` is read but its absence is tolerated (`readJsonFile` returns null, `:96,109`; contracts-gate falls back to the acceptance check, `contracts-gate.mjs:36-45`).
- **session-end**: launch resolved (`:16`) and `../bin/fc.mjs` present on disk, else `log(ctx, 'fc.mjs is not installed beside the hooks; evidence and report were not refreshed')` and exit 0 (`:17-21`).

---

## 3. LOCK COVERAGE

Both guards run through `runGuard`, which gates on `FILE_TOOLS` (`lib.mjs:15`):

```js
export const FILE_TOOLS = ['Edit', 'Write', 'NotebookEdit'];
```
`if (!FILE_TOOLS.includes(input.tool_name)) return 0;` (`lib.mjs:247`). The fragment matcher is the same three (`settings.fragment.json:44`).

Not intercepted: **Bash** (no PreToolUse matcher covers it anywhere in the fragment), and **MultiEdit** — the string `MultiEdit` does not occur anywhere under `flightdeck/**` on this branch. `Write` via shell (`sed -i`, redirects, `git checkout`) is unseen. Structural-check's matcher is `Edit|Write` only, so a `NotebookEdit` gets guarded but not structurally checked.

README `README.md:53-59`:

&gt; ## The hole the guards do not cover
&gt; The guards see the `Edit`, `Write` and `NotebookEdit` tools. A shell command — `sed -i`, a redirect, `git checkout` of a locked file — writes without passing through any of them, and no PreToolUse hook can stop it. Three backstops cover that gap, and a run should have all three:
&gt; - `permissions.deny` rules on the locked paths, which apply to the file tools immediately and cannot be talked past.
&gt; - A `sandbox.filesystem.deny` list naming the locked paths, which does apply to Bash and its children. `_sandbox_example` in the fragment shows the shape.
&gt; - `fc locked`, which compares the working tree against `lock_commit` and reports any locked path that changed, however it changed. It runs inside `fc verify`, so a shell write is caught before a run can be accepted.

`flightdeck/manuals/harness/hooks.md:60` records that backstop 2 "is optional and inactive until that step is taken" (install step 3a).

---

## 4. STOP GATE

Phase→gate map (`stop-gate.mjs:11`): `const GATE_FOR = { verify: 'acceptance-gate', contracts: 'contracts-gate' };` — every other phase returns 0 immediately (`:70-71`) with no event.

- `verify`: `acceptance-gate.mjs` runs `fc check &lt;acceptance id&gt;`, id resolved map → launch → `'T1'` (`acceptance-gate.mjs:25-29`).
- `contracts`: `contracts-gate.mjs` runs the checks of the plan unit with `kind === 'contracts'`, falling back to the acceptance id when `no_contracts`, no such unit, or no plan (`contracts-gate.mjs:33-46`), plus `fc boundary` as an `extra` item (`:49-60`).

Eight-block override (`stop-gate.mjs:13-15, 130-134`):
```js
const MAX_BLOCKS = 8;
...
const cap = Math.min(Number.isInteger(launch.ceilings?.stop_blocks) ? launch.ceilings.stop_blocks : MAX_BLOCKS, MAX_BLOCKS);
const count = blocks + 1;
if (count &gt;= cap) {
```
Rationale in `manuals/harness/hooks.md:17`: "Claude Code overrides a Stop hook after eight consecutive blocks, so the harness stalls first and records it."

Stall message and its exit code (`stop-gate.mjs:134-140`):
```js
if (count &gt;= cap) {
  const detail = `${ids.join(', ') || 'the gate'} still red after ${blocks} consecutive stop blocks in phase ${phase}`;
  record(ctx, 'stall', { blocks });
  record(ctx, 'trigger', { name: 'stop-gate stall', detail });
  err(`stall: ${detail}; the gate is releasing the turn. Escalate with fc launch escalate, or end the launch.\n`);
  return 0;
}
```
`return 0` → `process.exit(0)` (`lib.mjs:226`). The blocking path is `record(ctx, 'stop_block', …); err(...); return 2;` (`:142-144`).

RUNLOG reservation (`flightdeck/launch/RUNLOG.md:9`): "…spec conflicts carried to the next version: … **the stall message on exit 0 that Claude Code does not display**, and C3 one-line output versus validator lines…". `manuals/harness/hooks.md:26` states the general rule: stderr is shown on exit 2, and on "any other non-zero exit" the first stderr line is a notice — exit 0 is not listed as a stderr-displaying path.

- Bash: all roles except `spec-judge` (Read only) and `spec-attacker` (Read, Grep, Glob).
- Per-agent hooks: **none**. No `hooks:` key appears in any crew file (grep over `flightdeck/flightcrew/crew/` for `^hooks:` returns nothing). Likewise no `memory:` and no `disallowedTools:` in any role.
- Orchestrator Write/Edit: **no** — `tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, Agent` (`crew/orchestrator.md:5`); `crew/README.md:24` and `permissions.md:46` state it writes only through `fc`.

## 7. TWO PERMISSION SYSTEMS

Role reach lives in **both** places, split by kind: tool allowlist, model, turns, isolation and permission mode in the role file's frontmatter; command-level allow rules, agent-dispatch rules, workflow rules and the path deny rules in the project settings fragment. Neither expresses the other.

`manuals/harness/permissions.md:3`: "Unattended runs need boundaries they cannot talk past: the fragment's allow and deny lists, the per-role tool allowlists in the crew, worktree isolation, the sandbox, and `--allowedTools` on headless runs."

`:7`: "The fragment … must first be merged into the project's `.claude/settings.json` … **No allow, deny or hook rule below applies until it is done.**"

`:11`: "`acceptEdits` covers Edit, Write and NotebookEdit only. The orchestrator holds none of them: its `fc` writes run as Bash and are covered by the three `Bash(… fc *)` allow rules…"

`:42`: "The tools column is the frontmatter of `flightdeck/flightcrew/crew/&lt;role&gt;.md`, which `fc distribute --apply` copies to `.claude/agents/flightcrew/`; edit the source and redistribute."

`:37`: "`deny` and `ask` apply immediately; `allow` applies after workspace trust… Until it is granted, an interactive run prompts despite the allow list; this is why headless runs pass `--allowedTools`."

`:55-56`: "`permissionMode: acceptEdits` on the implementer means a worktree edit inside its paths never prompts; a prompt during implement is therefore always a boundary, a lock or a missing allow rule." / "Auto mode … is a backstop only."

Agreement checks that exist:
- `flightdeck/testbench/suites/schemas/run.mjs:501-502` asserts each crew `name` has a matching `Agent(&lt;name&gt;)` in `permissions.allow`. That is the only cross-check between the two systems, and it covers names only.
- `fc doctor --target &lt;dir&gt;` checks: agents byte-equal to source, every fragment hook command present in `settings.json`, hook interpreter resolvable, `worktree.baseRef === 'head'`, `.claude/worktrees/` gitignored, no crew-name collision under `.claude/agents/**` (`bin/cmd/doctor.mjs:221-279`; summarised at `permissions.md:92`). It does **not** compare a role's `tools` with the fragment's allow/deny lists, and does not detect that a deny rule contradicts a role's write mandate.
- `bin/cmd/doctor.mjs:19` requires only `['name','description','tools','model']` as crew frontmatter; `isolation`, `permissionMode`, `maxTurns` are asserted only in the testbench (`suites/crew/run.mjs:19-25, 77-86`), against a hardcoded expected table.

## 8. INSTALLATION

`fc distribute` copies crew and workflows, never a hook — `bin/cmd/distribute.mjs:1`: "copies the two distributable parts of flightcrew into a project's `.claude` directory: the crew definitions and the workflow scripts, **never a hook**, and prints the settings fragment the harness still needs by hand." Copy set built at `:53-65` (crew `*.md` with frontmatter → `agents/flightcrew/`, workflows `*.js` → `workflows/`); dry-run prints "would copy N files into &lt;target&gt; (no hook is ever copied)" (`:121`). `--apply` requires `--target` (`:106-109`). The fragment is only *printed*, with `node` replaced by `process.execPath` (`:76-94, 139-142`); the merge into `settings.json` is manual (`:141`).

Hooks run in place: `README.md:7` — "The scripts run in place from `flightdeck/flightcrew/hooks/`. Nothing is copied into `.claude/`; `$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` locates them from wherever a session starts, worktrees included."

README install section, verbatim (`hooks/README.md:34-41`):
&gt; ## Installing
&gt; 1. Merge `flightdeck/flightcrew/hooks/settings.fragment.json` into the project's `.claude/settings.json`: copy each key across, appending to any `hooks` list, `permissions.allow` and `permissions.deny` already there. Read the fragment from that path, or run `fc distribute --apply --target &lt;dir&gt;` (the `--apply` form requires `--target`, which is the project's `.claude` directory), which copies the crew and workflow files and prints the fragment with the absolute interpreter substituted. Drop the `_comment` and `_sandbox_example` keys as you merge — they document, they do not configure.
&gt; 2. Keep `worktree.baseRef` at `head`, or worker subagents branch from the remote default branch and never see the run's branch.
&gt; 3. Add `.claude/worktrees/` to the repository's `.gitignore`.
&gt; 4. Hooks in `.claude/settings.json` need workspace trust before they run: Claude Code asks for it the first time a session opens the directory, and until it is granted the hooks stay silent in every session however correct the settings are.
&gt; 5. Run `fc doctor --target &lt;dir&gt;` against the same `.claude` directory: it checks that the fragment's hook commands are present in the settings file and that the interpreter they name resolves. Bare `fc doctor` checks the flightcrew installation only and never opens `settings.json`.

`$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` dependency: every command string embeds `"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR"` (`settings.fragment.json:5` et seq.), and it is the sole root source in code (`lib.mjs:98`); the fragment's `_comment` (`:2`) says "the hook scripts run in place from flightdeck/flightcrew/hooks/, so nothing is copied and `$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` resolves them wherever the session starts, worktrees included."

**Were hooks installed for the two recorded runs? No, for either.**

`flightdeck/launch/flightcrew-buildout/report.md:71` (Orchestrator notes, `[stated]`):
&gt; "The hooks were not installed in the sessions that built this system, so no SessionStart, Stop or SubagentStop events were recorded; the nine agent starts are stated by hand and the phase changes are recorded by fc."

`:72`: "Units ran as parallel build sessions in the repository working tree rather than in per-unit worktrees, so no unit branches were created and `fc worker merge` was not used; every return records an empty commit list."

`events.jsonl` for run 1, each of nine `SubagentStart` lines carries `"source":"stated"` with `detail.reason` = `"dispatched as a parallel build session; the hooks were not installed for this run, so the start is recorded by hand"`. Event-source tally, run 1: `fc` × 15 (`escalation` 1, `gate` 2, `launch_end` 1, `phase` 4, `return` 7), `stated` × 9 (`SubagentStart`). Run 2 (`flightcrew-buildout-2/events.jsonl`): `fc` only — `gate` 2, `launch_end` 1, `phase` 6, `return` 2; **zero events with `source: hook` in either run**, and run 2's report has "## Orchestrator notes [stated] — (none recorded)". Both RUNLOG entries record `0 stop blocks` (`RUNLOG.md:7, 22`).

## 9. STRUCTURAL CHECK

Two implementations of the same idea:

- `hooks/structural-check.mjs` (PostToolUse, every edit of `Edit|Write`, **every phase**): reads `ctx.launch.json?.structural` (`:24`), takes `structural[path.extname(file)]` (`:25`), substitutes `{file}` with a single-quoted absolute path (`:13-15, 28`), runs `/bin/sh -c` with cwd = git toplevel of the envelope cwd (`:29-31`), maxBuffer 16 MiB, **no timeout**. Exit 2 with the last 20 combined lines on failure (`:37-39`); exit 2 with a message on spawn error (`:32-35`).
- `checks/gates/structural-gate.mjs`: same table and same `{file}` substitution (`commandFor`, `:34-39`), but adds `TIMEOUT_MS = 300_000` and `killSignal: 'SIGKILL'` (`:20, 50-56`), filters blank lines out of the tail (`:29-31`), and exposes the gate shape `run(context)` (`:66-78`) plus a CLI `main(argv)` (`:81-102`) that builds its context with `gateContext({ requireMap: false })`. It is **not** wired into the fragment and is **not** in `stop-gate.mjs`'s `GATE_FOR`.

Where the commands come from: the active launch's `launch.json` `structural` object. As recorded for run 1 (`flightdeck/launch/flightcrew-buildout/launch.json`):
```json
"structural": {
  ".mjs": "node --check {file}",
  ".js":  "node --experimental-default-type=module --check {file}",
  ".json":"node -e \"JSON.parse(require('node:fs').readFileSync(process.argv[1], 'utf8'))\" {file}",
  ".sh":  "sh -n {file}"
}
```
Keys include the leading dot (`manuals/harness/hooks.md:12`). No command for an extension = exit 0, nothing printed (`structural-check.mjs:26`; `structural-gate.mjs:47, 70-72`).

## 10. CONSTITUTION DELTA

Against `constitution-research:library/constitution/orchestration-tooling.md` "Frontmatter permissions" (lines 52–64 of the file), which requires each role file to declare six things:

| constitution requirement | built system |
|---|---|
| **Tools** allowlist per role | **Has.** Every crew file carries `tools:`; `doctor.mjs:19` requires it. |
| **Model and effort** ("which model tier … and how much reasoning") | **Partial.** `model:` on all ten roles; `maxTurns` on six. No reasoning-effort/thinking field on any role. `orchestrator` is `model: inherit`, i.e. inherited "from whoever started the run" — the case the constitution names as the thing to avoid. `permissions.md:88` documents an env override (`CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE=1`) that overrides every per-role `model`. |
| **Isolation** ("Workers always do") | **Has, one role.** `implementer` only. |
| **Memory scope** | **Lacks.** No `memory` key in any crew file; nothing declares persistence. |
| **Permission mode** | **Partial.** Only `implementer` and `test-builder` declare `permissionMode: acceptEdits`; eight roles declare none and inherit the session's `--permission-mode` (`permissions.md:9`). |
| **Role-scoped hooks** ("checks that run around this role's actions and no other's") | **Lacks / placed elsewhere.** No crew file has a `hooks:` key. Every hook is global in `settings.json`, dispatched by event and tool matcher, and the guards discriminate by *launch phase* (`lock-guard.mjs:8`, `boundary-guard.mjs:17`) and *path*, never by agent identity. `event-log.mjs:66-68` reads `agent_id`/`agent_type` for the record but nothing branches on them. |
| "together with the project's permission settings and sandbox configuration" | **Has, as the fragment**, but the sandbox is an example only (`settings.fragment.json:99-106`, "`_sandbox_example`"), documented as inactive until manually turned into a real rule (`hooks.md:60`, install step 3a). |

Against "Hooks and check runners" (lines 95–104):

| constitution requirement | built system |
|---|---|
| "Before an action: a hook that inspects the intended tool call and blocks it … a forbidden path, a destructive command or an out-of-scope edit" | **Has for paths, lacks for commands.** `lock-guard` + `boundary-guard` on PreToolUse `Edit\|Write\|NotebookEdit`. No PreToolUse hook on Bash, so "a destructive command" is not inspected (`README.md:53-59`). |
| "After an action: a hook that runs a linter, a type check or the relevant tests whenever a file changes" | **Has, narrowed.** `structural-check` runs a parse-level check per extension on `Edit\|Write`. No test run after an edit; tests run only at the Stop gate or via `fc check`. |
| "At the end of a turn: a hook that runs the definition of done and refuses to let the agent stop until it passes … the harness … ends the turn after eight consecutive refusals, so this hook is a gate, not a loop" | **Has, in two phases only.** `stop-gate` runs in `verify` and `contracts`; `implement`, `plan`, `targets`, `review`, `report` have no end-of-turn gate (`stop-gate.mjs:11, 70-71`). Against `orchestration-principles.md` "Permissions and blast radius" (lines 92–101): "Each role has its own allowlist" — has. "Filesystem and network are sandboxed so that a role's reach ends at its worktree" — the sandbox is an unapplied example; only the implementer has a worktree. "Irreversible actions are denied outright" — the deny list has two path rules and no command rules; `Bash(git commit *)`, `Bash(git switch *)`, `Bash(git add *)` are on the *allow* list for every role that holds Bash. "Workflows with side effects outside the repository are invoked by a human only" — all three workflows are on the allow list as `Workflow(fc-implement|fc-review|fc-explore)`, model-invocable. "An automatic action classifier is a backstop" — echoed at `permissions.md:56`.

## Factual tensions inside the built hook and permission model

1. **The deny rule contradicts the test-builder's mandate.** `Edit(flightdeck/launch/specs/**)` (`settings.fragment.json:96`, spec I14) blocks exactly the file `crew/test-builder.md:23` instructs the role to write, and the fallback check directory at `:22`. Recorded as an open conflict in `RUNLOG.md:9`.
2. **The stall message is written to stderr on exit 0** (`stop-gate.mjs:138-139`), and `manuals/harness/hooks.md:24-26` lists no exit-0 path that displays stderr. `RUNLOG.md:9` carries it as a spec conflict. The stall also records a `trigger` event, which then makes `runGuard` deny *every* subsequent edit (`lib.mjs:254-259`) — with no displayed explanation.
3. **The blast radius is split across two files that nothing reconciles.** Frontmatter declares tools/model/isolation; the fragment declares commands, agents, workflows and path denials. `fc doctor --target` compares hook commands and agent bytes but never the two permission surfaces; the only cross-check anywhere is name-level (`testbench/suites/schemas/run.mjs:501-502`).
4. **Guard coverage is narrower than the boundary it claims to enforce.** `FILE_TOOLS` is three tools (`lib.mjs:15`); Bash is allowed to nine of ten roles and is not intercepted. The README names three backstops (`README.md:55-59`), of which one (`permissions.deny`) covers only the same three tools, one (`sandbox`) ships as a documentation-only `_sandbox_example` and is inactive by default (`hooks.md:60`), leaving `fc locked` — a post-hoc detector at verify — as the only live coverage of the hole.
5. **`MultiEdit` appears in neither `FILE_TOOLS` nor the fragment matchers** anywhere under `flightdeck/**`, while the README frames the hole solely as "a shell command" (`README.md:55`).
6. **`NotebookEdit` is guarded but never structurally checked** — PreToolUse matcher `Edit|Write|NotebookEdit` vs PostToolUse matcher `Edit|Write` (`settings.fragment.json:44, 53`).
7. **Two structural implementations diverge.** The hook has no timeout (`structural-check.mjs:31`); the gate has `TIMEOUT_MS = 300_000` and `SIGKILL` (`structural-gate.mjs:20, 53-55`); the gate is unreachable from the fragment and from `stop-gate.mjs`'s `GATE_FOR`.
8. **The stop gate covers two of seven phases.** `implement` — the only phase in which a role holds general write access — has no end-of-turn gate (`stop-gate.mjs:11`).
9. **A missing tests-map pin silently disables the gate.** `stop-gate.mjs:78-88` writes one `hooks.log` line and exits 0; from the session's side this is indistinguishable from a green gate.
10. **Two enforcement records for a hook are the same record.** `structural-check` exit 2 and `stop-gate` exit 2 hold the turn; both are wrapped by `runHook`, which converts every thrown error into exit 0 (`lib.mjs:227-234`). A guard that crashes fails open.
11. **Neither recorded run exercised the hook or worktree model.** Hooks not installed for run 1 (`report.md:71`, nine `source: stated` events), no hook-sourced event in either run, units ran in the main working tree rather than per-unit worktrees (`report.md:72`), and `fc boundary` reported `1 outside` the allowed paths at verify (`report.md:31`) — the file `.claude/workflows/flightcrew-build.js`, written by the driving session (`report.md:67`). The lock/boundary guards, `isolation: worktree`, and the eight-block ceiling therefore have no observed run behind them.
12. **`fc doctor --target` can fail on a correct install.** `RUNLOG.md:16` (F11): the interpreter check spawns `&lt;first token&gt; --version` for every hook command and exits 2 on anything not an executable on PATH, "even though B30 does not list that condition" — while the fragment's own commands begin with a bare `node`, the token the README (`:46`) tells you to replace.</result>

[ASSISTANT 💬]
The hooks explorer is back. Under the two-state model most of what it found reads as one thing: every guard's job today is to consult phase state before it can enforce a freeze. What it found in detail:

- **Every hook needs a resolved launch.** The one root source is the project directory variable, the launch must be active and unique, and a missing tests-map pin silently disables the stop gate with a single log line, indistinguishable from green from inside the session.
- **The guards see three tools.** Edit, Write and NotebookEdit. Bash is allowed to nine of ten roles and is never intercepted. Of the three backstops the README names, the deny list covers the same three tools, the sandbox ships as a documentation example that is inactive by default, and the third is a post-hoc detector at verify. A guard that crashes fails open, since the wrapper turns every error into exit zero.
- **The deny rule blocks the test-builder.** The settings fragment denies edits under the canonical spec folder, which is exactly where the test-builder role is told to write the map and its fallback checks. Deny beats the role's own write tools.
- **Reach lives in two files nothing reconciles.** Tools, model, turns and isolation are in the role frontmatter. Command allows, agent dispatch, workflow allows and path denies are in the settings fragment. The only cross-check anywhere compares role names to agent allow entries.
- **Against the constitution's frontmatter model:** tools present on every role, isolation on the implementer only, no memory scope on any role, permission mode on two roles, no role-scoped hooks anywhere, and the orchestrator's model set to inherit, the one case the constitution names as the thing to avoid.
- **Against the constitution's hook model:** before-action hooks cover paths but never commands, the after-action hook is a parse check rather than a test run, and the end-of-turn gate runs in two of seven phases. The implement phase, the only one where a role holds general write access, has no gate.
- **Irreversible actions are on the allow list.** Git commit, add and switch are allowed to every role with Bash. All three workflows are model-invocable.
- **Nothing was ever exercised.** Neither run had hooks installed, no event in either run has a hook as its source, units ran in the shared tree, and the stall message the guides treat as a stall detector is written on exit zero, which Claude Code does not display.

Two things from this I'd put to you before the scaffold. Whether the sandbox filesystem deny list, which is the only mechanism that reaches Bash, is something you want in the model or out, since the constitution asks for sandboxing and the built system left it as an example. And whether role-scoped hooks are part of your vision, since the freeze hook you described works without knowing the role, but a worker-only test-after-edit hook would need one.

### A2. The B39 / runtime tension

Last line of each shipped script:

- `fc-explore.js:165` — `export default result;`
- `fc-implement.js:278` — `export default result;`
- `fc-review.js:497` — `export default result;`

Spec B39 (`launch/specs/flightcrew-v1/spec.v1.json`, node id `B39`, status `ok`):

&gt; "Every flightcrew/workflows/*.js passes node --experimental-default-type=module --check, begins with an export const meta whose name equals the filename, contains none of Date.now, new Date and Math.random, and every schema literal it passes to agent() equals the matching flightcrew/schemas/*.json."

What the `workflows` suite (T29) asserts — four cases, all `covers: ['B39']` (`testbench/suites/workflows/run.mjs:30-79`):

- `passes-node-module-check` — `node --experimental-default-type=module --check &lt;file&gt;` must exit 0 (`run.mjs:32-39`).
- `first-statement-is-export-const-meta-with-name-equal-to-filename` (`run.mjs:42-51`).
- `no-date-now-new-date-or-math-random` (`run.mjs:53-60`).
- `schema-literals-equal-the-schema-files` (`run.mjs:62-78`).

**The suite asserts nothing whatever about how a script ends** — `export default`, top-level `return`, or neither. Header comment `run.mjs:2`: "Scripts are read, never executed."

What the manuals say the runtime requires: `manuals/harness/claude-code-facts.md:58` lists the script API and states only that `export const meta = {name, description, phases}` "must be a pure literal and the first statement"; it names `agent`, `parallel`, `pipeline`, `phase`, `log`, `args`, `budget`, `workflow(name, args)`. **Neither `claude-code-facts.md` nor `manuals/harness/workflows.md` (65 lines) states any requirement about the ending at all** — no mention of `export default` and no mention of a top-level return. `workflows/README.md:7` asserts the opposite of the RUNLOG: it says the authoring contract in `claude-code-facts.md` covers "…`budget` and the default export" — but no such text exists in that manual.

The RUNLOG reservation (`launch/RUNLOG.md:9`):

&gt; "spec conflicts carried to the next version: B39 versus the workflow runtime (the shipped workflow scripts pass the suite but end with export default, which the runtime rejects), …"

Direct corroboration from the two scripts that actually ran: `.claude/workflows/flightcrew-build.js:128` ends `return { u0: { build: u0, verdict: u0v }, units: unitReport, integration, intVerdict }` and `.claude/workflows/flightcrew-targets.js:130` ends `return { fixtures, fixtureVerdict, suites: suiteReport, map }` — top-level `return`, no `export default`.

The conflict is not merely stylistic, it is unsatisfiable: running `node --experimental-default-type=module --check` on `flightcrew-build.js` yields `SyntaxError: Illegal return statement` (exit 1). So T29's first case and the runtime's top-level-return form cannot both be satisfied by one file.

### A3. What the scripts cannot do, and how state catches up

`workflows/README.md:9`:

&gt; "A script here only dispatches agents and returns payloads. It reads no file, runs no command, touches no git state and stamps no time: `Date.now()`, `new Date()` and `Math.random()` are unavailable in the workflow runtime, so a timestamp arrives through `args`. **After a workflow completes, the orchestrator writes each returned payload to a file and stores it with the `fc return` command for its kind — `fc return worker &lt;file&gt; --unit &lt;id&gt;`, `fc return critic &lt;file&gt; --pass &lt;n&gt;`, `fc return verifier &lt;file&gt; --pass &lt;n&gt;`, `fc return explorer &lt;file&gt; --id X&lt;n&gt;` — then lands each green unit with `fc worker merge &lt;unit&gt;` in wave order** — nothing a script returns is stored until the orchestrator stores it, and nothing a script did counts as evidence until a check has run."

The full persistence table is `manuals/harness/workflows.md:33-41` (halt → `fc launch escalate halt`; trigger → `escalate trigger`; red-pilot stop → `escalate blocked`; spec-conflict → `escalate spec-gap`; `unrouted` → orchestrator re-routes or `escalate blocked`; usage → `fc events usage`). `fc return` validates by kind and exits 2 on a mismatch (`workflows.md:48`).

What must be committed before `/fc-implement`: the rendered unit prompts. `workflows/README.md:17` — "`fc worker render &lt;unit&gt;` writes that file beside printing. Commit it before the dispatch, because a subagent worktree branches from HEAD and an uncommitted launch-folder file is invisible to the worker." Same rule at `manuals/harness/workflows.md:24`, `templates/kickoff/shape-workflow.md:4`, and the underlying facts at `manuals/orchestration/journey.md:33-34` ("Commit points the run relies on: after 2a, after 2b (`fc launch pin`), after G1 (plan), after wave 0, after each `fc worker merge`, at 9." / "Subagent worktrees branch from HEAD, so anything uncommitted in the launch folder is invisible to workers.").

### A4. Which kickoff part selects the shape

`flightdeck/flightcrew/templates/kickoff/shape-workflow.md` (6 lines, `&lt;!-- version: 2 --&gt;` at line 1). Line 3 states what the orchestrator keeps:

&gt; "The orchestrator hands a wave to a dynamic workflow script — the scripts are kept at flightdeck/flightcrew/workflows/ and run from the copies `fc distribute --apply` places in the harness directory's workflows folder — and keeps the session for the gates and the fc commands. This run takes the workflow shape because a wave holds more units than the implementers_concurrent ceiling… The orchestrator session keeps the three gates, every fc command and every stored return; only the dispatch mechanism moves into the script."

Line 4: "The scripts replace only the dispatching in conduct steps 1, 4 and 6; every fc command in those steps stays with the orchestrator…". Line 5: script phase lines "are the display and never evidence". Line 6: "Gates are never inside a script — the script ends and the session halts at the gate." Selection rule repeated at `manuals/harness/workflows.md:8` and `templates/kickoff/README.md:14`.

### A5. Tested by execution or only by parsing?

Only by parsing. T29 (`testbench/suites/workflows/run.mjs:2`) — "Scripts are read, never executed" — reads source text, runs `node --check` (a syntax check that does not evaluate), and uses `extract.mjs` (`firstStatement`, `metaLiteral`, `schemaLiterals`, `agentCallCount`) to pull the meta and schema literals out of the source. No suite invokes `agent()`, `parallel()` or the scripts themselves; the workflow runtime bindings (`args`, `agent`, `phase`, `log`) are never provided anywhere in the testbench. `fc distribute` copies the files but `manuals/harness/workflows.md:64` notes `fc doctor --target` "does not compare workflow copies".

### A6. Were they used in either recorded run?

No. Evidence:

- Both launches' kickoffs are shape-workflow (`launch/RUNLOG.md:5` and `:20` — `kickoff: base@1+shape-workflow@1+task-feature@1`; `launch/flightcrew-buildout-2/kickoff.md:1-3`; `launch.json:21`; `plan.json:9`).
- Event tallies contain no workflow/dispatch trace of the three scripts. Run 1 `flightcrew-buildout/events.jsonl`: `SubagentStart` ×9, `return` ×7, `phase` ×4, `gate` ×2, `escalation` ×1, `launch_end` ×1. Run 2: `phase` ×6, `gate` ×2, `return` ×2, `launch_end` ×1.
- The only occurrences of `fc-implement`/`fc-review`/`fc-explore` in either launch folder are inside `kickoff.md` prose (`flightcrew-buildout-2/kickoff.md:38`) and in the boundary/locked/evidence path listings of the three source files themselves. No `/fc-implement` invocation appears anywhere in the record.

What drove the build instead: `.claude/workflows/flightcrew-build.js` (128 lines, 39,577 bytes) and `.claude/workflows/flightcrew-targets.js` (130 lines, 32,824 bytes) — both committed on `flightcrew-buildout` outside `flightdeck/`. They are construction scaffolding, not part of the system: `flightcrew-targets.js` builds stage 2 (fixtures, suite library, the 29 locked suites, `tests-map.v1.json`) with phases `Fixtures`/`Suites`/`Map`; `flightcrew-build.js` builds the system in phases `Contracts`/`Build`/`Integrate` with units U0–U7 (matching `returns/U0.json`…`U6.json` in run 1). Both hard-code absolute machine paths (`const REPO = '~/Projects/flightdeck'`, `flightcrew-build.js:12`; `flightcrew-targets.js:14` even hard-codes a scratchpad session UUID). Their status as construction rather than system is what the run itself flagged: run 1's escalation records "fc boundary reports .claude/workflows/flightcrew-build.js outside the allowed paths; it was written by the session that drove this build and needs a decision before the boundary can be clean" (`flightcrew-buildout/events.jsonl:23`), and run 2 carried it as finding F9 (`flightcrew-buildout-2/report.md:40`, `review/pass-1.json:108`) and as a watch risk in the plan (`flightcrew-buildout-2/plan.json:85`, `plan.md:16`).

### B9. `MANIFEST.txt` and what T28 enforces

`flightdeck/flightcrew/MANIFEST.txt` is 264 lines: one repository-relative path per line under section-comment banners (`# ── flightcrew: the runner and its command modules ───`), covering `flightcrew/**`, `launch/README.md`, `launch/RUNLOG.md`, the spec folder, the buildout launch, `testbench/**` and `manuals/**`. Its own header (lines 1-4) says: "`fc doctor` and the testbench suite `manifest` read this file and check that every listed path exists and is not empty. A new file added under flightcrew/, launch/, testbench/ or manuals/ belongs on a line here."

T28 (`testbench/suites/manifest/run.mjs`, covers B38 and I13) enforces five things:
1. at least one path line, no whitespace inside a line (`run.mjs:83-91`);
2. every listed path exists, is a file and is non-empty (`run.mjs:94-109`);
3. every path is plain, repository-relative and starts `flightdeck/` (`run.mjs:112-121`);
4. every path in a hard-coded `REQUIRED` list (`run.mjs:39-68` — commands, validators, gates, hooks, 10 schemas, 10 crew roles, the three workflow scripts, 8 kickoff parts, 29 suite names, three fixture files, 13 manuals) appears in the manifest (`run.mjs:124-131`);
5. no `flightdeck/launch/` line other than `launch/specs/`, `launch/flightcrew-buildout/`, `README.md`, `RUNLOG.md`, `runs.keep` (`run.mjs:70, 133-138`).

**It does not lock the set.** There is no reverse-direction check: nothing walks the tree and asserts every existing file is listed. Adding a new file and not listing it passes (unless it happens to be on the 200-odd-entry `REQUIRED` list); removing a file fails only case 2 (path exists) if the line is left behind, and passes cleanly if the line is removed too, unless the path is in `REQUIRED`. `fc doctor` is weaker still — `checkManifest` (`bin/cmd/doctor.mjs:189-209`) only reports listed-but-missing paths. So the manifest is a required-subset check plus an existence check, not a locked file set, despite its own header's "belongs on a line here" instruction being unenforced.

Assembly and rendering: `fc launch new` and `fc launch kickoff` render `launch/&lt;L&gt;/kickoff.md` as a header block followed by `base.md`, one `shape-*.md`, one `task-*.md`, in that order; parts named `--kickoff base+shape-&lt;s&gt;+task-&lt;t&gt;` (or `--parts` on re-render), default `base+shape-session+task-feature` (`templates/kickoff/README.md:7`). The code: `partVersion()` reads `/^&lt;!--\s*version:\s*(\d+)\s*--&gt;/` from the first line (`bin/cmd/launch.mjs:117-119`); a part not in the library or without a version comment is a usage error (`launch.mjs:130-139`); a kickoff must start with `base` and name exactly one shape and one task (`launch.mjs:131, 165`). The version string is formed at `launch.mjs:166`: `parts.map((part) =&gt; `${part.name}@${part.version}`).join('+')` — e.g. `base@1+shape-workflow@1+task-feature@1`. It is written into `launch.json` at `kickoff.version` (`launch.mjs:285, 302`), mirrored into `plan.json`'s `kickoff_version` and the run-log entry (`templates/kickoff/README.md:19`). `kickoff.md` is rendered, never hand-edited (`kickoff/README.md:9`).

`constitution-fragment.md` (7 lines) is the block merged into the repository's own `CLAUDE.md` — "the project constitution — the repository's `CLAUDE.md`, into which `flightdeck/flightcrew/templates/constitution-fragment.md` is merged — says how the project always works" (`kickoff/README.md:3`). Its contents: launches live under `flightdeck/launch/`, `FLIGHTCREW_LAUNCH` semantics, `fc` is invoked by path and never installed, which manuals to read, the locked/allowed-path guard behaviour and the `fc launch escalate wrong-check` escape, and that plans/kickoffs/reports/evidence are rendered by `fc` and never hand-edited. It is installed by being printed for the human to paste: `fc distribute` prints it under the heading "add to the project instructions:" (`bin/cmd/distribute.mjs:146-149`) — i.e. nothing writes it anywhere; only the settings fragment and `.gitignore` line are printed alongside it in the same manual-step block.

### B11. Contradictions between manuals

**Phase moves, human vs agent.** `manuals/launch/launch-anatomy.md:91` heads a two-column table `| phase | human | orchestrator or agents |`. In it:
- `launch-anatomy.md:94` puts **`fc launch phase plan` in the human column**;
- `launch-anatomy.md:98` puts **`fc launch phase verify` in the orchestrator column**;
- `launch-anatomy.md:99` puts **`fc launch phase review` in the orchestrator column**;
- `launch-anatomy.md:100` puts **`fc launch phase report` in the orchestrator column** with `fc launch end` in the human column.

`journey.md` agrees on `phase plan` (stage 3, human — `journey.md:21`) and on verify/review/report (`journey.md:27, 28, 29`), and `crew/orchestrator.md:18` states the general rule: "Every phase change is `fc launch phase &lt;p&gt;`, except after a G1 or G2 approval, which moves the phase itself. Every gate decision is a human's." So the phase-move split is consistent in substance — but `launch-anatomy.md` never states the G1/G2 exception, and instead attributes the *result* of it to the human by listing "`fc launch gate G1 approve|exit`" in the human column (`:95`) without saying the approval itself performs the phase move, whereas `journey.md:23, 25` does say so ("`fc launch gate G1 approve` (phase to contracts)"). A reader of `launch-anatomy.md` alone would look for a missing `fc launch phase contracts` and `fc launch phase implement`; neither exists in either column of that table.

**Stage 9 actor.** `journey.md:29` gives the actor column of stage 9 (Report) as "`fc launch end`" — a command, not a role — while every other row names a human or an agent; `launch-anatomy.md:100` splits the same stage between human (`fc launch end`) and orchestrator (`fc launch phase report`), and `orchestrator.md:25` says "a human ends the run with `fc launch end &lt;outcome&gt;`".

**Which manual owns `shape-sessions`.** `manuals/harness/workflows.md:9` says "`flightdeck/manuals/orchestration/kickoff.md` carries `shape-sessions`", but the three shapes are also described together in `templates/kickoff/README.md:14`; `workflows.md` covers "the session and workflow pair" only, so `shape-session` is described in two manuals and `shape-sessions` in a third.

**`agent_type` rule stated three ways.** `manuals/harness/workflows.md:26` — "`agent_type` is `implementer` when `.claude/agents/flightcrew/implementer.md` exists, `general-purpose` otherwise" (a file test). `workflows/README.md:21` — "`implementer` where the crew has been distributed to the target directory, `general-purpose` where it has not — pass it explicitly in that case". `fc-implement.js:218` — `const agentType = args.agent_type ?? 'implementer'`, i.e. the default is unconditionally `implementer`; nothing detects the file, so the "otherwise" branch exists only if the caller supplies it. Meanwhile `fc-review.js` hard-codes `agentType: 'critic'`, `'implementer'`, `'verifier'` with no override at all — matching `workflows/README.md:29` ("This script's agent types are fixed") but not covered by `workflows.md`'s table, which lists only `model?` as fc-review's optional arg (`workflows.md:21`).

**Manifest instruction vs enforcement.** `MANIFEST.txt:4` says any new file under the four directories "belongs on a line here"; nothing checks that (see B9).

**Distribution target.** `workflows/README.md:5` says `fc distribute --apply` copies every `*.js` to `&lt;target&gt;/workflows/`, `&lt;target&gt;` defaulting to `$REPO/.claude`; `launch-anatomy.md:93` gives the once-per-repository form as `fc distribute --apply --target .claude`; `shape-workflow.md:3` says the copies land in "the harness directory's workflows folder" without naming it. Three phrasings for one path.

### B12. Pre-existing state documents on other branches

`flightdeck/STRUCTURE.md` is **absent from `flightcrew-buildout`** (`git cat-file -e flightcrew-buildout:flightdeck/STRUCTURE.md` → "path … does not exist in 'flightcrew-buildout'"). It exists on `main`.

On `main`, `flightdeck/STRUCTURE.md` says:

- `flightcrew/bin/` — "runners — runnable scripts needed for every launch" (`main:flightdeck/STRUCTURE.md:26`), with one subdirectory `worker/` (`:27`).
- `launch/` — "runs — orchestrated build runs, self contained" (`:35`), containing `example-launch/` with `checks/` and `specs/` (`:36-38`).
- `testbench/` — "tests — harnesses reusable across the git branch" (`:50`), with `benches/` (`rubrics/spec/fixtures/`, `validator-suite/fixtures/`) and `runs/` (`:51-57`).
- Invariants: "This map records directories only. Individual files are deliberately absent so it stays true as files churn." (`:7`); "Every folder that needs describing carries a `.keep` file whose name states that folder's default task" (`:8`); `testbench/tests.keep` "reserving `runs/` for local test results and requiring merge protection on the folder" (`:64`).

Which of those the built system contradicts:

- **`flightcrew/bin/` as "runnable scripts"** — the built `bin/` is a single entry point plus a command-module tree (`bin/fc`, `bin/fc.mjs`, `bin/cmd/*.mjs` ×19, `bin/worker/{render,return}.mjs`); `cmd/*.mjs` are not independently runnable scripts but subcommand modules of `fc.mjs`. The `worker/` subdirectory survives but with different contents (`main` has `bin/worker/render-worker-prompt.mjs`; the build has `render.mjs` and `return.mjs`).
- **`launch/` "self contained"** — the built `launch/` also holds `RUNLOG.md`, cross-run and beside the folders, which `launch/README.md:9` and `launch-anatomy.md:101` explicitly note ("which sits beside the launch folders, not inside one"); and `launch/specs/&lt;S&gt;/` is declared "the canonical, cross-run home of one spec" (`launch/README.md:7`), directly against "self contained". `example-launch/checks/` never materialised: neither committed launch has a `checks/` directory, and neither does `launch/specs/flightcrew-v1/`.
- **`testbench/` "harnesses reusable across the git branch"** — the built testbench is 29 suites pinned to one spec (`suites/*/run.mjs`, each header naming its `T&lt;n&gt;` and spec node), locked as targets of `flightcrew-v1` and listed in `tests-map.v1.json`'s `locked_paths`; only `benches/` retains the reusable-harness character. `runs/` survives but as `testbench/runs/.gitignore` rather than as a described keep-file folder.
- **"This map records directories only… Every folder that needs describing carries a `.keep`"** — the built tree adds `flightcrew/workflows/`, `flightcrew/hooks/`, `flightcrew/checks/gates/`, `flightcrew/checks/lib/`, `flightcrew/templates/kickoff/`, `manuals/harness/`, `manuals/launch/`, `manuals/orchestration/`, `testbench/suites/`, `testbench/lib/`, `testbench/fixtures/` — none carries a `.keep`; each is instead documented by a `README.md` (`flightcrew/README.md`, `hooks/README.md`, `crew/README.md`, `workflows/README.md`, `templates/kickoff/README.md`, `manuals/README.md`, `testbench/README.md`, `launch/README.md`). The surviving keeps are the six inherited ones (`blackbox/archive.keep`, `hangar/workspace.keep`, `missions/ideas.keep`, `radar/visuals.keep`, `manuals/documentation.keep`, `launch/runs.keep`, `flightcrew/orchestration.keep`, `bin/runners.keep`, `checks/checks.keep`, `crew/agents.keep`). The system substituted README-per-directory for keep-per-directory without a document recording the change — and `STRUCTURE.md` itself was not carried onto the branch, so nothing on `flightcrew-buildout` maps the tree.
- `main`'s branch note (`:68-70`) that `flightcrew/crew/spec-interviewer.md` "is deliberately empty. It is what the next launch builds" is superseded: the built crew has no `spec-interviewer.md`; the roster is `spec-builder`, `spec-judge`, `spec-attacker`, `explorer`, `test-builder`, `planner`, `orchestrator`, `implementer`, `verifier`, `critic` (`suites/manifest/run.mjs:10`), and `main`'s `worker.md`, `isolated-worker.md`, `reviewer.md`, `crew.json` are gone.

## Factual tensions

**Inside the built workflow scripts**

1. B39/T29 versus the runtime, and unsatisfiably so: the shipped scripts end `export default result;` (`fc-explore.js:165`, `fc-implement.js:278`, `fc-review.js:497`); the runtime form actually used in production is a top-level `return` (`.claude/workflows/flightcrew-build.js:128`, `flightcrew-targets.js:130`); and a top-level `return` fails T29's own `node --experimental-default-type=module --check` case (`SyntaxError: Illegal return statement`). No file can satisfy both the locked suite and the runtime.
2. Neither `manuals/harness/workflows.md` nor `manuals/harness/claude-code-facts.md` states any ending requirement, so the RUNLOG's "which the runtime rejects" is documented nowhere in the manuals it should have been recorded in — yet `workflows/README.md:7` claims `claude-code-facts.md` documents "the default export", which it does not.
3. The scripts have never been executed by anything: T29 reads them (`run.mjs:2`), the runtime bindings are never stubbed, and no recorded run invoked them (events show `SubagentStart`, `return`, `phase`, `gate` only). Every behavioural claim in `workflows.md:20-22` and `workflows/README.md:17-41` is untested.
4. `fc-implement.js`'s stop condition is not what the halt field implies: a red pilot fills `stopped_on` and leaves `halt` null (`fc-implement.js:239-240, 272-273`), so `halt` is a false negative for a stopped run; the README warns of this (`README.md:19`), the manual repeats it (`workflows.md:20`), but the field naming still invites the wrong test.
5. `fc-implement.js:237` searches the whole accumulated `returns` array for a halt, not just the current chunk, so once a halt exists every subsequent chunk in the same group short-circuits — but the loop that produced it has already dispatched the current chunk in full.
6. A synthesised halt is always `halt.kind: 'budget'` (`fc-implement.js:210`) regardless of cause; the causes recorded in `detail` are "returned nothing", "did not match the worker return shape" and "the dispatch did not complete" — none of which is a budget event. The schema's own enum offers `blocked` and `unsatisfiable`.
7. `fc-review.js`'s `unrouted` is reset each pass (`fc-review.js:183`) and returned as whatever the last executed pass produced, so findings that were unrouted in an earlier pass are silently dropped from the result the orchestrator is told to place (`workflows.md:41`).
8. `fc-review.js:214` omits the `model` override that every other agent call in the same script honours; `args.model` therefore does not reach the verifier.
9. The `violations()` validator is copied verbatim into all three scripts (`fc-explore.js:95-120`, `fc-implement.js:137-162`, `fc-review.js:67-92`) and implements only a subset of JSON Schema; the returns it accepts are not necessarily the returns `fc return` will accept, and `fc return` is the authority (`workflows.md:48`).
10. `agent_type` selection is described as a file test in the manual (`workflows.md:26`) but is a plain default in the code (`fc-implement.js:218`); `fc-review.js` cannot select at all.
11. `shape-workflow.md` is at `version: 2` in the library, but both committed launches record `shape-workflow@1` in `launch.json`, `plan.json` and `RUNLOG.md` — the shape part was revised after the runs that named it, and no re-render exists.

def sect(marker, prose):
    global body
    i=body.index(marker); j=i+len(marker)
    lines=body[j:].split('\n'); k=0
    while k<len(lines) and (lines[k].startswith('<!--') or lines[k]==''):
        if lines[k]=='' and k+1<len(lines) and lines[k+1].startswith('#'): break
        k+=1
    body=body[:j]+'\n'.join(lines[:k])+'\n'+prose.strip('\n')+'\n'+'\n'.join(lines[k:])

P['### 3. Unrequested decisions froze into interface\n']="""

**Why it matters.** The method's spec stage exists so that decisions are made before anything is frozen, by the human with help, and attacked from a fresh context.
