P['## Hooks and permissions\n']="""
The constitution asks two things of this layer. Each role's reach is declared in its own file's frontmatter: tools, model and effort, isolation, memory scope, permission mode and role-scoped hooks, so that reading the file is enough to know what the role can touch. And hooks enforce what instructions cannot, at three points: before an action, to block a forbidden path or a destructive command; after an action, to run a check whenever a file changes; and at the end of a turn, to refuse to let the agent stop until the definition of done passes. The built system has six hooks under `flightdeck/flightcrew/hooks/`: an event log, a lock guard, a boundary guard, a structural check, a stop gate and a session-end hook. A **guard** refuses a single tool call by printing a deny decision and exiting zero. A **gate hook** holds the turn by exiting two until a check passes. A **backstop** is a mechanism that catches what a guard cannot see, by a different route or after the fact. Every hook resolves a launch through one root source and, by the README's no-op rule, does nothing and says nothing when it cannot.
"""
P['### 4. Nothing sandboxes the shell\n']="""
**What.** The two guards intercept three tools, Edit, Write and NotebookEdit, per `flightdeck/flightcrew/hooks/lib.mjs:15` and the fragment's matcher at `settings.fragment.json:44`. Bash is in the tool list of nine of the ten roles and no hook intercepts it. `hooks/README.md:53-59` names the hole and three backstops: deny rules on the locked paths, which apply to the same three tools; a sandbox filesystem deny list, which does reach Bash and ships as `_sandbox_example` with the note that it documents and does not configure, recorded at `flightdeck/manuals/harness/hooks.md:60` as inactive until a manual step is taken; and the runner's locked-path check at verify, a detector after the fact. The fragment's allow list at `settings.fragment.json:69-92` grants `git add`, `git commit` and `git switch` to every role that holds Bash, and lists all three workflows as model-invocable. Against the constitution's three hook points, the before-action hooks cover paths and never commands, the after-action hook is a parse check per file extension rather than a test run, and the end-of-turn gate runs in two phases of seven.

**Why it matters.** The constitution's rule is that an agent with a capability will eventually use it, and that a rule an agent should follow is one it will eventually break, so every guarantee a run relies on must be enforced by something that does not consult the agent. A locked file that a shell command can rewrite is locked by instruction. The one backstop that would make it locked by enforcement is the sandbox, and it was left as an example. The constitution also asks that irreversible actions be denied outright and that workflows with side effects be human-invoked only; the allow list does the opposite on both. Locked paths remain the right mechanism for what a frozen status field cannot express, a test folder, a fixture, a library a check imports; what is missing is the layer that makes them hold against the shell.

**Effect on the system.** The lock's guarantee holds only while every implementer chooses the file tools over the shell. The critic's inputs, the diff boundary and the locked-path check would all report a shell edit afterwards, at verify, after the tokens are spent. There is no Bash sandboxing anywhere in the built system, and no PreToolUse hook on Bash.
"""
P['### 5. The gates fail open and fail silent\n']="""
**What.** Every hook runs through a wrapper, `hooks/lib.mjs:213-235`, that catches every thrown error, writes it to a log if a launch is known, and exits zero; a guard that crashes therefore permits the action it was about to refuse. The stop gate at `hooks/stop-gate.mjs:78-88` writes one log line and exits zero when no tests map is pinned or the map file is unreadable, which from inside the session is indistinguishable from a green gate. The gate runs only in the verify and contracts phases, `stop-gate.mjs:11`; the implement phase, the one in which a role holds general write access, has no end-of-turn gate. On the eighth consecutive block the gate writes a stall message to stderr and exits zero, `stop-gate.mjs:134-140`, and the run log records that Claude Code does not display stderr on exit zero; the stall also records a trigger event, after which the guard wrapper denies every subsequent edit with no displayed reason. Two structural implementations exist: the hook at `hooks/structural-check.mjs` has no timeout, and `checks/gates/structural-gate.mjs` has one and is wired to nothing.

**Why it matters.** The verification guide's fourth rung, a deterministic gate that refuses to end the turn until the check passes, is the floor for an unattended run, and the eight-block override is the stall detector the run abandons on. A gate that silently disables itself when its inputs are missing, that is absent from the phase it most needs to cover, and whose stall signal is invisible to the session it stalls, is a gate in name. The guides' rule that a hook is deterministic and cannot be forgotten assumes it also cannot fail open.

**Effect on the system.** An implement-phase session ends its turns freely. A verify-phase session with a missing pin passes its gate. A stalled run keeps going, now unable to edit anything, with the reason in a file nobody is told to read. Which of the two structural checks a run gets depends on nothing the run controls.
"""
P["### 6. A role's reach is declared in two places and nowhere fully\n"]="""
**What.** Tools, model, turn budget, isolation and permission mode are declared in each role's frontmatter under `flightdeck/flightcrew/crew/`. Command allows, agent dispatch allows, workflow allows and the two path deny rules are declared in `hooks/settings.fragment.json`. Neither expresses the other. The only cross-check anywhere, `flightdeck/testbench/suites/schemas/run.mjs:501-502`, asserts that each role name has a matching agent allow entry. `fc doctor` compares hook commands and agent bytes and never the two permission surfaces. One consequence is already recorded in the run log: the fragment denies edits under `flightdeck/launch/specs/**`, which is exactly where `crew/test-builder.md:22-23` tells the test-builder to write the map and its fallback checks, and a deny beats the role's own Write and Edit tools. Against the constitution's six frontmatter fields: tools appear on every role; isolation on the implementer only; memory scope on none; permission mode on two; role-scoped hooks on none; and the orchestrator's model is set to inherit, the case the constitution names as the one to avoid.

**Why it matters.** The constitution's rule is that a role and its permissions are one concern held in one file, so that reading the file is enough to know what the role does and what it can touch, and that nothing a role can do exceeds what is declared there. Two files with no reconciliation means the answer to what a role may do is the intersection of two documents that were written separately, and a contradiction between them is discovered by the role at run time. There are no role-scoped hooks in the built system: every hook is global, dispatched by event and tool, and discriminates by launch phase and path, never by which role is acting. A worker-only test-after-edit hook, or a critic that cannot write even if its tools were widened, cannot be expressed.

**Effect on the system.** The test-builder is blocked by the fragment from doing what its role file instructs. A reader of any role file learns its tools and not its commands; a reader of the fragment learns its commands and not its tools. Every role except the implementer shares the session's permission mode and working tree, and the orchestrator runs on whatever model started the session.
"""
P['## Workflows\n']="""

**Why it matters.** The repeatability principle is that the orchestration is a script, saved and rerun, so that a relaunch is a controlled experiment. P['## Documents and record\n']="""
The sources treat documents as the run's context and its memory. What an agent reads before acting must be true, because the agent has no way to test it; and what a run leaves behind must be a record of what happened, with its provenance marked, because the run log is written from it. The built system's manuals, README files, manifest and templates are that context and that record.

P['### 9. The manuals are command sequences\n']="""
**What.** Two hundred and forty-one lines across fourteen manuals contain a runner command, and four manuals hold most of them: `flightdeck/manuals/launch/launch-anatomy.md` with 51, `orchestration/journey.md` with 27, `harness/workflows.md` with 21 and `orchestration/review.md` with 20. **Why it matters.** A manual that describes conduct as a sequence of commands describes the interface of one program, and the runner problems document treats that program as a problem. ## 2. RENDER — `flightdeck/flightcrew/bin/cmd/launch.mjs`

- `partVersion(text)` (L118–121): `/^&lt;!--\s*version:\s*(\d+)\s*--&gt;/` against **the first line only**; returns a Number or null.
- `loadParts(ctx, spec)` (L129–141): splits the spec on `+`; refuses an empty list (`'a kickoff needs parts: base+shape-&lt;s&gt;+task-&lt;t&gt;'`), refuses when `names[0] !== 'base'`, refuses a missing file (`kickoff part not found: …`) and a missing version comment (`kickoff part has no version comment: …`). Parts are kept **in the order named**, `text.trim()`ed — so each part's `&lt;!-- version: N --&gt;` line is carried into the rendered file.
- `renderKickoff(ctx, launchDir, launchJson, partsSpec)` (L161–183): finds one part starting `shape-` and one starting `task-`; refuses otherwise (`a kickoff names one shape-&lt;s&gt; and one task-&lt;t&gt; part; got …`). Version = `parts.map(p =&gt; `${p.name}@${p.version}`).join('+')` — i.e. **in the order given on the command line, not a canonical order**. Body = `parts.map(part =&gt; part.text).join('\n\n')`; output = `${header}\n\n${body}\n`. Header comment: "Pure apart from the launch folder it reads the pins and the prior reports from, so re-rendering an unchanged launch restores exactly the bytes the last render wrote — which is what makes a hand edit to kickoff.md recoverable."
- Header fields (L175–180) and their sources:
  - `# Kickoff: ${task.name} · ${shape.name}` — the two part names.
  - `launch:` — `repoPath(ctx, launchDir)`.
  - `spec:` — `repoPath(launchDir + launchJson.spec.path)` + ` @ ` + `launchJson.spec.commit ?? 'draft'`.
  - `tests-map:` — same from `launchJson.tests_map`, or the literal `(none)` when `tests_map` is null.
  - `kickoff version:` — the assembled version string.
  - `read first:` — `path.join(ctx.launchDir, 'RUNLOG.md')`, always.
  - `prior reports:` — `priorReports()` (L145–152): every other launch folder whose `launch.json.spec.name` matches, that has a `report.md`, sorted by path; else `none`.
  - `write plan with: fc plan write` — a constant.
  - `evidence:` — `${launchRel}/evidence.html`, a constant suffix (not read from launch.json).
- `partsOf(launchJson)` (L186–189): strips `@N` off `launch.json.kickoff.version`; falls back to `DEFAULT_PARTS` when empty. `const DEFAULT_PARTS = 'base+shape-session+task-feature';` (L45).
- `writeKickoff` (L193–196): renders, writes to `launchJson.kickoff?.path ?? 'kickoff.md'`, returns the version.
- Flags: `fc launch new … [--kickoff base+shape-&lt;s&gt;+task-&lt;t&gt;]` (usage L29, parsed L257, used L301 as `flags.kickoff ?? DEFAULT_PARTS`); `fc launch kickoff [--parts …]` (usage L32, `kickoff()` L461–467, `flags.parts ?? partsOf(launchJson)`).
- Re-render points — exactly three: `newLaunch` (L301–308, rendered *before* the folder exists so a bad part leaves nothing written), `pin tests-map` (L450: `launchJson.kickoff.version = writeKickoff(ctx, dir, launchJson, partsOf(launchJson));`), and `fc launch kickoff` (L464). Nothing else writes kickoff.md.
- Never hand-edited: file header L7–8 — "Nothing here is hand-written by an agent: kickoff.md and the pinned copies are produced by these commands, which is why re-rendering a kickoff restores it byte for byte." Enforced only socially plus by the last Never entry in `base.md:27` ("hand-edit kickoff.md or plan.md (both are re-rendered from their sources)").

Header as rendered, `flightdeck/launch/flightcrew-buildout-2/kickoff.md:1-5` (the header block is 5 lines; line 6 is blank and line 7 is `&lt;!-- version: 1 --&gt;`):

# Kickoff: task-feature · shape-workflow

| shape-session | (unused) | 2 | n/a |
| shape-sessions | (unused) | 2 | n/a |
| task-migration / task-audit / task-agent | (unused) | 2 | n/a |

Every part used by either run is out of date relative to the library, in all three positions. Both rendered kickoff files still carry the embedded `&lt;!-- version: 1 --&gt;` markers at `kickoff.md:7`, `:14` (shape) and `:21` (task), so the file and the recorded string agree with each other and both disagree with the library. Nothing in the render, the validator or `fc verify` compares them: re-running `fc launch kickoff` would silently rewrite both kickoffs at `base@3+shape-workflow@2+task-feature@2` and leave `plan.json.kickoff_version` and the RUNLOG entries at `@1`.

---

## 4. VALIDATOR — `flightdeck/flightcrew/checks/validators/validate-kickoff.mjs`

Five rules (header comment L5–11; implementation L157–223):

- **kickoff-rule-1** (L170–175): the first line matches `/^Kickoff:\s*\S/` after `# `, and every label in `FIELDS` (L24) is present: `launch`, `spec`, `tests-map`, `kickoff version`, `read first`, `prior reports`, `write plan with`, `evidence`. Field parsing (`parseHeader`, L62–81) splits each line on runs of ≥2 spaces then on the first `': '`; the block ends at the first blank line, `&lt;!--` line or `## ` heading.
- **kickoff-rule-2** (L178–192): `spec` and `tests-map` paths resolve as files against the tree the kickoff sits in or the resolved root. `tests-map: (none)` is accepted only while the launch has no `tests_map` — otherwise "tests-map reads (none) but the launch has a tests map pinned; re-render the kickoff".
- **kickoff-rule-3** (L193–200): a recorded commit is `/^[0-9a-f]{7,40}$/`, or the literal `draft` when `launch.json.allow_draft === true`.
- **kickoff-rule-4** (L204–209): every whitespace/comma-separated token of `prior reports` resolves; `none` exempt.
- **kickoff-rule-5** (L212–220): the backticked single-word names under `## Roles` (`rolesNames`, L84–97; name pattern `/^[a-z][a-z0-9-]*$/`) each have `flightdeck/flightcrew/crew/&lt;name&gt;.md`; zero names is an error.

What it does **not** check: the `kickoff version` string's *shape* or its agreement with the library (only that the field exists); whether any `fc` command named in the body still exists (the manual admits this at `manuals/orchestration/kickoff.md:72`); the presence of `## Conduct`, `## Escalate`, `## Communication`, `## Budgets`, `## Outputs`, `## Never`; that the body was actually assembled from parts; whether the file matches a re-render; whether `launch`/`read first`/`write plan with`/`evidence` values point anywhere real (only that the labels exist); backticked names outside `## Roles`. `warnings` is always empty, so `--strict` can never differ from the default.

Wiring: `fc validate kickoff` → `bin/cmd/validate.mjs:23`; `validate-all.mjs:20` imports `checkKickoff`; `launch.mjs:516-518` makes `fc launch phase plan` refuse while it exits non-zero.

**Schema:** there is no `kickoff.schema.json`. `flightdeck/flightcrew/schemas/` holds `check-result`, `critic-findings`, `event`, `explorer-return`, `launch`, `plan`, `spec`, `tests-map`, `verifier-verdict`, `worker-return` — ten schemas, none for the kickoff. The only structured form of the kickoff anywhere is `launch.json.kickoff{path,version}` (two strings) plus `plan.json.kickoff_version` (one string); the document itself exists only as rendered markdown assembled from markdown parts.

---

## 5. WHAT IT SAYS — `base.md` v3 read closely

**Conduct steps and the fc commands each names**

1. `fc launch status`, `fc return explorer &lt;file&gt; --id X&lt;n&gt;`
2. `fc plan write &lt;json-path|--stdin&gt;`, `fc launch gate G1 approve|exit`
3. `fc worker render &lt;unit&gt;`, `fc return worker &lt;file&gt; --unit &lt;id&gt;`, `fc worker merge &lt;unit&gt;`, `fc launch gate G2 approve|exit`
4. `fc worker render &lt;unit&gt;`, `fc return worker`, `fc worker merge &lt;unit&gt;`
5. `fc launch phase verify`, `fc verify`, `fc verifier render`, `fc return verifier &lt;file&gt; --pass &lt;n&gt;`
6. `fc launch phase review`, `fc critic render --pass &lt;n&gt;`, `fc return critic &lt;file&gt; --pass &lt;n&gt;`, `fc verify` (re-run), `fc return critic --resolve F&lt;n&gt; --commit &lt;sha&gt;`
7. `fc launch phase report`, `fc launch end &lt;accepted|accepted-with-reservations|abandoned|partial&gt;` (`--units` for `partial`)

**Escalation list** (`base.md:12`) — five conditions and six kinds:

&gt; "Stop and ask a human when the spec is silent or contradictory on something a unit needs, when an implementer reports that a locked check is wrong or unsatisfiable, when an abandon trigger in the plan fires, when a permission or a tool blocks a required action, or when a ceiling is exceeded. Run `fc launch escalate &lt;kind&gt; --detail "…"` naming the finding, where `&lt;kind&gt;` is one of `spec-gap` …, `wrong-check` …, `trigger` …, `blocked` …, `budget` (a ceiling was exceeded) and `halt` (a worker returned a halt), then end the turn; propose nothing else in the same message."

Note `halt` is a sixth kind with no matching entry in the five-condition sentence.

**Roles** (`base.md:15`) — five backticked names, each with receives/never-receives: `explorer` (one question, its stage, the paths it may read → cited answer; never the plan or a unit's work); `planner` (spec, tests map, run log, "the roster at flightdeck/flightcrew/crew/README.md", explorer answers → plan content; never worker transcripts); `implementer` (one rendered dispatch: unit's spec nodes, checks by id, paths, branch → worker return; never the plan, the kickoff, another unit's dispatch); `verifier` (evidence, tests map, merged branch → verdict; never implementer reasoning); `critic` (pinned spec, diff since lock, evidence → findings; never the plan, the kickoff, the returns, earlier findings). Then: "Dispatch caps are defaults the plan may tighten and may not loosen: one question per explorer, one unit per implementer, and at most implementers_concurrent implementers at a time. Workers never message each other. Every dispatch is a rendered prompt, with one exception: a review-phase fix dispatch, which the conductor assembles from the finding, the spec node and that unit's checks, and nothing else."

**Communication** (`base.md:18`): summaries up / transcripts never; every return in its declared shape, written by the conductor to its file (`returns/` for worker, explorer, verifier; `review/` for critic passes) and stored through `fc return`; raw check output in the evidence, never paraphrased; "State what is checked, what is reviewed and what is merely stated, and keep the three apart"; evidence page rewritten "at every check, gate, phase change, return and ending".

**Budgets** (`base.md:21`): ceilings live in launch.json; the eight named dimensions are agents, concurrent implementers, turns per agent, gate iterations, stop blocks, critic passes, minutes, tokens-when-observed; "Defaults hold unless the plan tightens them. Exceeding a ceiling is an escalation."

**Outputs** (`base.md:24`): one branch per unit `&lt;launch&gt;/&lt;unit name&gt;` in its own worktree, landed by `fc worker merge`; every return stored through `fc return` at its fixed path; evidence page current at the end of every phase; `report.md` by `fc launch end` with the run-log stub inserted and mechanical fields filled; worktree/branch cleanup lines printed for the human.

**Never list** — six entries, all with an enforcement twin named:

| never | twin named |
|---|---|
| edit a locked path | lock-guard hook + `fc locked` |
| write outside allowed paths and the launch folder | boundary-guard hook + `fc boundary` |
| continue after an abandon trigger fired | "the guards deny every edit and `fc` refuses to dispatch" |
| resolve a spec conflict without a human | "`fc launch escalate` is the only route" |
| hand a worker anything beyond its rendered dispatch | `fc worker render`, plus the step-6 review-fix exception |
| hand-edit kickoff.md or plan.md | "both are re-rendered from their sources" — a *procedure*, not a hook or command; nothing denies the edit |

So six of six name something, but the sixth's twin is not an enforcement mechanism.

**fc command count in `base.md` v3:** 32 backticked `fc …` mentions, ~16 distinct commands: `fc launch status`, `fc launch gate`, `fc launch phase verify|review|report`, `fc launch escalate`, `fc launch end`, `fc plan write`, `fc worker render`, `fc worker merge`, `fc return explorer|worker|verifier|critic`, `fc verifier render`, `fc critic render`, `fc verify`, `fc locked`, `fc boundary`.

---

## 6. WHO READS IT

- **Told to read it:** the orchestrator, and only the orchestrator. `crew/orchestrator.md:6` `initialPrompt: "Run flightdeck/flightcrew/bin/fc launch status. Read the active launch's kickoff.md and follow it; do nothing else first."`; `:10` "The kickoff is your conduct: where it and your own judgement disagree, the kickoff wins."; `:14` lists `kickoff.md` first among what it reads; `:18` "Run `fc launch status`, read `kickoff.md`, and follow it." `crew/README.md:19` gives orchestrator "gets: kickoff, spec, map, plan, returns, prior reports". `manuals/orchestration/kickoff.md:3` "read by the orchestrator only"; `:10` table row "`kickoff.md` | the orchestrator only".
- **Told not to read it:** implementer (`crew/README.md:20` never-gets "other units, the whole plan, the kickoff"; `crew/implementer.md:16` "You do not read the plan, the kickoff, another unit's dispatch"); critic (`crew/README.md:22` "plan, kickoff, reasoning, prior findings"; `crew/critic.md:14` "You do not read the plan, the kickoff, any worker's reasoning or return, or an earlier pass's findings"); explorer (`crew/explorer.md:14` "You do not read a plan, a kickoff, a run log…"); spec-judge (`crew/spec-judge.md:17` "You receive no interview transcript, no kickoff…"). The verifier's never-list (`crew/README.md:21`) says "implementer reasoning, stored returns" and does **not** name the kickoff either way.
- **Partial exception — the planner:** `crew/planner.md:14` "Your dispatch also hands you the launch name, **the kickoff header block** (which carries the kickoff version string), the spec pin … and the launch's `ceilings` object"; `:23` "Set `shape` to the `shape-&lt;x&gt;` part named in the kickoff version and `kickoff_version` to that version string". So the header block travels to the planner; the body does not.
- **Dispatch templates:** none of `worker-dispatch.template.md` (headings: Intent, Scope, Constraints, Interfaces, Decisions, What this unit must make true, Checks that prove it, Paths, How to work, Return), `critic-dispatch.template.md` (Spec at commit, Diff since lock, Evidence, Locked paths changed since the lock, Return), `verifier-dispatch.template.md` or `explorer-dispatch.template.md` contains kickoff text or a kickoff placeholder.
- **`bin/worker/render.mjs`:** the sealed prompt draws from the spec, the checks and the launch data only. `render.mjs:9-14`: "A dispatch prompt is sealed… The worker prompt therefore carries the intent, every scope, constraint, interface and decision node, the behaviour and edge nodes the unit's spec_refs name and no others, each check by its id with the ids it covers, and never a check's command text. The critic prompt carries the pinned spec, the diff since the lock commit with the launch folder left out, the evidence summary and the locked-path change list, **and nothing from the plan, the kickoff or the returns**." Confirms the manual's `kickoff.md:16` "`fc worker render` never copies kickoff text."
- `crew/README.md:43`: "The run-chain roles receive their paths from the launch's kickoff header block … which names the launch folder, the pinned spec, the pinned tests map, the run log and the evidence page; every other run-chain input is rendered into the dispatch itself." — this says *roles* (plural) receive paths from the header, which sits against the "orchestrator only" rule and against the sealed-dispatch rule for implementer/critic/verifier/explorer.

## 7. WHAT THE KICKOFF OWNS vs LAUNCH.JSON OWNS

| item | kickoff text | launch.json | plan.json |
|---|---|---|---|
| ceilings | named but not valued (`base.md:21` lists the eight dimensions and points at launch.json; `implementers_concurrent` named by name in `base.md:6,15`, `shape-session.md:3`, `shape-workflow.md:3`, `shape-sessions.md:4`) | **owns the values** (`ceilings` object) | `expected_cost` inside them |
| model tiers | **absent from the whole library** | absent | **owns** `models.explore/unit/critic` (and `crew/README.md` carries the per-role defaults) |
| gate definitions (what a human reads) | **partly** — `base.md:4,5,9` state what the human reads at G1/G2/G3 | only `gates.G1/G2/G3 {status, at, note}` — state, not definition | **owns** `gates.G1/G2/G3` prose per run |
| gate mechanics (`fc launch gate`) | **owns** (`base.md:4,5`) | records the outcome | — |
| abandon triggers | referenced only ("when an abandon trigger in the plan fires", `base.md:12`; Never entry `base.md:27`) | absent | **owns** `abandon_triggers[]` |
| allowed / locked paths | referenced only ("write outside the allowed paths and this launch's folder", `base.md:27`); `task-audit.md:5` adds a rule about them | **owns** `paths.allowed/locked/enforce_boundary` | per-unit `paths[]` inside them |
| acceptance id | `task-feature.md:3` names it literally — "the acceptance check `T1` from the pinned tests map"; `base.md` never mentions it | **owns** `acceptance: "T1"` | via each unit's `checks` |

`launch.template.json:38-53`:

Actual values in both launches: `ceilings` identical — agents 12, implementers_concurrent 4, turns_per_agent 25, gate_iterations 3, stop_blocks 8, critic_passes 2, minutes 240, tokens null, expected_tokens null; `acceptance: "T1"`; G1 and G2 approved with human notes, G3 `pending` in both (neither launch.json records the ending gate).

## 8. CONTEXT vs TOOLING INSTRUCTION

Rough split of `base.md` v3 (27 lines, 6 blank/heading-only pairs; 12 content lines):

- **Tooling instruction — which command to run when:** the seven Conduct steps (L3–9) and the Escalate line (L12) — 8 of 12 content lines, and 30 of the 32 `fc` mentions. Almost every sentence in Conduct is verb + `fc` command + argument.
- **Context — what the orchestrator must know:** Roles (L15, information routing: who receives what, who never does), Communication (L18, where returns are written and what counts as evidence), Budgets (L21, where ceilings live and that exceeding one is an escalation). 3 of 12 lines, ~1 `fc` mention (`fc return` in L18).
- **Mixed:** Outputs (L24) — branch naming and worktree convention (context) plus `fc worker merge`, `fc return`, `fc launch end` (tooling). Never (L27) — prohibitions (context) each annotated with the enforcing hook or command (tooling awareness, not an instruction to run anything).

So roughly two-thirds tooling sequence, one-third routing/knowledge, with the shape and task parts (5–6 lines each) skewing further toward context: `shape-*` is mechanism plus what counts as progress; `task-*` is how to cut units and which risks to name, and names only `fc launch escalate`, `fc launch note`, `fc events append`.

**Hooks, permissions, sandbox, settings:** the kickoff never names a settings file, a permission rule, or a sandbox. It names hooks three times, always as an enforcement twin or a background actor — `base.md:5` "The stop-gate hook runs that unit's checks and the boundary in this phase without being invoked"; `base.md:27` "the lock-guard hook", "the boundary-guard hook"; `shape-session.md:5` "the events the hooks record in the launch folder's events file". "Permission" appears once, as an escalation condition (`base.md:12` "when a permission or a tool blocks a required action"), and once inside the `blocked` kind's gloss. "Worktree" appears in `base.md:24`, `shape-session.md:4`, `shape-workflow.md:4`. Nothing tells the orchestrator to configure, check or read any of them.

## 9. MANUAL — `flightdeck/manuals/orchestration/kickoff.md` (90 lines)

**Purpose** (L3): "the document the orchestrator wakes up to: its standing instructions for how to conduct a run of this shape"; rendered by `fc launch kickoff` "(called by `fc launch new` and `fc launch pin tests-map`)", never hand-edited, read by the orchestrator only; "Everything that defines correctness stays in the spec."

**The routing test** (L5–17): a four-row table (constitution / kickoff / pinned spec / plan) with reader and question; L14 "who must obey it? Everyone: the constitution. The judges of correctness: the spec. Only the conductor: the kickoff. This run only: the plan, or the dispatch itself."; L15 "A correctness line that exists only in the kickoff is invisible to the verifier and the critic"; L16 "`fc worker render` never copies kickoff text"; L17 "one home per rule".

**The library** (L19–28): three kinds of part; the `--kickoff` / `--parts` flags and the `base+shape-session+task-feature` default; when each shape is chosen; the version-comment rule and the three recording sites; "A conduct change is an edit to a part with its version bumped, then `fc launch kickoff`"; L27 "A healthy library shrinks in prose as the harness grows in enforcement."

**Anatomy** (L30–48): render order and a ten-block table mapping blocks to `base.md` headings; L32 gives the rationale for the order ("mission and pointers anchor the run, escalation survives a filling context, and prohibitions close `base.md`"); L47 "Pointers, not copies"; L48 "Every Never has an enforcement twin".

**Assembly and validation** (L50–55): the two render triggers, and the four validator rejections; L55 "`fc launch phase plan` refuses while `fc validate kickoff` exits non-zero" — matches `launch.mjs:516-518`.

**Writing a part** (L57–67), **Before sending it** (L69–79), **Anti-patterns** (L81–90): iteration doctrine — one change per run, versioned so the run log can attribute the next run's behaviour to it (L66); "Test a kickoff change the way a constitution change is tested: by whether behaviour shifts on the next run, not by rereading the prose" (L67); "It is shorter than the last version, or the reason it is not is written in the version-bump commit message for the part" (L79); L26 tells the human to record a mid-run correction in the run-log entry and treat it as a candidate line at the next version bump.

**Claims not matched by the library or the render:**

- L3 and L22 say the kickoff "is rendered by `fc launch kickoff` (called by `fc launch new` and `fc launch pin tests-map`)". Neither `newLaunch` nor `pin` calls the `kickoff` subcommand: `newLaunch` calls `renderKickoff` directly (`launch.mjs:301`) and `pin` calls `writeKickoff` (`launch.mjs:450`). The effect matches; the mechanism described does not.
- L23 "in every shape the orchestrator session, the gates, the `fc` commands and the stored returns are identical" — `shape-sessions.md:3-6` describes more than one Claude Code session, a `FLIGHTCREW_LAUNCH` env var, `fc launch note` stream assignments, and a per-session share of the concurrency ceiling; the session is not identical.
- L32 "the header block, then `base.md` (blocks 2 to 8)" implies blocks are separately addressable; the render (`launch.mjs:181`) joins whole part files, so `base.md`'s seven sections are one atom.
- L37 claims block 2 carries "the phases in order — `targets, plan, contracts, implement, verify, review, report, ended`". `base.md` names only `verify`, `review` and `report` as `fc launch phase` arguments; `targets`, `plan`, `contracts`, `implement` and `ended` never appear as a phase list in the kickoff.
- L38 lists the escalation trigger as "reached ceiling"; `base.md:12` v3 says "when a ceiling is **exceeded**" and glosses `budget` as "a ceiling was exceeded". (The v1 text as rendered says "reached", so the manual is describing the older part.)
- L54 describes only four validator rejections and omits kickoff-rule-1's missing-field and title rules.
- L62 "the library uses exactly two mechanisms: a halting step opens with the literal token `HALT:`… and prohibitions live only in the `## Never` list. No other emphasis mechanism is used." The parts also use bolded-by-convention lead labels `Dispatch:`, `Progress:`, `Stopping:` (`shape-*.md`) and backticked `kind:` tokens; and `task-audit.md:5`, `task-feature.md:4`, `task-migration.md:5` all carry prohibition-shaped sentences ("never let two units in the same parallel wave list overlapping paths", "the pinned map changes only by a re-pin, never by the orchestrator") outside any Never list.
- L77 "Every Never has an enforcement twin, or a trailing parenthetical … stating that no hook enforces it and why." The sixth Never's parenthetical — "(both are re-rendered from their sources)" — states neither an enforcer nor that none exists.
- L24's example version string `base@1+shape-session@1+task-feature@1` and L52's "`fc launch new` renders the header … with `tests-map: (none)`" both hold; but the manual nowhere states that the recorded version can drift from the library, which is the current state of both launches (§3).

## 10. THE TWO RENDERED KICKOFFS

`diff flightdeck/launch/flightcrew-buildout/kickoff.md flightdeck/launch/flightcrew-buildout-2/kickoff.md` returns exactly two hunks, both inside the 5-line header; lines 6–46 (the whole body: base v1, shape-workflow v1, task-feature v1) are byte-identical, as is line 1 (`# Kickoff: task-feature · shape-workflow`) and line 3 (`kickoff version: base@1+shape-workflow@1+task-feature@1`).

- Line 2: launch path `…/flightcrew-buildout` → `…/flightcrew-buildout-2`; spec path likewise, same commit `5f69a94` in both; tests-map `…/tests-map.v1.json @ 44aff6b` → `…/tests-map.v2.json @ 5cad9b9`.
- Line 4: `prior reports: none` → `prior reports: flightdeck/launch/flightcrew-buildout/report.md`.
- Line 5: evidence path `…/flightcrew-buildout/evidence.html` → `…/flightcrew-buildout-2/evidence.html`.

**Run-log risk line / reference to the previous launch:** neither kickoff carries one. The only run-log reference in either file is the constant header field `read first: flightdeck/launch/RUNLOG.md` (identical in both) and the body sentence at `kickoff.md:9` "Read … the run log named under read first". Nothing in the render mechanism can carry run-log content: `renderKickoff` never opens `RUNLOG.md`. The only launch-2-specific trace of run 1 anywhere is the `prior reports` field, which names run 1's `report.md` — and `launch.json.previous_launch` is `"flightcrew-buildout"` for run 2 (`null` for run 1), but `previous_launch` is never rendered into the header. The knowledge that run 1 abandoned at verify on `wrong-check` lives only in `RUNLOG.md:18-31`, in `plan.json.risks` for run 2, and in the human's G1 gate note ("risks carry run 1's run-log entry"), never in the kickoff.

## Factual tensions inside the built kickoff

1. **Version drift is unrecorded and undetectable.** Both launches record `base@1+shape-workflow@1+task-feature@1` in three places while the library carries `base@3`, `shape-workflow@2`, `task-feature@2`. No validator, no render path and no check compares a recorded version against the library, so a re-render of either launch would rewrite kickoff.md and `launch.json.kickoff.version` while `plan.json.kickoff_version` (`plan.schema.json:11`, required) and both RUNLOG entries stay at `@1`.
2. **`base.md` v3 line 5 tells the orchestrator to dispatch in the contracts phase**, and RUNLOG `:9` records the resulting spec conflict as an open reservation: "B27 worker render refusing the contracts phase the kickoff dispatches in". The kickoff instruction and the shipped `fc worker render` behaviour contradict each other, on the record.
3. **The escalation list is five conditions but six kinds.** `base.md:12` enumerates five stop conditions, then defines six `&lt;kind&gt;` tokens including `halt` ("a worker returned a halt"), which has no corresponding entry in the condition sentence; `shape-session.md:6` and `shape-workflow.md:6` are what actually route a halt.
4. **"Reached" vs "exceeded" a ceiling.** `base.md` v3:12/21 say "exceeded"; the rendered v1 text in both launches says "reached" (`kickoff.md:18`); the manual (`manuals/orchestration/kickoff.md:38,75`) says "reached". Three sources, two different thresholds.
5. **The sixth Never has no enforcement twin.** `base.md:27` "hand-edit kickoff.md or plan.md (both are re-rendered from their sources)" names a recovery property, not a hook or command, against `README.md:23` ("every never has its enforcement named beside it") and `manuals/orchestration/kickoff.md:48,77`.
6. **"Read by the orchestrator only" vs the planner's dispatch.** `manuals/orchestration/kickoff.md:3,10` and `crew/README.md` say orchestrator only; `crew/planner.md:14` says the planner's dispatch hands it "the kickoff header block", and `:23` requires the planner to derive `shape` and `kickoff_version` from it. `crew/README.md:43` widens this further to "the run-chain roles receive their paths from the launch's kickoff header block".
7. **"Nothing else reads them"** (`templates/kickoff/README.md:3`) is contradicted by the planner's header block and by `testbench/suites/templates/run.mjs`, which reads every part to assert its version line and the assembly order.
8. **The `## Roles` name rule is enforced one way only.** `README.md:20` says agent names appear in backticks under `## Roles` "and only there"; `rolesNames` (`validate-kickoff.mjs:84-97`) only scans inside `## Roles`, so a backticked crew name elsewhere in the document is neither checked nor forbidden by anything executable. `base.md` v3 in fact removed the backticks from `implementer`, `verifier` and `critic` in the Conduct steps (they were backticked in the rendered v1 at `kickoff.md:9-14`), which no rule required.
9. **The verifier's exclusion is unstated.** `base.md:15` says the verifier "never receives implementer reasoning" but does not say it never receives the kickoff, and `crew/README.md:21` likewise omits it — the verifier is the one crew role whose relation to the kickoff is undefined, while `manuals/orchestration/kickoff.md:15` asserts "neither ever sees the kickoff" of the verifier and the critic.
10. **The gate definitions live in two documents.** `base.md:4,5,9` state what the human reads at each gate; `plan.template.json:51-55` requires the plan to state the same thing per run; `manuals/orchestration/kickoff.md:17` says "one home per rule".
11. **No structured kickoff exists, but three files must agree about it.** The document has no schema and no JSON form; its only machine-readable projection is a version string duplicated into `launch.json`, `plan.json` and `RUNLOG.md`, with agreement enforced (via `shape`) only by validate-plan, and only between the plan and the launch — never against the library the string names.
12. **`evidence:` in the header is synthesised, not read.** `launch.mjs:179` hard-codes `${launchRel}/evidence.html` while `launch.json` never stores an evidence path, and kickoff-rule-1 checks only that the label exists — the one header field the validator cannot falsify is also the one the launch record does not own.</result>

[ASSISTANT 💬]
The built kickoff explorer is back. Set against the sources, the built library follows the shape the guides describe and misses on content, form and record.

**Where it follows the guides.** Base plus one shape plus one task, assembled by a script, a key-value header of pointers, read by the orchestrator only, a version string recorded in three places, a Never list with enforcement twins, and a README that says point never paste and prune on the same pass as you add.

**Where it departs.**

- **The base is a command sequence.** Eight of its twelve content lines are conduct steps and escalation, and thirty of its thirty-two runner mentions are there. Roughly two thirds of the base tells the orchestrator which command to type when. The guides' base carries the gate protocol, the escalation rules and the evidence requirements. Nothing in the built base names the phases as a list, and the manual claims it does.
- **The numbers left the kickoff.** Ceilings live in launch.json. Model tiers live in the plan and the crew README, and appear nowhere in the library. Abandon triggers live in the plan. Gate definitions live in both the base and the plan. The guides put default budgets, tiers and the stall rule in the kickoff with the plan tightening them. The built kickoff names the ceilings and points at launch.json for their values.
- **Version drift is undetectable.** Both runs record every part at version one. The library now carries base at three and every other part at two. No validator, render or check compares a recorded version to the library, so a re-render would silently rewrite both kickoffs while the plan and the log stay at one. The mechanism the guides rely on for attribution between runs, that kickoff seven is a diffable thing, exists as a string nothing verifies.
- **No structured form.** Ten schemas exist and none is for the kickoff. Its only machine-readable projection is the version string in three files and two pointer fields in launch.json. The header's evidence path is synthesised by the render and stored nowhere.
- **The record contradicts itself.** The kickoff dispatches in the contracts phase and the render command refuses that phase, an open reservation. The base defines six escalation kinds for five conditions. The rendered kickoffs say a ceiling reached, the library says exceeded, the manual says reached. The sixth Never's twin is a recovery property, not an enforcer. The manual says orchestrator only and the planner's dispatch hands it the header block.
- **The run log never reaches the kickoff.** The render never opens the log. The second run's kickoff differs from the first only in its header paths, and the knowledge that run one abandoned on a wrong check lives in the log, the plan's risks and a gate note, not in the document the orchestrator wakes up to. The guides have the kickoff point at the log as required pre-planning reading, which the header does, and that is the whole of it.

One thing the built system does that the guides do not: the shape modules are distinguished by dispatch mechanism and the task modules by how units are cut, including an agent-shaped task module the guides never name. That is an addition worth keeping in view.

Your YAML explorer is still out. When it lands I'll have the three kickoffs side by side and can propose the document's shape, with the eighty settings placed against the routing test.

## 4. OVERLAP WITH OTHER DOCUMENTS ON `main`

**vs `templates/plan.template.json`** — the largest overlap; the plan template carries a pointer *back* to the kickoff and duplicates several of its concerns:

- Kickoff pointer, explicitly one-directional: `"kickoff": { "path": "&lt;kickoff file used&gt;", "version": "&lt;integer&gt;" }`, with `plan.schema.json` stating "The kickoff this run is conducted under. Informational for the report; **the plan does not restate any of it**."
- Iteration ceiling — duplicated with an explicit precedence rule. Kickoff: `max_iterations_per_unit: 8`. Plan: `"iterations": "&lt;max attempts against this unit's checks before returning failed; defaults from kickoff when absent&gt;"`.
- Model tier: kickoff `models.{strong,standard,small}` and `models.overrides` vs plan `"model": "&lt;tier for the first attempt&gt;"`.
- Worker role: kickoff `dispatch.default_worker: worker-general` vs plan `"worker": "&lt;agent role from .claude/agents/&gt;"`.
- Diff boundary: kickoff `verification.diff_boundary.allowed_paths` vs plan `"owns": ["&lt;paths this unit may write; its diff boundary; no path in two units&gt;"]`.
- Parallelism: kickoff `dispatch.parallelism: 3` vs plan `"group": "&lt;parallel group; units sharing a group run concurrently&gt;"` and `"order": [[…wave 1…],[…wave 2…]]`.
- Approval/gate: kickoff `gates.plan.enabled` vs plan `"status": "&lt;draft | approved&gt;"` and the `approval` block.
- Kickoff's `planning.plan_must_include` list is, item for item, a prose restatement of the plan template's own field set (unit id/title, spec refs, checks, needs/produces, worker, owns, order).

**vs `templates/tests-map.template.json`**
- Baseline: kickoff `verification.baseline.required: true` ("every behaviour check must fail before implementation for the right reason") vs tests-map `"baseline": { "expect": "&lt;pass | fail: &lt;reason&gt;&gt;", "observed": …}` and the top-level `baseline` block.
- Check invocation: kickoff `verification.check_commands.{unit,contract,artefact,acceptance,lint,types,build}` (empty slots) vs tests-map `"command": "&lt;exact command; exit code is the verdict&gt;"` per check and `"kind": "&lt;acceptance | unit | contract | golden | schema | budget | constraint | boundary | structural&gt;"` — the kind vocabularies differ (kickoff has `artefact`, `lint`, `types`, `build`; the map has `golden`, `schema`, `budget`, `constraint`, `boundary`, `structural`).
- Locked test files: kickoff `verification.test_files_writable_by: [test-builder]` vs tests-map `"locked_paths": ["&lt;test directories, check scripts, the fixture, and this file; read-only to implementing agents during a run, enforced by hook&gt;"]`.
- Unverified behaviours: kickoff `pull_request.body_must_include: - unverified behaviours…` and `planning.plan_must_include: - mapped check ids per unit, or "unverified" with the spec's stated reason` vs tests-map `"unverified": [{ "ref", "reason", "decided_by": "human", "at" }]`.

**vs `templates/spec.template.json`**
- Freeze status: kickoff `references.spec: … # must be status: frozen with zero open questions` vs spec `"status": "&lt;draft | frozen&gt;"` and `"open_questions": [...]`.
- Scope-derived boundary: kickoff `diff_boundary.source: spec-scope` vs spec `"scope": [{ "id": "SC&lt;n&gt;", "kind": "&lt;in | out&gt;" }]`.
- Verification/acceptance: kickoff's `verification` block vs spec `"verification": {"id": "VER", …}` and `"acceptance": {"id": "ACC", …}` — the spec owns *what* proves done, the kickoff owns *how* checks are run. `flightdeck/manuals/spec/spec-conventions.md:75` states the intended separation: "Not the kickoff: how a run is conducted — tools, agents, gates, displays — never enters it".

**vs `templates/worker.template.md`**
- Iteration ceiling restated to the worker: "`Iteration ceiling: {{ceilings.iterations}} attempts, then return `failed` with the last failure output.`"
- Fence/boundary: "## Your fence — You may write only under: {{#each unit.owns}}" mirrors `verification.diff_boundary`.
- Blocked/contradiction escalation: worker template's "Writing outside your fence… is a blocked condition: stop and return `blocked`" and "A check that contradicts the spec text above… return `blocked`" pair with kickoff `dispatch.on_blocked: abandon-unit` and `dispatch.on_contradiction: halt`.
- Test immutability: worker "Tests, interface declarations, routes, schemas and migrations are fixed. Never edit, skip, weaken, or mock around them." duplicates kickoff `test_files_writable_by: [test-builder]`.
- Commit policy: worker "one atomic commit on your branch, message `{{unit.id}}: {{unit.name}}`" duplicates kickoff `git.commit_policy: atomic-per-unit`.
- Unit-slice context: worker "Everything you need is below; nothing outside this prompt is part of your task." duplicates kickoff `dispatch.worker_context: unit-slice`.

**vs `crew/crew.json`** — the orchestrator role declares the kickoff as an input and restates the budget set: `"parameters": ["kickoff_path", "spec_path", "tests_map_path", "crew_file (this file)", "run_directory", "prior_reports_for_this_spec (optional)", "budgets: max agents, max iterations per unit, spend ceiling, stall rule"]`, and `"context": {"receives": ["the kickoff", …]}`. Its purpose line: "Conduct the run as the kickoff describes". crew.json also owns per-role model tiers (`"model": {"tier": "strong", …}`) that the kickoff's `models` block says it "may override".

## 5. WHO READS IT

**Nothing on `main` reads it.** Evidence:
- `git grep -il liftoff main -- flightdeck/` returns only the file itself and the four-line `flightdeck/missions/shape-library.md`.
- `flightdeck/flightcrew/bin/worker/render-worker-prompt.mjs` reads only `--plan`, `--spec`, `--tests-map` and `flightdeck/flightcrew/templates/worker.template.md`; no YAML parser, no liftoff/kickoff input.
- `flightdeck/flightcrew/schemas/worker/worker-prompt.docspec.json` and `worker-agent.docspec.json` do not mention it.
- `flightdeck/flightcrew/checks/validators/validate-all.mjs` dispatches only to `validate-spec`, `validate-plan`, `validate-tests-map`, `validate-md`; there is no liftoff/kickoff validator and no liftoff schema.
- Nothing on `main` parses YAML at all; every schema and template is JSON or Markdown.

The only machine-visible trace is indirect: `plan.schema.json` **requires** a `kickoff: {path, version}` object on every plan, so a plan must cite *some* kickoff file — but the schema constrains only path+version, never the contents, and calls it "Informational for the report". `validate-md.mjs` mentions kickoffs generically in a comment ("kickoffs, or any other markdown document agents fill") and assumes a *markdown* kickoff, not YAML.

Conclusion: it stands alone as a human-authored design document.

## 6. WHAT IT LACKS — against the eight kickoff parts

## 7. DEFAULTS

The file **does not** formally distinguish required from optional. There is no `required:`/`optional:` marking, no type annotations, and no schema behind it. The distinction is carried entirely by convention in the written value:

- **Filled defaults (the majority, ~100 leaves):** a working value is already present and the comment explains the choice — `isolation: worktree`, `parallelism: 3`, `max_agents: 20`, `merge_policy: fast-forward-only`, `strong: opus`. The header comment makes these binding: "The orchestrator reads it first and treats every active value as an instruction; commented values are alternatives, not suggestions. Uncomment one alternative and comment the current default to change an option. Never leave two values active for the same key."
- **Empty slots the author must fill (~20):** `run.title: ""`, `references.spec_id: ""`, `spec_version: ""`, `tests_map: ""`, `prior_reports: []`, all seven `verification.check_commands.*: ""`, `diff_boundary.allowed_paths: []`, `models.overrides: {}`, `pull_request.reviewers: []`, `references.spec: specs/&lt;name&gt;.md` and `run.id: run-0001` (placeholder-shaped).
- **Sentinels rather than optionality:** `gate_timeout_minutes: 0 # 0 means wait indefinitely`; `spend_ceiling: 0 # … 0 means no spend ceiling (subscription)`; `tests_map: "" # … empty means none exists`.
- **Non-negotiables marked in prose, not structure:** `final.enabled: true # always; the final gate IS the pull request`; `on_contradiction: halt # always`; `findings_filter: none # the orchestrator never filters or softens findings`; `verdict_in_report: never`.

**Per-run vs standing:** no explicit marking, but the comments imply it. Per-run/per-attempt: `run.id` ("unique per run"), `run.attempt` ("increments per attempt at the same spec version"), `run.title`, the whole `references` block, `models.overrides` ("to raise one role **for this run**"), and everything interpolated from those. Standing: `git.base_branch: main # never touched by the run`, `permissions.*`, `reporting.*`, `review.*`, and the budget defaults. The comment on `models` states the layering rule directly: "tier per role; the crew file states the tier, this file may override". The comment on `permissions` states the enforcement layering: "blast radius per role; the harness enforces, this declares". `permissions.paths.write_denied_for_all` includes `flightdeck/liftoff*.yaml`, i.e. the kickoff declares itself immutable during the run.

---

## Shape, in plain terms

This kickoff is a single densely-commented settings file, not a document with parts. Where a markdown parts library would give you eight named prose sections you assemble and rewrite per run — a mission paragraph, a conduct sequence you can read top to bottom, escalation rules stated as sentences — this file gives you roughly 121 leaf keys under 16 top-level headings, where almost every key already holds a working default and the alternatives sit directly beneath it as commented siblings. Configuring a run means toggling comment characters, not writing prose; the header makes that the explicit contract ("Uncomment one alternative and comment the current default… Never leave two values active for the same key"). The consequence is that policy is exhaustively enumerated and machine-shaped, but narrative is absent: the mission is an empty `title` string and a three-value `purpose` enum, the conduct sequence exists only as the order of the sections, and the role roster is a set of bare ids pointing at `crew.json`. It reads as a control panel whose knobs happen to be commented in English — closer in spirit to `plan.template.json` (which cites it as `kickoff: {path, version}` and is told not to restate it) than to `worker.template.md`, which says the same rules again in the second person because a worker needs to be told, not configured. Nothing on `main` parses it; it is a design frozen at its first commit, still pointing at a directory layout the repository has since moved past.</result>

**Each of the three lacks what one of the others has.** The sources have the routing discipline and the parts, no structured form. Yours has the settings and the defaults, no prose and no versioning. [ASSISTANT 💬]
Now I can answer from the contract rather than from memory. Short version: yes to most of it, and the parts it cannot do are exactly the parts a state file was invented for.

**What a workflow script does deterministically**

- **Sequence and fan-out.** Phases, pipelines and parallel barriers are plain JavaScript control flow. The order of stages, what runs concurrently, what waits for what, and what stops the run on a condition are written once and execute the same way every time. That is the phase machine, without a phase field anywhere.
- **Budgets.** Concurrency is capped by the runtime per workflow. Per-agent turn budgets come from the agent definition. Token spend is a hard ceiling the runtime enforces: once spent reaches the target, further agent calls throw. Loops can read remaining budget and stop. That covers agents, concurrency, turns and tokens without a ceilings object or a budget command.
- **Gates between roles.** Structured returns validated against a JSON schema at the tool-call layer, so a worker's return either matches its shape or the model retries. A stage can refuse to continue on a red return, a refuted verdict or a spec-conflict finding, and stop the wave. The builder's own scripts already do this.
- **Isolation.** An agent call can take a worktree option and the runtime creates and removes the worktree. Per-stage model and effort are options on the call.
- **Repeatability.** Same script and same arguments replay from cache; a changed call and everything after it runs live. The clock and randomness are forbidden precisely so this holds. That is the constitution's repeatable principle implemented by the runtime rather than by discipline.

**What it cannot do, by design**

- **No file, shell or git access in the script.** The script dispatches agents and returns payloads. Everything that touches the repository is done by an agent it spawns.
- **No human input mid-run.** A permission prompt is the only pause. A gate that needs a human ends one workflow and starts the next.
- **One level of nesting.** A workflow can call a saved workflow, and that child cannot call another.

So the workflow replaces the sequencing, the budgeting, the isolation, the schema-validated handoffs and the stop-on-red logic. It does not replace the recording, the rendering or the human gate. Those stay as leaf scripts the spawned agents call, hooks that fire in the agents' sessions, and a page.

**Your proposal against that.** Here is the run folder, the spec and the plan, use workflow X with these modifiers. That works, and it is close to what the sources describe when they say the orchestration is a script, saved and rerun, invoked by name with the spec as its argument. Two consequences follow:

- **Phase state mostly dissolves.** The phase is where the script is. A run is the sequence of workflows invoked between human gates: one from targets to the plan gate, one from contracts to the interfaces gate, one for the waves to the evidence gate, and the review. What survives as state is only what a human decides between workflows, which is exactly what you said launch.json should hold: current run, gates passed, and nothing else.
- **The kickoff shrinks to arguments.** The runtime already takes an args object. The kickoff becomes the named workflow plus the modifiers it accepts: spec at commit, run folder, ceilings the plan may tighten, model tiers, shape choices. That is your omakase base with overrides, and it is machine-readable by construction. The prose the orchestrator reads becomes the agent definitions and the rendered dispatch prompts, which is where the sources put role conduct anyway.

**The one thing to watch.** The sources say the gated stages need a session that can stop and ask, and only the parallel waves are candidates for a script. Your model puts a workflow on every stage and a human gate between them. That is consistent with the runtime, since a workflow ending is a stop, but it means the orchestrator as a long-running conducting session largely disappears. What remains of it is the human, at a page, choosing the next workflow. Whether that is a loss or the point is your call, and it is the decision the kickoff document should record.

So yes, this abolishes most of the phasing state and most of the command scripting. The runner shrinks to the leaves the agents call, the kickoff becomes a workflow name plus arguments, and launch.json becomes an index of which workflow ran and what the human decided after it.

[ASSISTANT 💬]
**On the kickoff.** Yes, and the sources contain the seam that the builder resolved the wrong way. The constitution's tooling document has two adjacent entries. The liftoff prompt is implemented as a saved prompt or command, invoked with the spec as its argument. The dynamic workflow is a saved script that runs as a named command, the same shape every time. Those are two descriptions of one thing seen from two sides: the kickoff is the human-readable statement of how this run is conducted, and the workflow script is its executable form. The sources never say which lines of the conduct sequence are prose the orchestrator follows and which are steps the runtime executes. The builder answered by making the conduct sequence prose that tells the orchestrator to type commands, and putting every deterministic step behind those commands. So the kickoff kept its title and lost its content: the deterministic conduct moved into the runner, and what stayed in the kickoff was the instruction to invoke it. Your reading is right. The kickoff was always the seat of the run's deterministic shape. Its executable form is a script the runtime runs, not a program the orchestrator drives.

**On the workflow questions.**

- **Hooks.** The script has none and manages none. But every agent it spawns is a real subagent session in the same project, and project hooks fire inside it: a pre-tool-use guard fires on a worker's edit whether the worker was dispatched by a script or by hand. The event log's subagent start and stop events are exactly the hooks that would record a workflow's agents. One caution: the stop gate as built is a Stop hook, which holds the main session's turn. A worker inside a workflow ends with a subagent-stop event, not a session stop, so the gate that holds a worker until its checks pass would need to be wired to that event or expressed as the schema-validated return instead. The repository's Claude Code facts manual was verified against a specific version and would settle which events fire for spawned agents; I can have an explorer check it.
- **Locked files.** Enforced in the agents' sessions by the same guards and deny rules, not by the script. A worktree spawned by the script inherits the project settings. The sandbox deny list, if configured, reaches the worker's shell there too.
- **Acceptance and check commands.** The script cannot run a command. An agent it spawns runs the check and returns a structured result, or a hook in that agent's session runs it. So checks run inside agents, verdicts return as schema-validated payloads the script can branch on, and writing evidence to disk is a leaf script the agent calls. The builder's own three scripts already follow this: they return payloads and the orchestrator persists them afterwards. Under your model the agent persists its own return before it returns.
- **Custom agents.** Yes. An agent call takes an agent type resolved from the same registry as the Agent tool, meaning the crew files under the agents directory, and it composes with a schema: the custom agent's prompt gets a structured-output instruction appended. Model and effort are per-call overrides. So the crew definitions stay where they are, the script names which one each stage uses, and whoever writes the script sets that, not the orchestrator at run time.

Net: the workflow owns sequence, fan-out, budget, isolation and typed handoffs. Hooks own enforcement inside the agents. Leaf scripts own recording and rendering, called by the agents. The human owns the gates between workflows. There is nothing left over for a runner to own except scaffolding.

**Source against built, for the kickoff.** Five departures, each a problem.

- **Conduct became commands.** The sources' base carries the phase and gate sequence, the escalation rules and the evidence requirements as conduct. The built base spends eight of twelve content lines and thirty of thirty-two runner mentions telling the orchestrator which command to type. The deterministic part of conduct, which the sources place in a saved script, was placed in a runner and the kickoff was left holding the instruction to invoke it.
- **The numbers left the kickoff.** The sources have the kickoff carry default budgets, model tiers and the stall rule, with the plan tightening them. The built kickoff names the ceilings and points at launch.json for their values, has no model tiers at all, and leaves abandon triggers to the plan. Gate definitions ended up in both the base and the plan template, against the one-home rule the manual itself states.
- **The version is recorded and never verified.** Both runs record every part at version one in three places. The library now carries base at three and the others at two. Nothing compares the recorded string to the library, so a re-render silently rewrites the kickoff while the plan and the log keep the old string. The sources' whole attribution mechanism, kickoff seven is a diffable thing, is a string nothing checks.
- **No structured form.** Ten schemas exist, none for the kickoff. Its only machine-readable projection is a version string and two pointer fields. The header's evidence path is synthesised by the render and stored nowhere.
- **The run log never reaches it.** The render never opens the log. The two rendered kickoffs differ only in header paths. The knowledge that run one abandoned on a wrong check lives in the log, the plan's risks and a gate note, never in the document the orchestrator wakes up to, and the sources have the kickoff carry the log's known failure modes forward as pre-planning reading.

Your YAML on main departs on different points: no mission, no conduct sequence, no versioning, no reader, and about a hundred policy values that the routing test would send to the spec, the plan, the tests map, the role files and the settings.

**How much lifting a workflow can do at liftoff.** All of the conduct sequence. The script owns the order of stages, the fan-out, the stop-on-red, the budgets and the isolation, and it is invoked by name with the spec as an argument, which is the constitution's own description of the liftoff prompt. What it cannot own is the human gate and the recording, so liftoff under a workflow is the human invoking the first script from a page, and each later script starting after a gate.

**Versioning and iteration.** A workflow is a file under the project's workflows directory, so git versions it like the spec, and a run log can pin it at a commit the same way. The runtime records the script of every run under the session directory, so what ran is recoverable even if the file later changes. Iteration is cheap by design: edit one agent call and the unchanged prefix replays from cache, only the change and what follows runs live. That is the sources' one-change-per-retry rule with the runtime doing the attribution. What the runtime does not provide is a version field or a compatibility check between a saved script and the arguments a run passes it. That gap is where a kickoff schema sits.

**A JSON basis.** The arguments a workflow takes are already JSON, and the system already uses JSON Schema for the spec, the plan and the tests map. A kickoff as a JSON arguments object with a schema of its own gives you three things at once: a page can render and edit it, the script can validate it before spawning anything, and the version string becomes a field the schema requires. The builder's three scripts already inline a schema validator for returns, so validating arguments the same way is the same pattern pointed the other way. The absence today is exact: it would be the eleventh schema.

p='kickoff-problems.md'; body=open(p).read()
def sect(marker, prose):
    global body
    i=body.index(marker); j=i+len(marker)
    lines=body[j:].split('\n'); k=0
    while k<len(lines) and (lines[k].startswith('<!--') or lines[k]==''):
        if lines[k]=='' and k+1<len(lines) and lines[k+1].startswith('#'): break
        k+=1
    body=body[:j]+'\n'.join(lines[:k])+'\n'+prose.strip('\n')+'\n'+'\n'.join(lines[k:])
P={}
P['# Kickoff problems\n']="""
This document describes the problems of the flightcrew kickoff: the document the orchestrator wakes up to, which says how one run is conducted. It is one of a set of problem documents, each covering one domain, written to inform the plan of a later launch and the next version of the spec. It diagnoses. It proposes no remediation. The runner problems document covers the program the built kickoff drives, and the system problems document covers the workflow scripts' defects and the hooks; neither is restated here. The kickoff earns its own document because it sits on two of the three failure axes at once: it is itself the run's context, and it fixes most of the tooling the run relies on, so a fix on either axis passes through it.

Three kickoffs are compared. The method's sources, in the constitution and the orchestration guides in the library. The built library on branch `flightcrew-buildout` at commit `75b2b42`. And a YAML liftoff template on branch `main`, designed by the human before the build and withheld from it. Paths and line numbers refer to those revisions; the working tree may be on another branch, so read evidence with `git show <branch>:<path>`. Statements about the workflow runtime come from its authoring reference and from the facts manual the build verified against Claude Code 2.1.259.
"""
P['## Agent Invariants\n']="""
- The kickoff owns the conduct of one run and nothing else. Correctness lives in the spec, decomposition in the plan, and what every session must know in the constitution. The test for any line is who needs to obey it.
