P['## What the sources say\n']="""
The **kickoff**, which the constitution calls the liftoff prompt, is the fourth governing document of a run. The spec says what must be true. The plan says how, in what pieces, for this run. The constitution says how the project always works. The kickoff says how this run is conducted: which roles, in what order, on what budgets, with what gates. It is written by the human, maintained across runs, versioned like code, and read by the orchestrator only; the workers, the test-builder and the critic never see it. Every line in it passes one **routing test**: who needs to obey this? Everyone, the constitution. The judges of correctness, the spec. Only the conductor, the kickoff. This run only, the plan.

The sources give it eight parts, in a deliberate order: mission and pointers, the **conduct** sequence of stages with an explicit halt at each gate, escalation rules, roles and dispatch, communication and the evidence display, default budgets and the stall rule, the enumerated outputs, and a short absolute Never list each of whose lines has a hook or permission as its enforcement twin. Its form is markdown, assembled from a library of **parts**: a base carrying what every run shares, one shape module for the dispatch mechanism, one task module for the kind of work. A script renders the assembly with a key-value header of pointers, the spec at its frozen commit, the run log as required reading, the plan and evidence paths. It points and never pastes. No source gives it a JSON or YAML form. The assembled version is recorded in the plan header, the report header and the run log entry, so that when the log says version seven failed, seven is a diffable thing and eight is one reviewed change away. A healthy library shrinks as enforcement grows: correctness lines migrate to the spec template, universal lines to the constitution, enforceable lines to hooks. The pre-send checklist ends with the question of whether it is shorter than the last version.

The constitution's tooling document places two entries side by side. The liftoff prompt is implemented as a saved prompt or command, invoked with the spec as its argument. The dynamic workflow is a saved script that runs the same shape every time, invoked by name. These are one thing seen from two sides: the kickoff is the readable statement of a run's conduct and the workflow script is its executable form. The sources never draw the seam between them, never saying which lines of the conduct sequence are prose the orchestrator follows and which are steps the runtime executes. That undrawn seam is where the built system went.
"""
P['## Three kickoffs against the eight parts\n']="""
Two kickoffs were built without sight of each other or of the sources. The human's YAML on `main`, at `flightdeck/flightcrew/templates/liftoff.template.yaml`, has sixteen sections and about 121 active settings with 57 commented alternatives, nearly every key holding a working default. The builder's library on `flightcrew-buildout`, under `flightdeck/flightcrew/templates/kickoff/`, has a 27-line base and seven six-line modules. Each carried something the others lack.

| | The sources | The YAML on main | The built library |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mission and pointers | One line and a pointer header | Pointers exhaustive; mission an empty title and a three-value purpose | Pointer header rendered from the launch record; no mission line |
| Conduct sequence | Phases with a halt at each gate, as a checklist | Absent; inferable only from section order | Present as seven steps, each a runner command |
| Escalation | Named findings that halt the run | Present as policy enums | Present; six kinds for five conditions |
| Roles and dispatch | Roster by name, what each receives and must not | Delegated to the crew file by id; no per-role instruction | Present, with receives and never-receives per role |
| Communication and display | Summaries up; the evidence display's path and contents | Display contents and notify list | Present |
| Budgets and stops | Defaults here; the plan tightens them | The most complete section; ceilings, stall rule, on-ceiling | Ceilings named, values in the launch record; no model tiers |
| Outputs | Branch conventions, display finalised, log stub | Report sections, pull request body, footer flags | Present, as runner commands |
| Prohibitions | Short, each with an enforcement twin | Permissions block; network, shell, path denies | Six entries; five with a real twin |
| Form | Markdown parts, rendered, pointer header | One YAML file, toggled by commenting | Markdown parts, rendered, pointer header |
| Versioning | Assembled version recorded in three places | No version field | Version string in three places, never verified |
| Reader | The orchestrator only | Nothing on the branch parses it | The orchestrator; the header block also reaches the planner |
| Structured form | None | The whole file, with no schema | None; a version string and two pointer fields |

The built library also carries a task module for agent-shaped work that the sources never name, stating what each of four check classes owes. It has no counterpart in the sources and is worth keeping in view.
"""
P['### 1. Conduct became commands\n']="""
**What.** The base part at `flightdeck/flightcrew/templates/kickoff/base.md` has twelve content lines. Eight of them, the seven conduct steps and the escalation line, tell the orchestrator which runner command to type and when; thirty of the file's thirty-two runner mentions are there. The routing of information between roles, where returns are written, and where the ceilings live take the other three. The sources' base carries the gate protocol, the escalation rules and the evidence requirements; its worked example's conduct section names phases, what is presented at each gate, and that the run halts, with no command in it. The shape-workflow module at `templates/kickoff/shape-workflow.md` is the only text in the system that names the three workflow scripts, and it overlays a different dispatch on conduct steps one, four and six without the base saying those steps are replaceable. Both recorded runs selected that module; neither invoked a script.

**Why it matters.** The conduct of a run is deterministic by the method's own principle, and the runtime offers a form for it: a saved script that owns the order of stages, the fan-out, the stop on a red return, the budgets and the isolation, invoked by name with arguments. The sources describe the liftoff prompt in those same words, a saved command invoked with the spec as its argument. The builder had the two descriptions and the undrawn seam between them, and resolved it by placing every deterministic step behind a runner command and leaving the kickoff holding the instruction to invoke it. The kickoff kept its title and lost its content.

**Effect on the system.** The kickoff is where a system without a runner would do most of its deterministic work, and the built kickoff does none. Its conduct section cannot be read for what a run does without reading it for how the runner is driven. Its one module that reaches for the executable form describes scripts that have never run and contradicts the base it is assembled with. The runner problems document describes the program this left behind.
"""
P['### 2. The numbers have no single owner\n']="""
**What.** The sources put default budgets, model tiers and the stall rule in the kickoff, with the plan carrying this run's numbers and tightening them. In the built system, `base.md:21` names eight ceiling dimensions and says their values live in `launch.json`; model tiers appear nowhere in the library and are owned by the plan and the crew README; abandon triggers are owned by the plan; and what the human reads at each gate is stated in both `base.md:4-9` and `flightdeck/flightcrew/templates/plan.template.json:51-55`, against the one-home rule the kickoff manual states at `flightdeck/manuals/orchestration/kickoff.md:17`. The YAML on `main` has the opposite problem. Of its 121 settings, about 25 are pointers. Its verification block duplicates the tests map, its diff boundary duplicates the spec's scope, its plan-must-include list restates the plan template field by field, and its permissions block is what the constitution puts in role frontmatter and the settings fragment. The YAML and the plan template on `main` already argue about who owns the iteration ceiling, the model tier and the diff boundary, with a precedence comment on the plan's side. The built kickoff and `launch.json` argue about the ceilings.

**Why it matters.** Both attempts answered "everything the run needs" by enumerating, and neither settled the seam with the plan. Eighty settings and a command sequence with its values elsewhere are two shapes of the same weight. The routing test exists to decide ownership line by line, and applied to either attempt it moves most of the content out: to the spec, the tests map, the plan, the role files and the settings. What survives the test as conduct is small: the gates, the dispatch rules, the default budgets, the model tiers, the review policy and the ending policy. A base of defaults that a run overrides only where it differs is the sources' shrinking rule made structural.

**Effect on the system.** A value that lives in two documents drifts, and a reader cannot tell which governs. A value that lives in the wrong document is invisible to the role that needs it: a model tier in the plan is unknown to the kickoff that should default it, and a ceiling in the launch record is unknown to a page reading the kickoff. Neither attempt can be made smaller without first deciding, for each value, who needs to obey it.
"""
P['### 3. The version is recorded and never verified\n']="""
**What.** Both recorded runs carry the version string `base@1+shape-workflow@1+task-feature@1` in `launch.json`, in the plan and in the run log. The library at the branch tip carries `base.md` at version three and every other part at version two, after commit `acafec4` applied the review fixes. No validator, render path or check compares a recorded version to the library: `flightdeck/flightcrew/checks/validators/validate-kickoff.mjs` checks that the version field exists and nothing about its content. A re-render of either launch would rewrite `kickoff.md` and `launch.json` to the new versions and leave the plan's version field and both log entries at the old ones. The YAML on `main` has no version field at all, though the plan schema on that branch requires one.

The runtime offers what neither attempt built. A workflow is a file under the project's workflows directory, so git versions it exactly as it versions the spec, and a log can pin it at a commit. The runtime records the script of every run under the session directory, so what ran is recoverable even if the file later changes. An edit to one agent call reruns only that call and what follows, with the unchanged prefix replayed from cache, which is the sources' one-change-per-retry rule with the runtime doing the attribution. What the runtime does not provide is a version field on a workflow or a compatibility check between a saved script and the arguments a run passes it.

**Why it matters.** The sources' whole mechanism for improving a kickoff between runs rests on the version being a diffable thing: the log says seven failed on escalation, and eight is one reviewed change away. A version string that nothing verifies against the library is a label, and a library that moved while the string stayed makes every comparison between runs a comparison of the wrong documents.

**Effect on the system.** Both recorded runs are attributed to a kickoff that no longer exists in the form recorded. The next run of the same spec would be conducted under a different base with the same version string in its log entry unless someone re-renders, and re-rendering breaks the plan's agreement instead. Versioning by git commit, which the spec already uses and which a workflow file gets for free, is the mechanism the string was standing in for.
"""
P['### 4. No structured form exists\n']="""
**What.** The built system carries ten JSON schemas under `flightdeck/flightcrew/schemas/`, for the spec, the plan, the tests map, the launch record, the check result, the event and four agent returns. None is for the kickoff. The kickoff's only machine-readable projection is the version string and the two fields `path` and `version` in `launch.json`; the header's evidence path is synthesised by the render at `bin/cmd/launch.mjs:179` and stored nowhere. The document itself exists only as rendered markdown assembled from markdown parts. The sources give it no structured form either, though their header block of key-value pointers is the seed of one. The YAML on `main` is entirely structured and has no schema, no version field and no reader.

The runtime's arguments object is JSON, and the system already validates the spec, the plan and the tests map against JSON Schema. The three built workflow scripts each inline a schema validator to check the returns they receive. A kickoff expressed as the arguments a workflow takes, with a schema of its own, would be validated by the same mechanism pointed the other way, and would be the eleventh schema.

**Why it matters.** A page that renders, edits and hands back a kickoff needs a shape it can read. A script that refuses to run against arguments it does not understand needs the same shape. A version field a check can compare needs somewhere to live. Markdown parts give the orchestrator prose to follow and give everything else nothing. The absence is exact: every other document a run consumes has a schema, and the one that says how the run is conducted does not.

**Effect on the system.** The kickoff cannot be validated beyond its header labels, cannot be rendered by anything but the runner, cannot be edited by a page, and cannot be compared across runs except as text. The direction the human describes, a base of defaults with per-run overrides that later layers can read, has no home in the built system and none in the sources' form.
"""
P['### 5. The run log never reaches the kickoff\n']="""
**What.** The render at `bin/cmd/launch.mjs:161-183` never opens the run log; its header names the log's path as required reading, and that is the whole of the connection. The two rendered kickoffs, `flightdeck/launch/flightcrew-buildout/kickoff.md` and `flightcrew-buildout-2/kickoff.md`, differ only in their header paths: the launch folder, the map version, the prior report. Their bodies are byte-identical. The knowledge that the first run abandoned at verify on a wrong check lives in the log, in the second run's plan risks and in a gate note, and never in the document the orchestrator wakes up to. The sources have the kickoff carry the log's known failure modes forward as pre-planning reading so that they shape the plan before a worker is dispatched, and have the library shrink as rules migrate out of it.

**Why it matters.** The kickoff is the fix for the context axis where the cause was run conduct, and the run log is where that cause is recorded. A kickoff that changes between runs only in its pointers has not absorbed anything the previous run taught. The version string's three recording sites exist so that a conduct change can be attributed; a kickoff that never changes has nothing to attribute.

**Effect on the system.** Two runs of the same spec were conducted under the same conduct, and the second inherited the first's failure through the plan rather than through the document meant to carry it. The library grew from version one to three by the review's fixes, not by anything a run taught, and the runs that used it never saw the growth.
"""
P['### 6. The built kickoff contradicts its own system\n']="""
**What.** Five contradictions are on the record. `base.md:5` dispatches the contracts unit in the contracts phase, and the runner's render command refuses every phase but implement, an open reservation in `flightdeck/launch/RUNLOG.md:9`. `base.md:12` enumerates five conditions that stop the run and then defines six escalation kinds, the sixth having no condition. The library says a ceiling exceeded, the rendered kickoffs say a ceiling reached, and the kickoff manual says reached. The sixth Never at `base.md:27` gives as its enforcement twin the fact that the file is re-rendered from its sources, which is a recovery property and not an enforcer, against the manual's rule that every Never names one. The manual at `flightdeck/manuals/orchestration/kickoff.md:3` says the orchestrator alone reads the kickoff, and `flightdeck/flightcrew/crew/planner.md:14` hands the planner the kickoff's header block.

**Why it matters.** These are small, and each is the kind of thing a single execution or a single cross-check would have found. They matter because the kickoff is the one document the orchestrator is told wins over its own judgement, at `crew/orchestrator.md:10`. A contradiction between the kickoff and the tool it names, or inside the kickoff itself, is one the orchestrator has been told not to resolve.

**Effect on the system.** An orchestrator following the base to the letter reaches a step the runner refuses, an escalation kind with no trigger, and a threshold that two other documents state differently. The recorded runs did not meet these because no orchestrator followed the kickoff; the first run that does will.
"""
P['## Decisions the shape forces\n']="""
- Where the seam falls between the kickoff as prose the orchestrator reads and the workflow script as the conduct the runtime executes, since the sources describe both and never divide them.
- Whether the kickoff's structured form is the arguments a workflow takes, with a schema as its version and compatibility check, given that the runtime provides neither on a workflow itself.
- Which of the values in the three kickoffs survive the routing test as conduct, and which move to the spec, the plan, the role files and the settings.
- Whether the built task module for agent-shaped work, which the sources never name, is carried forward.
"""

# A. THE ROSTER

The sources use three overlapping vocabularies. The constitution's "Agent roles" list has **fourteen** roles; the agents guide's roster has **seven** ("Seven roles cover a full run"); `piecing-it-together`'s "Sessions and agents" table has **nine** contexts plus the human. Merged below, with the name each source uses.

### 1. Spec interviewer / Interviewer
- **Names**: `Spec interviewer` (orchestration-tooling), `Interviewer` (piecing-it-together table).
- **Job**: "extracts the spec from the human by asking and never by drafting, one question at a time. Any answer the human defers is written into an Open Questions section verbatim, not paraphrased." (orchestration-tooling, Agent roles)
- **Stage**: 1. **Sees**: "the idea, the spec template, the run log". **Must not see**: "—". **Form**: "interactive session". (piecing-it-together, Sessions and agents)
- **Returns**: `specs/&lt;name&gt;/spec.md @ commit`, status frozen.

### 2. Spec attacker
- **Names**: `Spec attacker` (orchestration-tooling), `Spec attacker` (piecing-it-together).
- **Job**: "reads the draft in a fresh context with the mandate to assume it is defective. Every finding is filed as an Open Question for the human to resolve; the attacker surfaces and never decides."
- **Stage**: 1. **Sees**: "the draft spec, the reviewer mandate". **Must not see**: "the interview". **Form**: "fresh session".
- Mandated by orchestration-principles, Adversarial attack: "The spec draft, before it is frozen: attacked for gaps, contradictions and unstated assumptions."

### 3. Spec judge
- **Name**: `Spec judge` (orchestration-tooling only; no counterpart in the HTML guides).
- **Job**: "reads the attacked spec and rules on whether it is ready to freeze. A ruling of not ready returns it to the human with the reasons."
- **Stage**: 1 (the freeze gate).

### 4. Test builder / Test-writer / Test writer
- **Names**: `Test builder` (orchestration-tooling), `Test-writer` (agents guide roster), `Test writer` (piecing-it-together table), `test-writer` (kickoff worked example).
- **Job (constitution)**: "derives the executable targets from the frozen spec, one check per behaviour and per edge. Before any work starts it runs the baseline and proves that every check fails, and fails for the right reason rather than from a missing import or a typo."
- **Job (agents guide)**: tagline "**Defines done** — Test-writer — Writes the target before anyone can aim past it." Body: "Derives checks from the spec's numbered behaviours and edge cases, before implementation starts and without sight of the plan's internals. Its output is the locked target the run iterates against. Where the spec is too vague to test, it reports that as a spec finding rather than guessing."
- **Permissions**: badges "read · write (tests only) · run". Kickoff example: "test-writer (writes tests/ only)".
- **Isolation / form**: "a session or subagent run to completion before implementers start; its files then locked by a PreToolUse hook"; "fresh session or subagent" (piecing-it-together).
- **Model tier**: "Everything upstream of the workers stays on the strongest model: the orchestrator, the test-writer, the reviewer." (core-stages, Model tier)
- **Stage**: 2. **Sees**: "the frozen spec, the fixture, the codebase". **Must not see**: "any plan or implementation" — "It never sees a plan or an implementation."
- **Returns**: "tests mapped to B/E numbers · acceptance script · diff boundary paths · baseline check results".
- **Separation rule (verification guide, "Separating writer from implementer")**: "The two sessions must not share context: a test-writer that has seen the implementation plan writes tests for the plan; a test-writer that has seen only the spec writes tests for the spec."

### 5. Main orchestrator / Orchestrator
- **Names**: `Main orchestrator` (orchestration-tooling), `Orchestrator` (agents guide, piecing-it-together, core-stages).
- **Job (constitution)**: "plans the run, holds each gate, dispatches workers and merges their results. It never writes code, never edits a test, and never grades its own work."
- **Job (agents guide)**: "**Coordination** — Orchestrator — Holds the goal; touches nothing." Body: "Reads the spec and the kickoff, decomposes the work, fixes interfaces, dispatches roles, and synthesises results into evidence for the human's gates. It plans and judges; it does not implement, and it does not read what workers read. Its context is the run's scarcest resource, so everything reaches it as a summary or a result."
- **Permissions**: "read (sparingly) · no write".
- **Form**: "the main session, or the script of a dynamic workflow, which holds the loop and intermediate results outside any context window"; "fresh session; plan mode at 4".
- **Stages**: 4–9 (piecing-it-together); main character of 4, 5, 7 (core-stages).
- **Sees**: "kickoff, spec, test mapping, constitution, prior reports, worker returns". **Must not see**: "worker transcripts, the interview, the reviewer's reasoning". Also from orchestration-principles: "The orchestrator never reads a worker's transcript. It receives handoffs, nothing else."
- **Returns**: `runs/&lt;id&gt;/plan.json` (stage 4), interfaces commit + protected path set (stage 5), merges and `runs/&lt;id&gt;/checks/` (stage 7).
- **Only the orchestrator reads the kickoff**: "The kickoff's defining property is that only the orchestrator ever sees it."

### 6. Explorer
- **Names**: `Explorer` in all three.
- **Job (constitution)**: "answers one codebase question with a short, cited return. Its purpose is to keep the raw investigation, the files read and searches run, out of the orchestrator's context."
- **Job (agents guide)**: "**Before the plan** — Explorer — Reads widely so nobody else has to." Body: "Searches and analyses the codebase, git history, docs and logs, and returns a summary sized for the orchestrator. Cheap and fast by design; thoroughness is a parameter, not a virtue. Multiple explorers can fan out across questions in parallel."
- **Permissions**: "read · run (read-only)"; "an explorer cannot write" (orchestration-tooling, Frontmatter permissions); "a worker cannot merge; an explorer cannot write" (orchestration-principles).
- **Model / form**: "the built-in Explore subagent (read-only, Haiku by default, with quick / medium / very thorough levels), or a custom read-only researcher with web tools added"; "subagent, read-only tools, small model"; kickoff example "explorer (read-only, haiku)".
- **Stage**: 4. **Sees**: "the codebase". **Must not see**: "—".
- **Returns**: "an explorer hands off an answer with citations, not the search that found it" (orchestration-tooling, Handoffs).

### 7. Planner
- **Name**: `Planner` (agents guide only — the constitution folds planning into the Main orchestrator, and piecing-it-together has no separate planner row).
- **Job**: "**Before the work** — Planner — Turns spec plus codebase into an approach." Body: "Produces the plan the human approves at the first gate: files to change, order, risks, and the decomposition into units. Read-only by construction so that planning cannot leak into doing. Can be asked for two variant plans when the approach is genuinely uncertain."
- **Permissions**: "read · no write".
- **Form**: "plan mode in the session, or the built-in Plan subagent gathering context before a plan is presented."
- **Stage**: 4.

### 8. Interface builder
- **Name**: `Interface builder` (orchestration-tooling only; core-stages calls the actor "the orchestrator, or one worker in sequence").
- **Job**: "writes the seams exactly as the spec states them, before any parallel work begins. Signatures and stubs only, no behaviour; a contradiction between the spec and the codebase halts the run rather than being adapted around."
- **Stage**: 5. **Sees** (core-stages): "the plan's interfaces list · the spec's interfaces section · the contract checks". **Produces**: "one commit on the run branch · the protected path set". **Ends at**: gate 2.
- Stub rule: "The stub raises; it never returns. A stub that returns plausible data, an empty result or a fake redirect, lets a behaviour test pass falsely and lets a worker build against fake behaviour."

### 9. Worker (general) / Implementer / Worker
- **Names**: `Worker (general)` (orchestration-tooling), `Implementer` (agents guide roster, kickoff example), `Worker` (piecing-it-together, core-stages).
- **Job (constitution)**: "implements one unit to its mapped checks in an isolated worktree. It fixes causes and never symptoms, and stops the run for a human if it meets a contradiction."
- **Job (agents guide)**: "**Does the work** — Implementer — Builds one unit against a fixed contract." Body: "The only role with general write access, and there are usually several of them, each owning one unit with its own pass/fail. An implementer receives the spec, its unit's contract and its unit's checks; it does not receive the other units. It iterates until its checks pass or its budget runs out, and reports evidence, not narrative."
- **Permissions**: "read · write · run". Kickoff example: "implementer (worktree, sonnet, maxTurns 20)".
- **Isolation**: "worker subagents with `isolation: worktree` so parallel edits cannot collide; each opens a small PR or commits atomically to its branch"; "Each worker declares worktree isolation in its frontmatter and receives a temporary checkout of its own."
- **Model tier**: "The default is a smaller tier for workers, with escalation driven by the plan's flags: size L, a risk mark, or a unit with entries in `decisions` gets the stronger model."
- **Stages**: 5–6 (piecing-it-together); 6 (core-stages).
- **Sees**: "one unit, its interfaces, its checks, the worker template"; core-stages: "**Each worker sees** — its rendered prompt only". **Must not see**: "other units, the plan as a whole, test files as writable".
- **Returns**: "unit commits · structured returns · events"; foundation rule: "**Worker return shape** — every worker ends by returning unit, spec refs, artefacts, status."
- **Accountability**: "Workers answer upward, never sideways. Each is accountable to the orchestrator for its unit and its checks, and never coordinates with another worker."

### 10. Worker (strong) / escalation retry
- **Name**: `Worker (strong)` (orchestration-tooling only; core-stages calls it "escalation on failure").
- **Job**: "makes one escalation retry on a unit the general worker failed, on a stronger model, from a clean state, with the failure evidence in hand. It inherits the evidence and not the approach; a second failure ends attempts on that unit."
- Core-stages: "A useful kickoff rule is escalation on failure: a worker that hits its iteration ceiling is retried once on the stronger tier before returning blocked."
- Principles: "Retries are capped per unit, with the escalation path fixed: one stronger attempt from a clean state, then the run stops for a human."

### 11. Adversary (build unit) / per-unit adversary / fix-worker
- **Name**: `Adversary (build unit)` (orchestration-tooling); "A per-unit adversary, if wanted" (core-stages).
- **Job**: "attacks a completed unit before merge, asking what the checks missed. It looks where units cheat: scope quietly narrowed, edges weakened, behaviour added that nobody asked for."
- Principles: "Each completed unit, before merge: attacked for what its checks missed, and for where it cheated by narrowing scope, weakening edges or adding behaviour nobody asked for."
- **Routing (core-stages)**: "Findings go to the orchestrator, never straight to the worker whose context is the thing being challenged. The reviewer returns a structured result; the orchestrator dispatches a fresh fix-worker with the finding, the spec entities it cites, the unit's checks and the diff, and nothing of the original worker's reasoning." "The orchestrator does not adjudicate: a finding the fix-worker disputes stays open and reaches the report marked disputed." "Per-unit review is usually reserved for risk-flagged units."
- **Stage**: 6, before merge.

### 12. Run verifier / Verifier
- **Names**: `Run verifier` (orchestration-tooling), `Verifier` (agents guide, piecing-it-together).
- **Job (constitution)**: "refutes the final green. It assumes done is wrong and goes looking for the proof; its failure to find any is what makes the green credible."
- **Job (agents guide)**: "**Confirms done** — Verifier — Runs the checks and tries to refute the result." Body: "Mostly not an agent at all: hooks, gates and scripts run the deterministic checks, and they should, because determinism is the point. The agent form of the verifier exists for the last rung of the ladder: a fresh model that re-runs the evidence and actively tries to refute the claim of done, so the agent doing the work is not the one grading it."
- **Permissions**: "read · run". **Form**: "Stop hooks and `/goal` for the deterministic part; a verification subagent or a self-checking workflow stage for refutation"; "optional subagent asked to refute".
- **Stage**: 7. **Sees**: "the merged branch, the check results". **Must not see**: "the implementer's reasoning".
- Core-stages: "A verification subagent, if the kickoff asks for one, runs here: given the merged branch and the check results and told to try to refute them. It is a refinement on top of the deterministic gate, not a substitute for it."
- The deterministic half is the Stop hook: "**Main character** — the Stop hook"; "The orchestrator cannot declare done; only the command can."

### 13. Reviewer / Critic
- **Names**: `Reviewer` (orchestration-tooling, piecing-it-together), `Critic` (agents guide roster, review guide, kickoff example).
- **Job (constitution)**: "judges the full diff against the spec's intent from a fresh context. It exists to catch the work that passes every check and is still the wrong work."
- **Job (agents guide)**: "**Judges the work** — Critic — Challenges the result, not the reasoning it never saw." Body: "Receives the spec and the diff in a fresh context, with an adversarial mandate bounded to correctness and stated requirements. Reports gaps by spec number. Read-only by construction: a critic that can fix things becomes an implementer with opinions, and its findings stop being findings."
- **Permissions**: "read (diff + spec) · no write". Worked frontmatter: `tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash`, `model: opus`, `maxTurns: 15`. "`Bash` is included so the critic can run the checks itself rather than trust reported output — running is not writing." Review guide checklist: "The critic's frontmatter is read-only-plus-shell, strongest model, turn-budgeted."
- **Stage**: 8. **Sees** (piecing-it-together): "spec, diff, reviewer mandate". **Must not see**: "the orchestrator's context, worker transcripts". **Form**: "subagent, fresh, strong model".
- **Inputs (review guide, "The sealed room")** — Inside the room: "**The spec, at its frozen commit** — The sole definition of right. Intent, numbered behaviours, scope, non-goals."; "**The full diff** — The result on its own terms, including test-file changes — which should be none."; "**The evidence** — Raw check output and what was not checked, so judgement starts where determinism stopped."; "**Read access and a shell** — To open surrounding code and re-run checks itself. Running is not writing."
- **Kept outside**: "**The implementer's reasoning** — Every line of it argues for the conclusion under review."; "**The plan's internals** — The critic judges the result against the spec, not fidelity to an approach."; "**The kickoff** — Conduct rules are not correctness, and they bias toward the run's momentum."; "**Prior findings and fixes chatter** — Each re-review is a fresh room, or it inherits its own last verdict."
- **Mandate, two halves**: adversarial — "assume the diff contains at least one gap and look for it"; bounding — "gaps that affect correctness or the stated requirements; not style, not hypothetical robustness, not improvements" plus the exit "if there are none, say 'no gaps' and stop." "A mandate without that sentence cannot be satisfied by sound work, which means it manufactures findings by construction."
- **Return shape**: "A finding is a claim with an address: the spec number it bears on, the file and line, and one sentence on what is missing." Frontmatter description: "Returns a list of correctness gaps referencing spec behaviour numbers, or 'no gaps'."
- **Finding types (four)**:
  - "**→ implementer, fix** — **Correctness gap** — A numbered behaviour or edge case not satisfied, or satisfied more narrowly than the spec states."
  - "**→ implementer, revert** — **Scope violation** — A change outside the spec's fence that the diff-boundary check could not classify… Reverted, not debated."
  - "**→ human, decide** — **Spec conflict** — The diff and the spec cannot both be right, or two spec lines collide when implemented. This is an escalation, never something the loop resolves silently."
  - "**→ run log, no action** — **Observation** — Real but out of mandate… explicitly not fed back into the loop, or the over-engineering door reopens."
- **Timing / cadence**: "Review runs once, at the end, on the whole. Attacks run at every stage, on the parts." (principles) One re-review only: "**One re-review, fresh room** — New dispatch, new diff, no memory of the first verdict."
- **Repertoire of passes** (review guide): correctness/bug hunt (`/code-review`, every run), spec alignment (custom critic, every run), simplification (`/simplify`), security (read-only security-reviewer subagent, strongest model), design/conventions (skill against DESIGN.md).

### 14. Report assembler / Assembler / Scribe
- **Names**: `Report assembler` (orchestration-tooling), `Assembler` (piecing-it-together), `Scribe` (agents guide, marked "Optional").
- **Job (constitution)**: "joins the recorded artefacts into the report with the provenance of each marked and no verdict of its own. An abandoned run's report is assembled exactly as an accepted run's would be."
- **Job (agents guide)**: "**Optional** — Scribe — Keeps the evidence where the human will read it." Body: "Maintains the evidence display from check outputs and critic findings, and drafts the mechanical fields of the run-log entry at the end. Worth splitting out on large runs so the orchestrator's context is not spent on formatting; on small runs the orchestrator does it."
- **Permissions**: "read · write (display + log)". **Model**: "a small subagent on a cheap model, or hook scripts appending to the display and `RUNLOG.md` stub directly."
- **Stage**: 9. **Sees**: "events, checks, plan, findings". **Must not see**: "—". **Form**: "skill invoked by hook or final step".
- **Returns**: `runs/&lt;id&gt;/report.md` · PR · frozen evidence page.

### 15. The human ("You")
- Listed in the piecing-it-together roster: **Stage** "1, 2, 3, G1, G2, G3, 10"; **Sees** "the display, then the report"; **Must not see** "the transcripts, until something needs diagnosing"; **Form** "—".

---

# B. OPTIONAL AND MERGEABLE

**The mergeable set and the never-merge rule (agents guide, roster closing paragraph):**

&gt; "The minimum viable cast for a run that earns its cost: orchestrator, one explorer pass, test-writer, implementers, a deterministic gate, one critic pass. The planner is folded into the orchestrator on small runs; the scribe is folded into hooks. What must never be folded together: test-writer with implementer, and critic with anything."

Preceding it: "Seven roles cover a full run. Small runs merge some of them; no run should merge the ones whose separation it depends on."

Other explicit optionality in the sources:
- **Scribe** is labelled "Optional" in the roster badge itself.
- **Verifier**: "Mostly not an agent at all: hooks, gates and scripts run the deterministic checks" — the agent form is optional; piecing-it-together lists it as "optional subagent asked to refute", and core-stages: "A verification subagent, if the kickoff asks for one, runs here… a refinement on top of the deterministic gate, not a substitute for it."
- **Per-unit adversary**: "A per-unit adversary, if wanted"; "Per-unit review is usually reserved for risk-flagged units; the whole-diff review after the core covers the rest."
- **Interface builder** collapses into the orchestrator: stage 5 main character is "orchestrator, or one worker in sequence"; piecing-it-together: "the orchestrator (or a single worker) writes the seams".
- **Report assembler** collapses into a hook: "The session-end hook or a final orchestrator step runs the assembler".

Never-merge, restated elsewhere:
- Constitution invariant: "The orchestrator directs; it never writes code, never edits a test, never grades its own work."
- Principles invariant: "No agent grades its own work. The judge sees the result and the criteria, never the reasoning."
- Review guide: "a critic that can edit becomes an implementer with opinions, and its findings stop being findings — the frontmatter allowlist, not a polite instruction, is what makes this true."

---

# C. THE THREE SEPARATIONS

Agents guide, "Why roles, not just workers":

&gt; "So the question when designing a team is not 'how many agents do I want' but 'which separations does this run's quality depend on'. Three separations do most of the work: **the definer of done is separated from the doer** (test-writer vs implementer), **the judge is separated from the judged** (critic vs implementer), and **the coordinator is separated from the content** (orchestrator vs everyone). Every role in the cast below serves one of those three, or exists to protect the orchestrator's context."

The pairs each protects:

| Separation | Pair | What it protects, quoted |
|---|---|---|
| Definer of done vs doer | test-writer ↔ implementer (also test-writer ↔ planner/orchestrator, since it must not see the plan) | "the test-writer's tests describe the spec *because* it never saw the implementation plan"; "A test written after describes what was built. A test written before describes what was wanted." |
| Judge vs judged | critic ↔ implementer; verifier ↔ implementer | "the critic's judgement is independent *because* it never saw the implementer's reasoning"; "so the agent doing the work is not the one grading it" |
| Coordinator vs content | orchestrator ↔ everyone (explorer, workers, critic) | "the explorer can read three hundred files *because* none of them land in the orchestrator's context"; "The orchestrator's context is gapped from the workers'. It sees handoffs and check results; it does not see how a worker got there." |

The mechanism under all three: "The mechanism underneath every role is context isolation. A subagent runs in its own context window with its own system prompt, its own tools and its own model; it receives only what it is given and returns only what it reports."

Plus the fourth structural rule, vertical accountability: "Accountability runs vertically. Each agent answers to the orchestrator for one output in one declared shape; agents do not negotiate with each other. Handoffs travel through files and schemas, not through shared conversation. A team that chats horizontally is a team whose contexts are contaminating one another, which quietly dissolves the separations the roles were built for."

---

# D. DISPATCH

## Kickoff guide — dispatch rules (part 4 of the kickoff anatomy)

&gt; "**4 · Roles and dispatch — Who does what**
&gt; The roster available (by agent name, pointing at `.claude/agents/`), what each is for, and the dispatch rules: workers get their unit's contract, checks and the relevant spec sections only; the critic gets spec plus diff and nothing of the reasoning; the test-writer runs before any implementer. Caps on parallel dispatch live here as defaults the plan can tighten but not loosen."

Checklist item: "**Dispatch rules state what each role receives — and what it must not.**"

Worked example conduct lines:
&gt; "3. Wave 0: contracts and contract tests. Dispatch the test-writer for all unit checks; on completion, tests are locked (hook enforced).
&gt; 4. Waves 1..n: dispatch one implementer per unit, worktree-isolated, with its contract, its checks, and spec sections for its behaviours.
&gt; 5. Proof: integrate, run the spec's e2e command, dispatch the critic with the spec and the full diff."
&gt; "## Roles (.claude/agents/) — explorer (read-only, haiku) · test-writer (writes tests/ only) · implementer (worktree, sonnet, maxTurns 20) · critic (read-only, opus). Dispatch cap: 4 implementers concurrent. Workers never message each other."

Document routing matrix (who reads what): CLAUDE.md → everyone; kickoff → orchestrator only; spec → all judges of correctness; plan → orchestrator, with "Half dots: workers receive the spec sections and plan unit relevant to their unit, not the whole document." Routing test: "**who needs to obey this?** Everyone → `CLAUDE.md`. The judges of correctness → the spec. Only the conductor → the kickoff. This run only → the plan, or the dispatch message itself."

## Core-stages — the three prompt layers

&gt; "Not the plan. The plan unit is data; the prompt is rendered from it at dispatch time, from three layers each kept in one place."

| Layer | Lives in | Carries | Varies |
|---|---|---|---|
| Agent definition | `.claude/agents/worker.md` | "Role, tools allowed and denied, model tier, worktree isolation, the return shape" | never |
| Worker template | `orchestration/templates/worker.md` | "The sections, the rules, the order; the place the 'must not see' boundary is implemented, because what is not a slot cannot reach the worker" | per project |
| The fill | `plan.json` resolved against `spec.json` | "The unit's spec entities verbatim, interface signatures, paths, check names and command" | per unit |

Corresponding principle (orchestration-principles, Context engineering): "Template every recurring input. The spec, the plan, the tests map, the worker brief and the liftoff prompt are templates with slots, and a brief is rendered from them by a script, never composed freehand by the orchestrator. **What is not a slot cannot reach the worker**, so the boundary on what a role sees is structural rather than instructed, and the brief a worker was given is a recorded file rather than a recollection."

## The worker prompt slots, verbatim

```
// worker.md — slots; nothing else reaches the worker

&lt;unit id and name&gt;
&lt;spec entities, verbatim: the behaviours and edges this unit is accountable for&gt;
&lt;interfaces consumed: signatures, marked read-only&gt;
&lt;interfaces produced: already stubbed, to be implemented&gt;
&lt;paths this unit may write&gt;
&lt;checks that must be green, and the exact command&gt;
&lt;rules: tests and interfaces are read-only · outside "owns" is out of bounds ·
        on a contradiction between a test and the spec, stop and return blocked&gt;
&lt;iteration ceiling&gt;
&lt;return shape: unit · spec refs · artefacts written · status · blocked-on&gt;
```

## The return shape

From the slot list: `unit · spec refs · artefacts written · status · blocked-on`.
From piecing-it-together's foundation: "**Worker return shape** — every worker ends by returning unit, spec refs, artefacts, status."

## What the orchestrator does and does not supply

&gt; "The orchestrator does not tell the worker how. It tells the worker what it is accountable for, what proves it, and where the fence is; the decomposition, the ordering and the fences are the orchestrator's contribution, all upstream of the prompt. The procedural part, how to implement B5 in this codebase, is the part the model is better at than a prompt-writer at the unit level, and leaving it out is not withholding guidance."

&gt; "Render the prompt deterministically, with a small skill or script over the two JSON files, rather than having the orchestrator compose it freehand. Freehand composition is where orchestrator context leaks into workers and where a slot is quietly dropped under context pressure. It also makes the report's agents table honest: the task a worker was given becomes a recorded file rather than a stated recollection."

Principles echo: "The orchestrator supplies the target, never the method: objective, interfaces, boundaries and the check that decides pass or fail. There are no build instructions."

## Plan unit — the dispatch record (core-stages)

```
{ "id", "name",
  "spec_refs": ["&lt;B|E ids&gt;"],   // what this unit is accountable for
  "owns": ["&lt;paths&gt;"],          // the only paths it may write — its diff boundary
  "needs": ["&lt;I-ids&gt;"], "produces": ["&lt;I-ids&gt;"],
  "checks": ["&lt;check names&gt;"],  // its stop condition, from the test map
  "worker": "&lt;role&gt;", "model": "&lt;tier&gt;",
  "group": "&lt;wave id&gt;", "size": "S|M|L",
  "flags": ["produces-interface","modifies-existing","risk","human-decision"],
  "decisions": ["&lt;a call made where the spec was silent&gt;"] }
```

---

# E. ROLE FILE

## Constitution — Frontmatter permissions (orchestration-tooling)

&gt; "Each role file opens with a block that declares everything the role is allowed to reach, and that declaration is the role's blast radius: whatever is not granted there cannot be done, however the role is prompted. The role and its permissions are one concern held in one file, so that reading the file is enough to know both what the role does and what it can touch. The block must declare:
&gt; - **Tools**: the allowlist of tools and commands the role may call. A reviewer has read tools only; a worker has edit and its build and test commands; an explorer cannot write.
&gt; - **Model and effort**: which model tier the role runs on and how much reasoning it is given, so that budgets are fixed per role rather than inherited from whoever started the run.
&gt; - **Isolation**: whether the role runs in a temporary worktree of its own. Workers always do.
&gt; - **Memory scope**: whether the role persists anything between runs, and where. Most roles persist nothing.
&gt; - **Permission mode**: how the harness treats the role's actions when no human is present to approve them.
&gt; - **Role-scoped hooks**: checks that run around this role's actions and no other's, such as a test run after every edit a worker makes."

Backing invariant: "Every role's reach is declared in its own file, and nothing a role can do exceeds what is declared there."

## Agents guide — frontmatter fields

&gt; "In Claude Code a role becomes a markdown file: YAML frontmatter for configuration, body as the agent's entire system prompt." "Subagents live in `.claude/agents/` (project) or `~/.claude/agents/` (personal), and the body of the file is the whole of what the agent knows about how to behave: subagents receive their own system prompt plus basic environment details, not the parent session's prompt, and they do not inherit the parent's skills. Whatever a role needs, its file must say."

&gt; "Only `name` and `description` are required, but the fields that matter for team design are the ones that encode the role's boundaries:"

| Field | Role-design use (quoted) |
|---|---|
| `description` | "Written for the dispatcher, not the human: it is the logic by which the orchestrator picks this agent. State when to use it and what it returns." |
| `tools` | "An allowlist. Omit it and the agent inherits everything, which is almost never what a role wants. The badge set above translates directly: a critic gets `Read, Grep, Glob`; an implementer adds `Write, Edit, Bash`." |
| `disallowedTools` | "A denylist subtracted from the rest; the quick way to make a role read-only without enumerating." |
| `model` | "`haiku`, `sonnet`, `opus`, a full model ID, or `inherit` (the default). This is where tiering happens: cheap models for wide reading and formatting, the strongest for judging. `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL` overrides all of it for a session, useful as a cost ceiling." |
| `maxTurns` | "A per-agent budget: the number of agentic turns before the subagent stops. The team-level stall rule, expressed locally." |
| `skills` | "Skills injected into the agent's context at startup, in full. How a role carries its domain knowledge without the parent's." |
| `isolation` | "`worktree` gives the agent its own checkout and branch, created and cleaned up by the runtime. The default for anything that writes code." |
| `permissionMode / memory / mcpServers / hooks` | "Permission behaviour, opt-in memory, external tools, and per-agent hooks, for the roles that need them." |

**Worked example (the critic), verbatim:**

```
---
name: critic
description: Reviews a completed diff against the spec. Use after an
  implementer reports done and its checks pass. Returns a list of
  correctness gaps referencing spec behaviour numbers, or "no gaps".
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
model: opus
maxTurns: 15
---
You are an adversarial reviewer. You will be given a spec file and a diff.
Assume the diff contains at least one gap and look for it.

Check, in order:
1. Every numbered behaviour and edge case in the spec is implemented.
2. Nothing outside the spec's scope section changed.
3. No test file was modified.
4. No error is suppressed rather than handled.

Report only gaps that affect correctness or stated requirements — not
style, not hypothetical robustness. For each gap: the spec number, the
file and line, and one sentence on what is missing. If there are none,
say "no gaps" and stop.
```

&gt; "Two details in that file carry more weight than they look. `Bash` is included so the critic can run the checks itself rather than trust reported output — running is not writing. And the output shape is stated in both the description and the body, because the orchestrator will consume it programmatically and an unstated shape becomes a different shape every run."

## The eight design rules, quoted verbatim

&gt; "**One job, one definition of done.** An agent's body should fit on a screen and end with what it returns. If the prompt needs sections, the role needs splitting.
&gt;
&gt; **Tools follow the role, never the convenience.** Every tool an agent holds is a way its role can be corrupted. A critic with Edit will eventually fix instead of report; an explorer with Write will eventually 'tidy something up'. Scope first, widen only on evidence from the run log.
&gt;
&gt; **State the output shape explicitly.** The parent receives only the result, so the result's format is the interface. For anything consumed downstream, make it a schema and validate it at the handoff.
&gt;
&gt; **Write descriptions for the dispatcher.** Delegation is driven by the description. 'Use this agent when…' phrasing, non-overlapping with sibling agents, and honest about what comes back. Overlapping descriptions produce misrouting that looks like model failure.
&gt;
&gt; **Tier models by role, not by pride.** Wide reading, formatting and mechanical transforms go to cheap models; judging, planning and hard implementation go to the strongest. The verifier's deterministic parts go to no model at all.
&gt;
&gt; **Give every agent a budget.** `maxTurns` per agent, caps on parallel count in the kickoff or workflow script. A role without a budget is where a run's cost surprise comes from.
&gt;
&gt; **Summarise on the way up.** Instruct every role to return conclusions sized for a coordinator, with pointers to files for the detail. Many agents returning verbose results still drowns the parent.
&gt;
&gt; **Version the roster with the project.** Agent files are setup, like the spec template and the hooks. They are checked in, reviewed, and improved through the run log, not edited ad hoc mid-run."

Review guide corroborates the last: "The critic's agent file is versioned with the roster, and it changes through this loop, not mid-run."

## Team shapes (the four stagings, agents guide)

"One session / Subagents in-session"; "Scripted / Dynamic workflow"; "Parallel sessions / Sessions in worktrees"; "Experimental / Agent teams". "The roles do not change; the coordination mechanism does." "Choose the smallest shape that fits the run, and let the run log justify moving up." On agent teams: "the vertical-accountability rule matters more here, not less, because messaging makes horizontal chatter easy."

---

# F. BLOCKED AND CONTRADICTION

**Universal invariant (orchestration-tooling, Agent Invariants):** "A contradiction between the spec and the codebase halts the run for a human. No agent adapts around it."

### Worker / implementer — returns blocked
- Constitution: "It fixes causes and never symptoms, and **stops the run for a human if it meets a contradiction**."
- Worker prompt rule slot: "`&lt;rules: … on a contradiction between a test and the spec, stop and return blocked&gt;`"
- Core-stages, "When a worker meets the wiring": "**Discovers the wiring is wrong for its unit** — It must not route around the contract; that produces code that satisfies the tests while not doing what the spec meant. It stops, returns `status: blocked` with the contract it needs changed and the spec entity that requires it. **Exit** Either the spec's interfaces section or the plan's reading of it was wrong, and only a human says which."
- Also: "**Tries to edit a locked file** — The block-writes hook refuses the write before it happens and the worker sees why. Nothing goes red because nothing changed." "**Breaks a contract in a shared file** — The contract test goes red in the worker's own check run. It cannot edit the test, so the only way back to green is to undo its change. The worker fixes its own mistake."
- Piecing-it-together: "A worker that cannot satisfy a test, or that finds the test contradicts the spec, stops and reports rather than resolving it; that report is an **exit** for a human decision." And: "A worker reporting that a test contradicts the spec is an exit, not a bug for the worker to resolve. Either the test or the spec is wrong, and only a human can say which."
- **How the block reaches the human** (core-stages): interactive shape — "the blocked status is the worker's return value landing in the orchestrator's context… stop dispatching, do not resolve the contract yourself, write the block to the run directory, ask the user… What makes this deterministic is a `PostToolUse` hook on the subagent tool that reads the returned result, appends a blocked event to `events.jsonl` on a match, and injects a line into the orchestrator's context saying dispatch must halt". Workflow shape — "A block there is a stop condition the script handles: skip dependents, finish or stop the wave, return the block as the final result to the session, which then asks. A block almost always means a spec or plan change, which means a new run."

### Test-writer / test builder — reports a spec finding
- Agents guide: "Where the spec is too vague to test, it reports that as a spec finding rather than guessing."
- Verification guide: "Where the spec is not precise enough to write the check, that is a finding about the spec, and the right response is to fix the spec, not to guess."
- On its own product being wrong: "Pre-written tests can be wrong. When an implementer reports that a test contradicts the spec or cannot be satisfied, that report should stop the run for a human decision rather than be resolved by the agent. **Silent resolution in either direction is how a locked target becomes a locked mistake.**"

### Critic / reviewer — files spec-conflict
- Review guide, finding types: "**→ human, decide** — **Spec conflict** — The diff and the spec cannot both be right, or two spec lines collide when implemented. This is an escalation, never something the loop resolves silently — the same rule that governs a wrong locked test."
- Routing consequence: "The orchestrator can route the first two kinds without judgement, must halt on the third, and must *not* act on the fourth."
- Checklist: "Spec conflicts are wired to escalate, not resolve."
- Disputes: "Disputed findings have exactly one adjudicator: the human at the gate, reading the finding and the implementer's objection side by side. The loop never argues with itself."
- Loop cap: "a loop still producing correctness gaps on pass three is not converging, and that is an abandon signal for the run, not a reason for pass four."

### Interface builder — halts
- Constitution: "Signatures and stubs only, no behaviour; **a contradiction between the spec and the codebase halts the run rather than being adapted around.**"
- Principles, Checkpoints: "2. The interfaces. Written as stubs before parallel work begins; **a contradiction with the spec halts here.**"
- Core-stages gate 2 exit: "If the seams are wrong the fix is upstream, in the spec's interfaces section or the plan's reading of it, never in the code."

### Spec attacker / spec judge
- Attacker: "Every finding is filed as an Open Question for the human to resolve; **the attacker surfaces and never decides.**"
- Judge: "A ruling of not ready returns it to the human with the reasons."

### Orchestrator
- Kickoff guide escalation section: "Name the findings that halt the run for a human decision rather than being resolved by improvisation: a spec gap or contradiction, a pre-written test the implementer believes is wrong, an abandon trigger from the plan firing, a needed action that permissions block. **An orchestrator without escalation rules does not stop being confused — it stops *reporting* that it is confused.**" And: "Escalations name the finding and propose nothing else in the same message."
- Prohibitions: "never resolve a spec contradiction silently."
- Stage 7 stall: "After eight consecutive blocks Claude Code overrides the hook and ends the turn… Either way the number is a stall detector. **Exit** The useful question at exit is which check kept failing, and the report says."

### Verifier / Stop hook
- "The orchestrator cannot declare done; only the command can."
- Verification guide: "Claude Code overrides the hook after eight consecutive blocks. Treat that override as a stall detector: a run that hits it has a problem the check cannot fix, and the right response is to abandon and diagnose."

---

# G. ANTI-PATTERNS (agents guide, verbatim)

&gt; "**The generalist blob** — One agent, all tools, doing exploration, implementation and review in one context. Every separation the roles exist for is gone; the run self-confirms by construction.
&gt;
&gt; **The critic who saw the plan** — A reviewer given the implementer's reasoning, or run in the implementing session's context. It will review the intention instead of the result, and approve.
&gt;
&gt; **The implementer who grades itself** — Done declared by the agent that did the work, with no deterministic gate and no refutation. The exact self-confirmation orchestration is supposed to remove.
&gt;
&gt; **Horizontal chatter** — Workers passing context to each other directly. Contamination spreads, accountability blurs, and the orchestrator loses the ability to say which unit failed.
&gt;
&gt; **Agent sprawl** — A roster of eighteen specialists, most unmaintained, with overlapping descriptions the dispatcher cannot tell apart. Fewer, sharper roles beat many vague ones; retire agents the way the run log retires findings.
&gt;
&gt; **Inherit-everything tools** — Omitted tool lists on every agent, so every role can do everything and the badges above are fiction. The allowlist is the role.
&gt;
&gt; **The unbounded specialist** — No `maxTurns`, no cap on parallelism, no stall rule. One stuck agent quietly spends the run's budget on a loop nobody is watching.
&gt;
&gt; **Prompt-only isolation** — 'Do not modify tests' written in the body of an agent that holds Edit and write access to the test directory. Boundaries that matter are enforced by tools, hooks and worktrees, not by asking nicely."

(The review guide adds a parallel list for the critic specifically — the briefed reviewer, the continuing conversation, the helpful critic, chasing everything, the unreferenced review, the reviewer stack, narrative acceptance, review as the only defence — and the kickoff guide a third for conduct: the everything-document, the pasted library, correctness smuggled into conduct, the silent kickoff, prose where a hook belongs, CLAUDE.md's twin, the stale pointer, gates as suggestions.)

## What the sources treat as the irreducible cast

The sources converge on a cast that is defined by separations rather than by headcount. The agents guide states the floor outright — "orchestrator, one explorer pass, test-writer, implementers, a deterministic gate, one critic pass" — and is explicit that the planner folds into the orchestrator and the scribe folds into hooks on small runs, while "What must never be folded together: test-writer with implementer, and critic with anything." One member of that floor is not an agent at all: the deterministic gate is a Stop hook running the acceptance command, and the guide says of the verifier that it is "mostly not an agent at all… because determinism is the point," which is why the constitution's Run verifier and the guide's agent-form Verifier are both described as refinements laid on top of the gate rather than substitutes for it. The constitution's longer fourteen-role list does not contradict this; it names as separate agents several things the guides describe as phases of the orchestrator or of a hook — spec judge, interface builder, worker (strong), adversary, report assembler — and it justifies the split by the same reasoning: "Under attended work one person wore all of them in turn, carrying the same context between them; here each is a separate agent with a context of its own, so that the assumptions of one hat cannot leak into another." The irreducible cast, in the sources' own logic, is therefore the smallest set of contexts that keeps the three separations intact — someone who defines done before anyone builds, several who build one fenced unit each and cannot touch the definition, something deterministic that decides when the building stops, someone in a sealed room who judges the result against the spec and cannot fix what it finds, and a coordinator that sees only summaries and never grades its own work — with everything else in the roster being an optimisation of context or cost that the run log is expected to justify.</result>

The sources roster is in. The compact result:

- **Three vocabularies, one cast.** The constitution names fourteen roles, the agents guide seven, the map page nine. The differences are mostly the same hats split or folded: interface builder, spec judge, strong worker, per-unit adversary and assembler are separate agents in the constitution and phases of the orchestrator or of a hook in the guides.
- **The floor.** Orchestrator, one explorer pass, test-writer, implementers, a deterministic gate, one critic pass. The planner folds into the orchestrator on small runs. The scribe folds into hooks. One member of the floor is not an agent: the gate is a stop hook running the acceptance command.
- **The never-merge rule.** Test-writer with implementer, and critic with anything. Backed by the invariant that no agent grades its own work and the orchestrator never writes code, edits a test, or grades its own work.
- **Three separations** that every role serves: definer of done from doer, judge from judged, coordinator from content. The mechanism under all three is context isolation, and the fourth rule is vertical accountability: agents answer upward, never sideways.
- **Dispatch is rendered, not composed.** Three layers: the agent file that never varies, the template per project that implements the must-not-see boundary because what is not a slot cannot reach the worker, and the fill per unit from plan and spec. The worker's nine slots and its return shape are quoted verbatim.
- **What a role file must declare.** Tools, model and effort, isolation, memory scope, permission mode, role-scoped hooks; a description written for the dispatcher; the output shape stated in both description and body. Eight design rules, from one job one definition of done to version the roster with the project.
- **Blocked and contradiction, per role.** Worker returns blocked with the contract it needs and the spec entity requiring it. Test-writer reports a spec finding rather than guessing. Critic files a spec-conflict that only a human resolves. Interface builder halts. Attacker surfaces and never decides. Orchestrator escalates, names the finding and proposes nothing else.

[ASSISTANT 💬]
That changes the reading, and it splits the two cases I had paired.

The spec-builder holds the ask-user-question tool. A subagent cannot ask the human anything, so the spec-builder cannot be dispatched by an orchestrator or a workflow. It has to be the session itself, started with the agent flag, and the sources say the same thing in their own words: the interviewer is an interactive session, and the attacker and judge are what it dispatches from inside that session. So the spec-stage dispatcher is you by necessity, not by omission. The README's fault is smaller than I stated: it named the human's act as if it were a component, and it did not say that the spec-builder is a session agent rather than a subagent, or that this is why.

The test-builder is the opposite case and stays a gap. It needs no human. It reads a frozen spec, writes checks and a map, and returns. It could be dispatched by an orchestrator, a workflow stage or a render command, and none of those exists for it. Its inputs list names no run folder because nothing was ever going to hand it one.

For the crew document that gives a cleaner cut. The roles divide into session agents, which the human starts because they must talk to the human, and subagents, which something dispatches with a rendered prompt. The spec-builder is the only role in the first group. Everything in the run chain is in the second, and the test-builder is the one member of the second group with no dispatcher. That is also the fact a later page would build on: the page constructs the session invocation for the first group and hands arguments to a workflow for the second.

# Cross-roster sections

## 9. `crew/README.md` in full (46 lines, no frontmatter — so `fc distribute` skips it)

- **The distribute instruction** (`:3`): "Each file's frontmatter is its identity — `name`, `description`, `tools`, `model`, and the extras the role needs — and its body is the system prompt that role runs under. `flightdeck/flightcrew/bin/fc distribute --apply --target &lt;repo&gt;/.claude` copies every file here that carries frontmatter to `&lt;target&gt;/agents/flightcrew/`, where `&lt;target&gt;` is the harness directory receiving the copies; this README carries none, so it stays behind." Matches `bin/cmd/distribute.mjs:53-63` ("every crew file that carries frontmatter (a file without it is documentation, not an agent)").
- **The dispatch paths** (`:5`): "`fc worker render &lt;unit&gt;` writes the unit dispatch, `fc critic render --pass &lt;n&gt;` the critic's, `fc verifier render` the verifier's, and the spec-stage dispatcher passes the fixed paths listed below."
- **The two chains** (`:7`): "The spec chain (`spec-builder`, `spec-judge`, `spec-attacker`) turns an intention into a frozen spec. The run chain (`test-builder`, `planner`, `orchestrator`, `implementer`, `verifier`, `critic`) turns a frozen spec into a finished, proven build. The `explorer` serves both chains and stands outside the split… A role reads only what its dispatch names; the 'must not see' column is as binding as the 'sees' column, because a role that reads the plan or another role's reasoning stops being an independent witness."
- **The roster table** (`:11-22`) — ten rows, columns role / stage / sees / must not see / tools / model / turns / isolation / returns. Selected "gets / never gets": spec-builder gets "intention or draft, template, schema, run log, explorer returns, judge and attacker output", never "repository source files other than the template, schema and run log its dispatch names; prior specs; history"; spec-judge gets "the rubric, the draft", never "everything else"; spec-attacker gets "the draft, the project", never "everything else"; explorer gets "the codebase, one question", never-column "—"; test-builder gets "frozen spec, fixture, codebase, the testing manuals at `flightdeck/manuals/testing/`", never "plan, implementation, interview"; planner gets "spec, tests-map, run log, this roster, explorer returns", never "worker transcripts"; orchestrator gets "kickoff, spec, map, plan, returns, prior reports", never "worker transcripts, interview, critic reasoning"; implementer gets "the one dispatch `fc worker render` produced for its unit", never "other units, the whole plan, the kickoff"; verifier gets "evidence, map, merged branch", never "implementer reasoning, stored returns"; critic gets "spec at commit, diff since lock, evidence", never "plan, kickoff, reasoning, prior findings".
- **Extras** (`:24`): "The implementer is the only role given worktree isolation, and it carries `permissionMode: acceptEdits`, as does the test-builder. The orchestrator carries an `initialPrompt` and holds no `Write` or `Edit`: it writes through `fc plan write`, `fc launch note` and `fc return`."
- **Fixed spec-stage paths** (`:28-39`): template `templates/spec.template.json`; schema `schemas/spec.schema.json`; rubric `manuals/rubrics/spec/spec-readiness-rubric.md`; validator `checks/validators/validate-spec.mjs`; linter `checks/validators/spec-readiness-lint.mjs`; canonical folder `flightdeck/launch/specs/&lt;spec-name&gt;/`; optional run log `flightdeck/launch/RUNLOG.md`. "The spec-stage roles read no manual at session time — their conventions are encoded in their definitions." (`:28`) "no run edits the spec file it holds: a launch is given a pinned copy, and the spec-builder's interview subdirectory `interview/` inside that folder is never copied into one." (`:41`)
- **Run-chain inputs** (`:43`): from the kickoff header block naming launch folder, pinned spec, pinned tests map, run log and evidence page; "every other run-chain input is rendered into the dispatch itself".
- **What is not a role** (`:45-46`): "Report assembly is a command, not a role: `fc launch end` renders `report.md` and `evidence.html`, and the SessionEnd hook refreshes them. No report states an acceptance verdict."

def sect(marker, prose):
    global body
    i=body.index(marker); j=i+len(marker)
    lines=body[j:].split('\n'); k=0
    while k<len(lines) and (lines[k].startswith('<!--') or lines[k]==''):

P['## What the sources say\n']="""
The constitution names fourteen roles, the agents guide seven, the map page nine. The differences are the same hats split or folded: the interface builder, spec judge, strong worker, per-unit adversary and report assembler are separate agents in the constitution and phases of the orchestrator or of a hook in the guides. The guides state the floor outright: an orchestrator, one explorer pass, a test-writer, implementers, a deterministic gate and one critic pass. The planner folds into the orchestrator on small runs and the scribe folds into hooks. One member of the floor is not an agent: the gate is a stop hook running the acceptance command.

What the cast protects is three **separations**, pairs of roles the method keeps in different contexts so that one cannot bias the other. The definer of done is separated from the doer, the test-writer from the implementer. The judge is separated from the judged, the critic from the implementer. The coordinator is separated from the content, the orchestrator from everyone. The never-merge rule follows: the test-writer is never merged with the implementer, and the critic is never merged with anything. The mechanism under all three is context isolation, a subagent receiving only what it is given and returning only what it reports, and the fourth rule is that accountability runs upward and never sideways.

A role is started in one of two ways. A **session agent** is the session itself, started by the human with the agent flag, because it must talk to the human or conduct the run. A **subagent** is dispatched by something else with a prompt, cannot ask the human anything, and returns once. A subagent's prompt is a **sealed dispatch**: rendered by a script from three layers, the agent file that never varies, a template per project that implements the must-not-see boundary because what is not a slot cannot reach the worker, and the fill per unit from the plan and the spec. Freehand composition is where context leaks and slots drop. The role file itself declares tools, model and effort, isolation, memory scope, permission mode and role-scoped hooks; its description is written for the dispatcher; and its output shape is stated in both the description and the body, as a schema validated at the handoff.

[ASSISTANT 💬]
The explorer is out on the built ending. The source side I already hold from the first round, so here is the standard the built ending will be measured against, stated once so the scaffold can cite it:

- **Three endings and a forbidden fourth.** Accept and merge. Abandon and retry. Partial acceptance, unit by unit, on the hard condition that a landing unit stands only on wave-zero contracts and never on an abandoned unit. The fourth, fix it up and keep going, is not an ending but a refusal to choose one.
- **The abandonment sequence.** Stop at the finding and dispatch nothing new. Freeze the evidence. Write the run log entry, the ten lines, now not tomorrow. Make the setup change and commit it alongside the entry. Clear the ground: delete the run's branches, remove its worktrees, prune.
- **The salvage rule.** One question decides what carries: is this artefact setup or output. Spec and tests carry. Proven contracts and factual explorer findings carry. Plan, partial implementation and transcript do not. The next orchestrator meets the failure only through the run log, never through inherited conversation.
- **The merge sequence.** Wave order. An integration branch rebased on current main with the full end-to-end proof rerun. Re-verify after skew. One PR per unit or one squashed commit per unit. CI says it again. Close the run: evidence archived at the merge commit, success entry written, worktrees removed, branches deleted, spec status pointed at the landing commit.
- **The report and the log.** The report is assembled the same way whether the run was accepted or abandoned, carries every fact for the decision and never makes it. The human writes the diagnosis from the report. The report can exist without the log; the log is worthless without the report.
- **The retry.** One change per retry, same frozen spec, same kickoff except the edit. Retry when the diagnosis is specific. Demote to a single session when the task never warranted the orchestra. Shelve after three failures on the same axis.
- **The merge gate is the shortest gate.** Integration proof green on the rebased state, CI green, cost line closed. A merge that needs discussion is a review that ended too soon.

When the explorer lands I'll put the built end command, the land command, the stub mechanics, the human's command count and what survives against that list, and scaffold the endings document as the seventh.
